There comes a time in every properly made boy’s life when he feels a fierce desire to go somewhere and dig for buried treasure. This feeling suddenly seized Tom one day. He went out to find Joe Harper, but could not find him. Then he looked for Ben Rogers; Ben had gone fishing. Soon he came across Huck Finn the Red-Handed. Huck would do. Tom led him to a private spot and told him his plan in confidence. Huck was willing. Huck was always ready to join any adventure that promised fun and needed no money, because he had far too much of the kind of time that is not money. “Where’ll we dig?” Huck said.

“Oh, almost anywhere.”

“Why, is it buried all over?”

“No, it surely isn’t. It’s buried in very special places, Huck—sometimes on islands, sometimes in rotten chests under the end of a branch on an old dead tree, right where the shadow falls at midnight; but mostly under the floors of haunted houses.”

“Who buries it?”

“Why, robbers, of course—who did you think? Sunday-school superintendents?”

“I don’t know. If it was mine, I wouldn’t bury it; I’d spend it and enjoy myself.”

“So would I. But robbers don’t do things that way. They always hide it and leave it there.”

“Don’t they ever come back for it?”

“No, they mean to, but usually they forget the signs, or else they die. Anyway, it stays there a long time and gets rusty; then, after a while, somebody finds an old yellow paper that tells how to find the signs—a paper you have to puzzle over for about a week, because it’s mostly marks and hieroglyphics.”

“Hyro—what?”

“Hieroglyphics—pictures and things, you know, that don’t seem to mean anything.”

“Have you got one of those papers, Tom?”

“No.”

“Well then, how are you going to find the signs?”

“I don’t need any signs. They always bury it under a haunted house, or on an island, or under a dead tree with one branch sticking out. Well, we’ve searched Jackson’s Island a little, and we can search it again sometime; and there’s the old haunted house up the Still-House branch, and lots of dead-branch trees—loads of them.”

“Is it under every one of them?”

“How you talk! No!”

“Then how will you know which one to dig under?”

“Dig under all of them!”

“Why, Tom, that’ll take all summer.”

“Well, what of it? Suppose you found a brass pot with a hundred dollars in it, all rusty and gray, or a rotten chest full of diamonds. What then?”

Huck’s eyes shone.

“That’s splendid. Plenty splendid enough for me. Just give me the hundred dollars, and I don’t want any diamonds.”

Among the public buildings in a certain town—which, for many reasons, it would be wise not to name, and to which I shall give no invented name—there stood one institution once common to towns both large and small: a workhouse. In this workhouse, on a day and date I need not repeat, since they can be of no possible interest to the reader at this point, was born the mortal whose name appears at the head of this chapter.

For some time after the parish surgeon brought him into this world of sorrow and trouble, it was very doubtful whether the child would live long enough to receive a name. Had he not done so, these memoirs would probably never have been written; or, if they had, they would have filled only a page or two, and would have had the priceless advantage of being the shortest and most accurate example of biography in the literature of any age or country.

I do not claim that being born in a workhouse is, by itself, the happiest or most desirable event that can happen to anyone. But in this particular case, it was the best thing that could possibly have happened to Oliver Twist. The truth was that there was considerable difficulty in persuading Oliver to begin breathing—a troublesome habit, though custom has made it necessary for a comfortable life. For some time he lay gasping on a small flock mattress, balanced rather unevenly between this world and the next, with the advantage clearly on the side of the latter. If, during that short time, Oliver had been surrounded by attentive grandmothers, worried aunts, skilled nurses, and deeply learned doctors, he would certainly and without question have been killed very quickly. But there was no one present except an old pauper woman, made somewhat hazy by an unusual allowance of beer, and a parish surgeon who handled such matters by contract. So Oliver and Nature settled the question between them. After a few struggles, Oliver breathed, sneezed, and announced to the workhouse inmates that a new burden had been placed upon the parish, by raising as loud a cry as could reasonably be expected from a male infant who had possessed that useful appendage, a voice, for no more than three minutes and a quarter.

Anne had not entered Kellynch since leaving Lady Russell’s house in September. There had been no need, and on the few occasions when it might have been possible for her to visit the Hall, she had managed to avoid it and get away. Her first return was to take up her place again in the modern, elegant rooms of the Lodge, and to delight its mistress.

Lady Russell’s pleasure at seeing her again was touched with some anxiety. She knew who had been often at Uppercross. But fortunately, either Anne had grown fuller and better-looking, or Lady Russell imagined that she had; and, as Anne accepted her compliments, she amused herself by linking them to her cousin’s quiet admiration, and hoping she might be granted a second spring of youth and beauty.

Once they began to talk, Anne quickly became aware of a change in her own mind. The matters that had filled her heart when she left Kellynch, which she had felt were neglected and had been forced to suppress among the Musgroves, had now become only secondary concerns. Lately she had scarcely thought even of her father, her sister, or Bath. Their affairs had been overshadowed by those of Uppercross; and when Lady Russell returned to their old hopes and fears, expressing satisfaction with the house taken in Camden Place and regret that Mrs Clay was still with them, Anne would have been ashamed for anyone to know how much more she was thinking of Lyme, Louisa Musgrove, and all her friends there. The Harvilles’ home and friendship, and Captain Benwick, interested her far more than her father’s house in Camden Place or her sister’s closeness with Mrs Clay. She was actually obliged to make an effort to meet Lady Russell with even the appearance of equal concern over subjects that naturally had the strongest claim upon her.

At first there was some awkwardness when they spoke of another matter. They had to discuss the accident at Lyme. Lady Russell had been there barely five minutes the previous day before a complete account of it all had poured out upon her; yet it still had to be discussed. She had to ask questions, regret the recklessness, mourn the outcome, and both of them had to mention Captain Wentworth’s name. Anne knew she did not manage it as well as Lady Russell. She could not say his name and look directly into Lady Russell’s eyes until she found the means of briefly telling her what she thought of the attachment between him and Louisa.

The powerful voice—unearthly, we might term it, since we could not possibly connect it with any contrivance of pipe or key—ceased its resonant strain, and the girl, as she turned to aid her elderly companion, finally noticed us.

He was her father; from childhood onward, she had guided his sightless footsteps. They were Saxon Germans, who, having emigrated there only a few years earlier, had made fresh connections among the neighbouring villagers. Near the time when the pestilence began, a young German student had come among them. Their artless tale was readily guessed. He, a nobleman, loved the beautiful daughter of the poor musician, and had followed them in their escape from the persecutions of his own friends; but soon the great leveller arrived, scythe undulled, to cut down with the grass the lofty flowers of the field. The young man fell early. She lived on for her father's sake. His blindness allowed her to maintain a deception, first born of chance—and now, solitary creatures, the only survivors in that country, he knew nothing of the alteration, nor understood that, when he heard his child make music, the silent mountains, unfeeling lake, and unconscious trees were, save himself, her only hearers.

On the very day of our arrival, she had been seized by the symptomatic sickness. The thought of abandoning her old, blind father alone upon the vacant earth filled her with paralysing terror; yet she lacked the courage to reveal the truth, and the extremity of her despair roused her to extraordinary efforts. At the usual hour of vespers, she conducted him to the chapel; and, though she trembled and wept for him, she performed, with neither fault of rhythm nor mistake of note, the hymn composed in celebration of the creation of the adorned earth, which was soon to become her grave.

We seemed to her as visitors sent from heaven; at the sight of deliverance, her strained courage and scarcely upheld resolution gave way. With a cry, she sprang toward us, clasped Adrian's knees, and, saying only, “O save my father!” amid sobs and hysterical exclamations, released the long-barred flood of her grief.

Poor girl!—she and her father now rest side by side beneath the tall walnut-tree where her lover lies, and which she had indicated to us in her last moments. Her father, finally made aware of his daughter's peril, and unable to behold the changes in her beloved face, stubbornly retained her hand until death had made it cold and rigid. Nor afterward did he stir or utter a word, until, twelve hours later, merciful death bore him to his unbroken rest. Beneath the turf they lie, with the tree for their memorial;—that sacred place remains clear to my recollection, enclosed by rugged Jura and the distant, boundless Alps; the church spire they once attended still rises among the sheltering trees; and though her hand is cold, I still fancy that the strains of holy music they cherished drift around them, comforting their mild spirits.

“But when I saw you become the object of another’s love; when I imagined that you might be loved in some way other than as a sacred emblem and image of beauty and virtue; or that you might love another with a more passionate affection than you felt for me, then the fiend within me awoke. I sent your lover away, and from that moment I have known no peace. I sought sleep and rest in vain; my eyes would not close, and my blood was forever in turmoil. I woke to a new life as one who dies in hope might awaken in Hell. I will not stain your imagination by describing my struggles, my rage against myself, and my despair. Let a veil be drawn over the unimaginable feelings of a guilty father; the secrets of a heart so tortured must not be made common. Everything was uproar, crime, remorse, and hatred, yet still the deepest love; and what first roused me to the firm resolve to conquer my passion and restore her father to my child was the sight of your bitter, sympathetic grief. That brought me here: I thought that if I could awaken again in my heart the sorrow I had felt at losing your mother, and the many memories of her that had slept for seventeen years, then all love for her child would die away. In a moment of heroism, I resolved to go alone; to leave you, the life of my life, and not see you again until I could do so without guilt. But it could not be done: I valued my strength too highly, or my love too little. I would certainly have died if you had not hurried to me. If only I had truly been extinguished!

“And now, Mathilda, I must make my final confession. I have been miserably mistaken in believing I could conquer my love for you; I never can. The sight of this house, these fields and woods where my first love lived seems only to have increased it. In my madness I dared tell myself—Diana died in giving her birth; her mother’s spirit passed into her body, and she should be Diana to me. With every effort to cast it off, this love clings more closely—this guilty love, more unnatural than hatred, which withers your hopes and destroys me forever.

Better to have loved despair, and safer to have kissed her.

No time or distance can tear from my soul what has become part of it. Since arriving here, I have not ceased for a moment to feel the hell of passion planted within me, burning until all is cold, rigid, and dead.

He had, indeed, been entirely unaware of his own influence. He had gone after her into the shrubbery with no thought of exerting it. In his concern to discover how she endured Frank Churchill’s engagement, he had come with no selfish purpose—no purpose beyond trying, should she give him the opportunity, to comfort or advise her.—All that followed had been the work of the instant, the direct consequence of what he heard upon his feelings. The charming conviction of her complete indifference to Frank Churchill, of her heart being wholly free from him, had produced the hope that, in time, he might win her affection himself;—yet it was not an immediate hope—he had merely, in a moment when eagerness overcame judgment, ventured to ask whether she would not forbid his endeavour to attach her.—The higher hopes that unfolded by degrees were all the more delightful.—The affection which he had asked leave to awaken, if possible, was already his!—In less than half an hour, he had risen from a state of utter distress to something so nearly perfect happiness that it could be called by no other name.

_Her_ alteration was as great.—That single half-hour had bestowed on both the same dear certainty of being loved, and had removed from both an equal measure of ignorance, jealousy, and distrust.—On his part, there had been a jealousy of long duration, dating from Frank Churchill’s arrival, or even from the expectation of it.—He had loved Emma and been jealous of Frank Churchill from nearly the same time, one feeling probably having revealed the other to him. It was jealousy of Frank Churchill that had driven him from the country.—The party at Box Hill had determined his departure. He would spare himself the sight of such attentions, permitted and encouraged, ever again.—He had gone away to become indifferent.—But he had chosen the wrong place. There was too much family happiness in his brother’s home; woman appeared there in too engaging a shape; Isabella resembled Emma too closely—differing only in those conspicuous inferiorities which invariably set the other before him in greater brilliance—for much progress to be made, even if his stay had been longer.—Still, he had remained resolutely, day after day—until the post of that very morning brought the account of Jane Fairfax.—Then, along with the satisfaction which he must feel—nay, which he did not hesitate to feel, having never considered Frank Churchill at all worthy of Emma—there was such tender concern, such acute anxiety for her, that he could remain no longer. He had ridden home in the rain, and, directly after dinner, walked up to learn how this sweetest and best of all beings, faultless despite all her faults, endured the revelation.

What sort of life could be theirs while Fate still kept this dreadful destiny poised in the balance? The marriage had to be delayed, whatever the cost. On that point he was firmly determined. Deeply as he loved the girl, and though the slightest touch of her hand, as they sat side by side, sent every nerve in him trembling with delicious happiness, he saw no less plainly where his duty lay, and understood fully that he had no right to marry before he had carried out the murder. Once that was done, he could stand at the altar with Sybil Merton and place his life in her keeping without any fear of guilt. Once that was done, he could clasp her in his arms, certain that she would never need to blush for him or bow her head in disgrace. Yet it had to be done first; and the sooner, the better for them both.

Many men in his circumstances would have chosen the primrose path of dalliance rather than the hard ascent of duty; but Lord Arthur was too scrupulous to put pleasure before principle. His love contained more than passion alone; Sybil represented to him everything good and noble. For an instant he felt a natural horror of the deed demanded of him, but it quickly vanished. His heart assured him that it was not a sin but a sacrifice; his reason told him that no other path remained. He must choose between living for himself and living for others, and however dreadful the burden imposed upon him, he knew he must not allow selfishness to prevail over love. Sooner or later, all of us are summoned to make that same choice—the same question is put to every one of us. It came to Lord Arthur early—before the calculating cynicism of middle age had spoiled his nature, or the shallow, fashionable egotism of the day had eaten into his heart—and he did not hesitate to do his duty. Happily, too, he was no dreamer or idle dilettante. Had he been, he would have faltered like Hamlet and allowed indecision to ruin his purpose. But he was practical by nature. To him life signified action rather than reflection. He possessed the rarest of all gifts: common sense.

By now the wild and troubled emotions of the night before had wholly subsided, and he looked back almost shamefacedly on his frantic roaming from street to street and his violent anguish of feeling. The very genuineness of his suffering now made it appear unreal. He marvelled that he could have been foolish enough to rant and rave against the inevitable.

How this troubling matter might be put right, and how they might be received as cousins again, became the question; and it was one which, in a more sensible way, neither Lady Russell nor Mr Elliot considered unimportant. “Family connections were always worth maintaining, good society was always worth seeking; Lady Dalrymple had taken a house in Laura Place for three months, and would be living there in style. Sir Walter, however, chose his own method, and at last wrote a very elegant letter, full of explanation, regret, and entreaty, to his right honourable cousin. They paid calls in Laura Place; they had cards from the Dowager Viscountess Dalrymple and the Honourable Miss Carteret, to display wherever they would be most noticed; and “Our cousins in Laura Place”—“Our cousin, Lady Dalrymple and Miss Carteret”—were mentioned to everyone.

Anne was ashamed. Even if Lady Dalrymple and her daughter had been very agreeable, she would still have been ashamed of the excitement they caused; but they were nothing at all. They had no distinction of manner, accomplishment, or intelligence. Lady Dalrymple had gained the reputation of “a charming woman” because she smiled and gave a polite reply to everyone. Miss Carteret, with even less to say, was so plain and awkward that she would never have been tolerated in Camden Place except for her birth.

Lady Russell admitted that she had expected something better; but still, “it was an acquaintance worth having”; and when Anne ventured to give Mr Elliot her opinion of them, he agreed that they were nothing in themselves, yet continued to insist that, as family connections, as good society, as people who would gather good society around them, they had value. Anne smiled and said,

“My idea of good company, Mr Elliot, is the company of intelligent, well-informed people who have a great deal to say; that is what I call good company.”

Her half-brother had plenty of money again, but debts and fresh madness soon wasted it most terribly. There were greater differences between him and her than there had been between him and his father, and it is believed that he held a deep and deadly grudge against her for having influenced their father’s anger. My father believes that no man who was not a true gentleman at heart has ever, since the world began, been a true gentleman in manner. He says that no varnish can conceal the grain of wood, and that the more varnish is applied, the more clearly the grain shows through. Well, this man pursued Miss Havisham closely and claimed to be devoted to her. I believe she had shown little feeling before then, but whatever capacity for feeling she had came out at that time, and she loved him passionately. He persuaded her to buy her brother’s share in the brewery—which his father had foolishly left him—at an enormous price, saying that, once he was her husband, he must own and manage the whole business. Your guardian was not then among Miss Havisham’s advisers, and she was too proud and too much in love to accept advice from anyone.

Dawn had come when I put the Manuscript down. The rain had nearly stopped; the world was gray and mournful, and the spent storm was sighing and sobbing itself into repose. I went to the stranger’s chamber and listened at his door, which stood a little open. I heard his voice, and knocked. No answer came, yet the voice continued. I looked in. The man was lying on his back in bed, speaking in broken phrases but with animation, emphasizing them with his arms, which he flung about restlessly, as delirious sick folk do. I entered quietly and bent over him. His mutterings and exclamations continued. I spoke—only a word, to attract his notice. His glassy eyes and ashen face kindled at once with pleasure, gratitude, joy, and welcome:

“Oh, Sandy, you have come at last—how I have yearned for you! Sit beside me—do not leave me—never leave me again, Sandy, never again. Where is your hand?—give it to me, dear, let me hold it—there—now everything is well, all is peace, and I am happy once more—we are happy once more, are we not, Sandy? You are so dim, so shadowy, only a mist, a cloud; but you are here, and that is blessedness enough; and I have your hand; do not take it away—it is only for a little while, I shall not need it long.... Was that the child?... Hello-Central!... she does not answer. Sleeping, perhaps? Bring her when she wakes, and let me touch her hands, her face, her hair, and bid her good-bye.... Sandy! Yes, you are there. I lost myself for a moment, and thought you had gone.... Have I been ill long? It must be so; it seems like months to me. And such dreams! such weird and dreadful dreams, Sandy! Dreams as real as reality—delirium, of course, but so real! Why, I thought the king was dead, I thought you were in Gaul and could not return, I thought there had been a revolution; in the wild madness of those dreams, I thought that Clarence and I, with a handful of cadets, fought and destroyed the whole chivalry of England! Yet even that was not the strangest thing. I seemed to be a being from a far-off age yet unborn, centuries ahead, and even that was as real as all the rest! Yes, I seemed to have flown back from that age into ours, then forward into it again, and to have been left, a stranger and desolate, in that strange England, with an abyss of thirteen centuries gaping between me and you! between me and my home and friends! between me and all that I hold dear, all that could make life worth living!

“If I cannot live upon that, I shall not ask any man to help me along. Is that satisfactory?”

A tremendous burst of applause followed, and from its midst the king’s voice rang out:

“Take off his bonds and free him! But I said:

“That an ordinary man should be disgraced before the world is nothing; but it would dishonor the _king_ if those who saw his minister naked did not also see him rescued from his shame. If I might request that my clothes be returned—”

“They are unsuitable,” the king interrupted. “Bring garments of another kind; dress him as a prince!”

My scheme had succeeded. I wished to hold matters as they stood until the eclipse became total; otherwise they would begin urging me again to banish the darkness, and naturally I could not do that. Sending for the clothing bought me some time, though not enough. So I was forced to find another pretext. I said that it was only natural the king might alter his mind and partly regret what he had done in his excitement; therefore I would permit the darkness to deepen for a while, and if, after a reasonable interval, the king remained of the same mind, the darkness would be sent away. Neither the king nor anyone else liked that arrangement, but I had to stand firm.

It became darker and darker, blacker and blacker, while I wrestled with those clumsy sixth-century garments. At length it was utterly dark, and the crowd groaned in terror as they felt the chill, uncanny night wind moving through the place and saw the stars appear and glitter overhead. At last the eclipse was complete, and I was greatly relieved, though everyone else was miserable—which was only to be expected. I said:

“The king, through his silence, still abides by the terms.” Then I raised my hands—held them so for a moment—and said, with the most dreadful solemnity: “Let the enchantment melt away and depart without harm!”

For a moment there was no answer in that profound darkness and sepulchral stillness. But when the sun’s silver edge thrust itself forth a minute or two later, the gathering burst into a mighty cry and surged down like a flood to overwhelm me with blessings and thanks; and Clarence, certainly, was not the last wave of it.

We reached Kishan on the 7th of July. Throughout our journey the weather had been clear. Every day, before sunrise, we quitted our nightly encampment, and watched the shadows withdraw from hill and vale before the golden glory of the advancing sun. The soldiers who accompanied us drew, with national liveliness, eager pleasure from the spectacle of lovely nature. The rising of the star of day was greeted with triumphant music, while birdsong, caught in fragments, filled the pauses between the strains. At noon, we set our tents in some shaded valley, or in an embowered mountain wood, where a brook murmuring over pebbles invited grateful sleep. Our evening march, quieter, was still more pleasing than the restless spirit of the morning. When the band played, they unconsciously selected airs of tempered passion; the lover's farewell, or a lament for absence, was succeeded and concluded by some solemn hymn, harmonizing with the peaceful beauty of evening and raising the soul to lofty and religious meditation. Often every sound was hushed, that we might hear the nightingale, while fireflies moved in brilliant measure, and the gentle cooing of the aziolo promised fair weather to the travellers. Did we cross a valley? Soft shadows enclosed us, with rocks coloured in lovely tints. If we climbed a mountain, Greece, like a living map, lay spread below, her famous peaks dividing the ether, her rivers tracing silver threads across the fertile country. Almost fearful to draw breath, we English travellers gazed in ecstasy upon this magnificent prospect, so unlike the sober colouring and melancholy charms of our native landscape. When we left Macedonia, the rich yet low plains of Thrace offered fewer beauties; nevertheless, our journey remained interesting. An advance guard announced our approach, and the country people were soon astir to pay honour to Lord Raymond.

“It would look like flight, my darling. I must not press them too hard; it would arouse suspicion.”

“Look back, look back! See whether we are being followed!”

“The road is clear, my dearest. So far, no one is following us.”

Houses in groups of two and three pass us by: lonely farms, ruined buildings, dye works, tanneries, and the like; open country and rows of leafless trees. Hard, uneven paving lies beneath us, with soft, deep mud on either side. Sometimes we drive into the mud at the edge of the road to avoid the stones that rattle and shake us; sometimes we become stuck there in ruts and boggy places. Then our impatient agony is so great that, in our frantic fear and haste, we want to get out and run—hide—do anything rather than stop.

Out of the open country, and back among ruined buildings, lonely farms, dye works, tanneries, and the like; cottages in twos and threes, rows of leafless trees. Have these men tricked us and brought us back by another road? Is this not the same place all over again? Thank Heaven, no. A village. Look back, look back! See whether we are being followed! Hush! The posting-house.

Slowly, our four horses are taken out. Slowly, the coach stands in the little street without horses, seeming unlikely ever to move again. Slowly, the new horses appear, one at a time. Slowly, the new postilions follow, sucking and braiding the lashes of their whips. Slowly, the old postilions count their money, add it wrongly, and reach unhappy totals.

The dog raced wildly around the place in terror, while all the other dogs howled after him, knocking into and crashing against everything in their path, until there was complete confusion and a terrible racket. Sir Dinadan was so pleased with his trick that he kept telling, over and over, until everyone was tired of it, how the wonderful idea had come to him. It nearly convinced me that no new joke is possible. Everybody laughed at these ancient things—but they always do; I had noticed that in later centuries. It was at Warwick Castle that I encountered the curious stranger I am about to describe. Three things drew me to him: his open simplicity, his remarkable knowledge of ancient armor, and the peacefulness of his company—for he did all the talking. We found ourselves, as shy people often do, at the rear of the group being conducted through the castle, and he immediately began saying things that interested me. As he spoke, softly, pleasantly, and fluently, he seemed to slip imperceptibly out of this world and time into some distant age and long-forgotten land; gradually he cast such a spell over me that I seemed to walk among the ghosts and shadows, dust and decay, of a gray antiquity, conversing with one of its relics. Just as I might speak of my closest friends or enemies, or my most familiar neighbors, he spoke of Sir Bedivere, Sir Bors de Ganis, Sir Launcelot of the Lake, Sir Galahad, and all the other great names of the Round Table—and as he continued, how very, very, indescribably old, faded, dry, musty, and ancient he came to seem! At last he turned to me and said, as casually as one might mention the weather or any ordinary matter—

“You know about the transmigration of souls; do you know about the transposition of epochs—and bodies?”

I said I had never heard of it. He was so little concerned—just as people are when discussing the weather—that he did not notice whether I answered him or not. There was a brief silence, at once broken by the droning voice of the paid guide:

“Ancient hauberk, dating from the sixth century, from the time of King Arthur and the Round Table; said to have belonged to the knight Sir Sagramor le Desirous; observe the round hole in the chain mail over the left breast; cannot be explained; believed to have been made by a bullet after firearms were invented—perhaps maliciously by Cromwell’s soldiers.”

My companion smiled—not a modern smile, but one that must have vanished from common use many, many centuries ago—and murmured, apparently to himself:

“Know this well: I saw it happen.” Then, after a pause, he added, “I did it myself.”

By the time I had recovered from the electric shock of that remark, he had disappeared.

He walked quickly towards Portland Place, glancing back from time to time as if afraid someone was following him. At the corner of Rich Street, two men were reading a small notice posted on a hoarding. A strange curiosity came over him, and he crossed the road. As he approached, the word “Murder,” printed in black letters, caught his eye. He recoiled, and a dark flush rose in his cheeks. It was an advertisement offering a reward for information leading to the arrest of a man of medium height, between thirty and forty, wearing a billycock hat, a black coat, and checked trousers, with a scar on his right cheek. He read it again and again, wondering whether the miserable man would be caught and how he had received the scar. Perhaps one day his own name would be posted on the walls of London. Perhaps one day a price would be put on his head as well.

The thought sickened him with terror. He turned sharply and hurried away into the night.

He scarcely knew where he went. As he walked home towards Belgrave Square, he met the great wagons heading for Covent Garden. The carters in white smocks, with cheerful sunburned faces and coarse curly hair, marched sturdily along, cracking their whips and occasionally calling to one another. On the back of a huge grey horse, leading a clattering team, sat a plump boy with a bunch of primroses in his battered hat, gripping the mane tightly in his small hands and laughing. The great heaps of vegetables looked like jade against the morning sky, like green jade against the pink petals of some marvellous rose. Lord Arthur was strangely moved, though he could not say why. There was something unspeakably sad in the delicate beauty of dawn, and he thought of all the days that rise in loveliness and end in storm. And these country people, with their rough, good-natured voices and easy ways—what a strange London they must see: a London untouched by the sin of night and the smoke of day, a pale, ghostly city, a deserted town of tombs. He wondered what they thought of it, and whether they knew anything of its splendour and shame, its fierce, flame-coloured pleasures and dreadful hunger, of all it creates and destroys from morning until evening.

As was to be expected, spasms and a severe headache immediately followed an experiment so hasty and perilous. Yet these, along with the other impediments to breathing, being by no means grave enough to endanger my life, I resolved to bear them as well as I might, since I was leaving them behind at every moment in my descent toward the denser layers near the moon. This descent, however, remained exceedingly violent; and it soon became dreadfully clear that, though I had likely not erred in expecting an atmosphere whose density corresponded with the satellite’s mass, I had been mistaken in imagining that this density, even at the surface, could in any way sustain the immense weight carried in my balloon’s car. Yet it ought to have done so, and to the same extent as at the earth’s surface, the actual gravity of bodies on either planet being assumed to bear the same ratio as the atmospheric condensation. That it did not, however, was sufficiently proved by my headlong fall; and why it did not can only be accounted for by referring to those possible geological disturbances of which I have spoken before. In any event, I was now near the planet and descending with the most frightful violence. I therefore lost no instant in casting out, first my ballast, then my water-kegs, then my condensing apparatus and gum-elastic chamber, and finally every object in the car. But all was useless. I continued to fall with dreadful swiftness, and was now less than half a mile from the ground. As a final expedient, having thrown away my coat, hat, and boots, I cut the car itself loose from the balloon, it being of considerable weight; then, grasping the net-work with both hands, I had scarcely time to notice that the entire country, as far as sight extended, was densely dotted with tiny dwellings, before I plunged headlong into the very center of a fantastically appearing city, and among a vast multitude of ugly little people. Not one of them spoke a syllable or made the slightest effort to help me; instead, they stood like a company of fools, grinning absurdly and looking sidelong at me and my balloon, their arms planted akimbo.”

The little man's body was disproportionately broad, giving his whole figure a highly absurd roundness. His feet, naturally, could not be seen at all, though a hard substance of suspicious character occasionally stuck through a tear in the bottom of the car—or, more properly speaking, the top of the hat. His hands were enormously large. His hair was very gray and gathered into a queue behind him. His nose was remarkably long, crooked, and inflamed; his eyes full, bright, and sharp; his chin and cheeks, though wrinkled by age, broad, puffy, and doubled. Yet no trace of ears, of any sort or description, could be found anywhere on his head. This strange little gentleman wore a loose sky-blue satin coat, with matching tight breeches fastened at the knees by silver buckles. His waistcoat was made of some vivid yellow fabric; a white taffeta cap sat jauntily to one side of his head; and, to complete his attire, a blood-red silk handkerchief wrapped his throat and fell gracefully over his chest in a fantastical bow of extraordinary size.

Having descended, as I have said, to within about a hundred feet of the earth's surface, the little old gentleman was suddenly overcome by a fit of alarm and seemed unwilling to come any closer to solid ground. He therefore threw out some sand from a canvas bag, which he raised with great difficulty, and at once became stationary. Then, hurried and agitated, he drew a large morocco pocketbook from a side pocket of his coat. He held it suspiciously in his hand, stared at it with an expression of extreme surprise, and was plainly astonished by its weight. At last he opened it and took out an enormous letter, sealed with red wax and carefully tied with red tape, which he dropped exactly at the feet of the burgomaster, Superbus Von Underduk. His Excellency bent down to pick it up. But the aeronaut, still deeply disturbed and apparently having no further business in Rotterdam, began at that moment to make brisk preparations for departure. Since he needed to cast off some ballast in order to rise again, he threw out half a dozen bags, one after another, without troubling to empty them. Every one, most unfortunately, landed on the burgomaster's back and rolled him over and over no fewer than twenty-one times before every man in Rotterdam. It should not be imagined, however, that the great Underduk allowed such impertinence from the little old man to go unpunished.

“Certainly; it would be both rude and cruel of me to trouble you with my curiosity.”

Soon after, he asked whether I thought the breaking ice had destroyed the other sledge. I answered that I could not say with any certainty, because the ice had not broken until nearly midnight, and the traveller might have reached safety before then; but I could not know.

From that time, new life seemed to fill the stranger’s failing body. He was extremely eager to go on deck and watch for the sledge we had seen before; but I persuaded him to stay in the cabin, since he was much too weak to endure the bitter air. I promised that someone would keep watch for him and tell him at once if anything new came into view.

This is my journal of this strange event up to the present day. The stranger has slowly regained his health, but he is very quiet and seems troubled whenever anyone but me enters his cabin. Still, his manner is so gentle and pleasing that all the sailors have become interested in him, though they have spoken with him very little. As for me, I am beginning to love him like a brother, and his constant, profound sorrow fills me with sympathy and pity. He must have been a noble man in happier days, for even now, ruined as he is, he remains so appealing and kind.

I said in one of my letters, my dear Margaret, that I would find no friend on the wide ocean; yet I have found a man who, before misery broke his spirit, I would gladly have had as the brother of my heart.

“Perhaps we are not testing the matter fairly,” he said. “The paper lies upon a flat surface, whereas the human throat is cylindrical. Here is a piece of wood whose circumference is nearly that of a throat. Wind the drawing about it, and repeat the experiment.”

I did so; yet the difficulty became still plainer than before. “This,” I declared, “is the impression of no human hand.”

“Now read,” said Dupin, “this extract from Cuvier.”

“The account of the fingers,” I said, when I had finished reading, “agrees exactly with this sketch.”

Its heavy oak door stood unbarred. Inside was a small chamber, cold as an icehouse, its natural walls of solid limestone damp with a chilly sweat. It was romantic and mysterious to stand there in the deep darkness and look out at the green valley shining in the sun. But the solemn effect soon faded, and the rough play began again. The instant anyone lit a candle, everyone rushed at its owner; a struggle and a brave defense followed, but the candle was quickly knocked down or blown out, followed by delighted laughter and another chase. But everything must end. Before long, the procession filed down the steep slope of the main passage, the flickering line of lights faintly showing the towering rock walls almost to where they met sixty feet overhead. He was short in stature, yet wonderfully upright, and his voice was the most melodious I had ever listened to. He opened his lecture with a review of the history of chemistry and the several advances achieved by learned men, uttering with enthusiasm the names of its most eminent discoverers. He next glanced briefly at the science in its current condition and defined many of its basic expressions. Having performed a few preliminary experiments, he ended with an encomium on modern chemistry, whose language I can never forget:

“The old instructors in this science,” he said, “held out impossibilities and accomplished nothing. Modern teachers promise little; they understand that metals cannot be changed into one another, and that the elixir of life is a fantasy; yet these philosophers, whose hands appear fit only to meddle with filth, and whose eyes to bend over microscope or crucible, have truly wrought miracles. They enter nature’s secret retreats and reveal her labour in her concealed places. They rise to the heavens; they have found the circulation of the blood and the character of the air we breathe. They have gained powers new and nearly boundless; they can summon the thunders of heaven, imitate the earthquake, and even deride the unseen world with its own shadows.”

These were the professor’s words—or rather, let me call them the utterances of fate—spoken for my ruin. While he continued, I felt my soul contending with a tangible foe; the separate keys composing the mechanism of my being were struck in turn; chord followed chord, until my mind held but one thought, one idea, one aim. So much has been achieved, cried the soul of Frankenstein—more, vastly more, shall I accomplish; following the path already traced, I will open a new road, investigate powers unknown, and disclose to the world creation’s profoundest mysteries.

That night I did not close my eyes. My inward being was in revolt and confusion; I sensed that order would emerge from it, though I lacked the strength to bring it forth. Gradually, after morning broke, sleep overtook me. I awoke, and the thoughts of the preceding night seemed like a dream. Nothing remained except a determination to resume my former studies and give myself to a science for which I thought I possessed a natural aptitude. That same day I visited M. Waldman. In private his manner was still gentler and more engaging than before an audience, since the dignity visible in his bearing during a lecture gave way, in his own home, to the utmost warmth and kindness.

The next day he did not leave the house. In fact, he spent most of it in his own room, sick with a frantic fear of death, yet indifferent to life itself. The feeling that he was being hunted, trapped, and tracked down had begun to rule him. If the tapestry so much as stirred in the wind, he trembled. Dead leaves blown against the leaded windows seemed like his own wasted promises and desperate regrets. When he shut his eyes, he saw again the sailor’s face looking through the misty glass, and horror seemed to place its hand upon his heart once more.

But perhaps it had only been his imagination that had summoned revenge from the night and set those ugly shapes of punishment before him. Real life was chaos, but imagination had a terrible logic. Imagination made remorse follow sin wherever it went. Imagination made every crime produce its twisted offspring. In the ordinary world of facts, the wicked were not punished and the good were not rewarded. Success went to the strong, and failure was forced on the weak. That was all. Besides, if a stranger had been lurking around the house, the servants or gamekeepers would have seen him. If footprints had been found in the flower-beds, the gardeners would have reported them. Yes, it had been only imagination. Sibyl Vane’s brother had not returned to kill him. He had sailed away in his ship, perhaps to sink in some winter sea. At least he was safe from him. Why, the man did not know who he was, and could not know. The mask of youth had saved him.

Yet if it had only been an illusion, how terrible it was to think that conscience could create such dreadful phantoms, give them visible shapes, and make them move before one’s eyes. What kind of life would his be if, day and night, shadows of his crime looked at him from quiet corners, mocked him from hidden places, whispered in his ear while he sat at a feast, and woke him with icy fingers as he slept? As the thought moved through his mind, he turned pale with fear, and the air suddenly seemed colder. Oh, in what a mad hour he had killed his friend! How horrible even the memory of it was! He saw it all again. Every dreadful detail returned with greater horror. From the black cave of time, terrible and wrapped in scarlet, rose the image of his sin.

During his brief stay, Emma had scarcely seen him; but she had seen enough to feel that the first encounter was behind them, and to conclude that he had not improved under the blend of resentment and self-importance now visible in his manner. Indeed, she was beginning to wonder greatly that she had ever found him agreeable at all; and the sight of him was so closely tied to unpleasant feelings that, except as a moral punishment, a lesson, a useful humiliation for her own mind, she would have been grateful for the certainty of never seeing him again. She wished him well; but he caused her pain, and his happiness twenty miles away would give her the greatest satisfaction.

The discomfort of his remaining in Highbury, however, would surely be reduced by his marriage. It would prevent many pointless anxieties and smooth over many awkward situations. A Mrs. Elton would excuse any alteration in their dealings; their former intimacy could fade without notice. It would be almost like beginning again with mere civility.

Of the lady herself, Emma thought very little. She was good enough for Mr. Elton, certainly; accomplished enough for Highbury—pretty enough, perhaps, to seem plain beside Harriet. As for family connections, Emma was entirely at ease, convinced that, despite all his boastful claims and contempt for Harriet, he had achieved nothing. On that point, the truth seemed discoverable. What she was must remain uncertain; but who she was could be learned; and, leaving aside the ten thousand pounds, she did not seem at all Harriet’s superior. She brought no name, no lineage, no influential relations. Miss Hawkins was the younger of two daughters of a Bristol—merchant, of course he had to be called; but since the profits of his commercial life appeared so modest, it was not unfair to suppose that the status of his trade had been modest too. She had been accustomed to spend part of every winter in Bath; but Bristol was her home, in the very centre of Bristol. Though her father and mother had died some years before, an uncle remained—connected with the law. Nothing more honourable was claimed for him than that he was connected with the law; and the daughter had lived with him. Emma supposed him to be some attorney’s drudge, too dull to advance. And all the grandeur of the connection appeared to rest on the elder sister, who was very well married to a gentleman of great consequence near Bristol, who kept two carriages! That was the conclusion of the story; that was Miss Hawkins’s glory.

A few days later, Virginia and her curly-haired escort went riding across Brockley meadows. While forcing her way through a hedge, she tore her riding habit so badly that, when she returned home, she decided to go upstairs by the back staircase to avoid being seen. As she hurried past the Tapestry Chamber, whose door happened to be open, she thought she saw someone inside. Assuming it was her mother’s maid, who sometimes brought her sewing there, Virginia looked in to ask her to mend the habit. To her great surprise, however, it was the Canterville Ghost himself. He sat by the window, watching the faded gold of the yellowing trees drift through the air and the red leaves whirl wildly down the long avenue. His head rested on his hand, and his entire posture expressed the deepest dejection. He looked so lonely and so dilapidated that little Virginia, whose first impulse had been to flee and lock herself in her room, felt sorry for him and resolved to comfort him. Her footsteps were so soft, and his sadness so profound, that he did not notice her until she spoke.

‘I am very sorry for you,’ she said, ‘but my brothers are going back to Eton tomorrow, and then, if you behave yourself, nobody will bother you.’

‘It is ridiculous to ask me to behave myself,’ he replied, turning in astonishment toward the pretty little girl who had dared to speak to him. ‘Completely ridiculous. I must rattle my chains, groan through keyholes, and walk about at night, if that is what you mean. It is my only reason for existing.’

‘It is no reason to exist at all, and you know you have been very wicked. Mrs. Umney told us, on the first day we came here, that you had killed your wife.’

‘Well, I freely admit it,’ said the Ghost irritably, ‘but it was entirely a family matter and concerned no one else.’

‘It is very wrong to kill anyone,’ said Virginia, who sometimes possessed a gentle Puritan seriousness inherited from some old New England ancestor.

‘Oh, I detest the shallow harshness of abstract morality! My wife was very plain, never had my ruffs properly starched, and knew nothing about cooking. Why, there was a buck I shot in Hogley Woods—a magnificent pricket—and do you know how she had it served at table? Still, it does not matter now; it is all over. And I do not think it was very kind of her brothers to starve me to death, even though I did kill her.’

All the young people were eager to see Lyme. Captain Wentworth spoke of going there again himself; it was only seventeen miles from Uppercross, and though it was November, the weather was not at all bad. In short, Louisa, the keenest of them all, had decided they should go. Besides the pleasure of having her own way, she now felt it was a point of honor to stand by her decision, and she overcame all her father’s and mother’s wishes to postpone the trip until summer. So they were to go to Lyme—Charles, Mary, Anne, Henrietta, Louisa, and Captain Wentworth.

Their first careless plan had been to leave in the morning and return that night. But Mr. Musgrove would not agree, for the sake of his horses; and when they considered it sensibly, they saw that a November day would leave little time to see a new place after allowing seven hours, as the roads required, for the journey there and back. They therefore decided to stay the night and were not expected home until dinner the following day. This was thought a great improvement. Although they all met at the Great House for breakfast rather early and left very punctually, it was well past noon before the two carriages—Mr. Musgrove’s coach carrying the four ladies, and Charles’s curricle, in which he drove Captain Wentworth—came down the long hill into Lyme and entered the town’s even steeper main street. It was clear that they would have only enough time to look around before the day’s light and warmth disappeared.

After finding rooms and ordering dinner at one of the inns, the obvious next step was to walk straight down to the sea. They had come too late in the year for any of the entertainment or activity Lyme might offer as a resort. The public rooms were closed, nearly all the visitors had gone, and hardly anyone remained except the local residents. Since the buildings themselves offered little to admire, a visitor’s eye would naturally seek the town’s striking setting: its main street seeming almost to rush into the water; the walk to the Cobb around the pleasant little bay, lively in season with bathing machines and visitors; the Cobb itself, with its old features and recent improvements; and the beautiful line of cliffs stretching eastward from the town. A very unusual visitor indeed would fail to find enough charm in Lyme’s immediate surroundings to wish to know it better.

That hour passed; the sun climbed high in the sky, but the cottagers did not appear. I shook with fear, imagining some dreadful disaster. The cottage was dark inside, and I heard no movement; I cannot describe the agony of waiting.

“Soon two countrymen passed by. They stopped near the cottage and began talking with angry gestures, but I could not understand them, because they spoke the language of the country, not that of my protectors. Shortly afterward Felix came with another man. I was surprised, for I knew he had not left the cottage that morning, and I listened anxiously, hoping his words would explain these strange events.

“‘Do you understand,’ his companion said, ‘that you must pay three months’ rent and lose the vegetables from your garden? I do not wish to treat you unfairly, and so I ask you to take a few days to consider your decision.’

“‘It is completely useless,’ Felix replied. ‘We can never live in your cottage again. My father’s life is in great danger because of the dreadful event I have told you about. My wife and sister will never recover from their terror. I beg you, do not argue with me any longer. Take back your house and let me flee this place.’

“Felix shook violently as he spoke. He and his companion entered the cottage, stayed there a few minutes, and then left. I never saw any of the De Lacey family again.

“For the rest of the day, I remained in my hovel, numb with complete despair. My protectors had gone, breaking the only bond that connected me to the world. For the first time, revenge and hatred filled my heart. I made no effort to control them; instead, carried along by their force, I turned my thoughts toward harm and death.

I then went from shop to shop, buying whatever was needed to alter his appearance. When that was done, I made my own way to Little Britain. Mr. Jaggers was at his desk, but when he saw me come in, he rose at once and stood before the fire.

“Now, Pip,” he said, “be careful.”

“I will, sir,” I replied. As I had walked there, I had thought carefully about what I meant to say.

“Don’t involve yourself,” said Mr. Jaggers, “and don’t involve anyone else. You understand—anyone. Don’t tell me anything: I don’t want to know anything; I am not curious.”

Of course, I saw that he knew the man had arrived.

“I only want, Mr. Jaggers,” I said, “to make sure that what I have been informed is true. I have no wish for it to be untrue, but I may at least confirm it.”

Mr. Jaggers nodded. “But did you say ‘told’ or ‘informed’?” he asked, tilting his head and looking not at me but, as if listening, at the floor. “Told would suggest spoken communication. You cannot have spoken communication with a man in New South Wales, you know.”

“I will say informed, Mr. Jaggers.”

“Good.”

“I have been informed by a person named Abel Magwitch that he is the benefactor who was so long unknown to me.”

“That is the man,” said Mr. Jaggers, “in New South Wales.”

“And no one else?” I asked.

“And no one else,” said Mr. Jaggers.

“I am not so unreasonable, sir, as to hold you responsible for my mistakes and false conclusions; but I had always supposed it was Miss Havisham.”

“As you say, Pip,” Mr. Jaggers replied, looking coolly at me and biting his forefinger, “I am not responsible for that at all.”

“And yet it seemed so much like it, sir,” I pleaded, my heart sinking.

“Not the smallest piece of evidence, Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, shaking his head and gathering up his coat-skirts. “Judge nothing by appearances; judge everything by evidence. There is no better rule.”

“I have nothing more to say,” I said with a sigh, after standing silent for a while. “I have confirmed my information, and that is the end of it.”

“And Magwitch—in New South Wales—having finally revealed himself,” said Mr. Jaggers, “you will understand, Pip, how strictly, in all my dealings with you, I have kept to the plain facts. There has never been the slightest departure from the plain facts. You know that, do you not?”

“Quite, sir.”

“When Magwitch—in New South Wales—first wrote to me—from New South Wales—I told him that he must not expect me ever to depart from the plain facts.”

In the days of my youth, discontent had never entered my thoughts; and if at any time I was oppressed by _ennui_, the view of nature's beauty, or the contemplation of what was noble and sublime in the works of man, could invariably engage my heart and restore buoyancy to my spirits. But I am a stricken tree; the lightning has pierced my soul; and I then felt that I was destined to live on, displaying what I shall shortly cease to be—a wretched image of ruined humanity, an object of pity to others and of horror to myself.

We remained for a long time at Oxford, wandering through the surrounding country and seeking out every place connected with the most stirring period of English history. Our small expeditions of discovery were frequently extended by the new objects continually appearing before us. We saw the grave of the celebrated Hampden and the field where that patriot was slain. For a moment my soul rose above its degrading and miserable apprehensions, to meditate upon the sacred principles of liberty and self-devotion for which these scenes stood as monuments and memorials. For an instant I ventured to cast aside my fetters and survey the world with a liberated and exalted spirit; but the iron had penetrated my flesh, and I fell back once more, trembling and despairing, into my unhappy self.

We quitted Oxford reluctantly and went on to Matlock, our next resting-place. The landscape around this village bore a stronger resemblance to that of Switzerland; yet all was upon a lesser scale, and the verdant hills lacked the diadem of far-off white Alps that ever accompanies the pine-clad mountains of my native land. We explored the marvellous cavern and the small natural-history cabinets, where the curiosities were arranged in the same fashion as in the collections at Servox and Chamounix. When Henry uttered the latter name, I trembled, and hastened away from Matlock, which had thus become linked with that dreadful scene.

From Derby, continuing our northward course, we spent two months in Cumberland and Westmorland. I could now nearly imagine myself amid the Swiss mountains. The small remnants of snow still resting upon the northern mountain slopes, the lakes, and the rush of the rocky streams were all sights familiar and beloved to me. Here we likewise formed several acquaintances, who almost succeeded in beguiling me into happiness. Clerval's pleasure was proportionately greater than my own; his mind enlarged in the society of gifted men, and within himself he discovered capacities and resources greater than he could have supposed he possessed while he kept company with his inferiors.

“April 19th. This morning, to my great joy, at about nine o’clock, with the moon’s surface terribly close and my fears at their height, the pump of my condenser finally showed clear signs that the atmosphere was changing. By ten, I had reason to think its density had increased greatly. By eleven, the apparatus required very little work; and at twelve, though somewhat hesitant, I dared to unscrew the tourniquet. Finding no ill effect from this, I at last opened the gum-elastic chamber and removed it from around the car. As might have been expected, spasms and a violent headache immediately followed an experiment so sudden and dangerous. But since these and the other difficulties of breathing were not severe enough to threaten my life, I resolved to bear them as well as I could, knowing that I would soon leave them behind as I approached the denser layers near the moon. This approach, however, was still extremely rapid; and it soon became alarmingly clear that, although I had probably been right in expecting an atmosphere denser in proportion to the satellite’s mass, I had been wrong in believing that this density, even at the surface, would be enough to support the great weight in my balloon’s car. Yet it should have done so, and to the same degree as on the earth’s surface, if the actual gravity of bodies on either world were in proportion to the density of the atmosphere. My swift fall proved that this was not so; why it was not so can only be explained by those possible geological disturbances I mentioned before. In any case, I was now very near the planet and descending with terrible force. I lost no time in throwing overboard first my ballast, then my water-kegs, then my condensing apparatus and gum-elastic chamber, and finally every object in the car. But it was useless. I still fell with dreadful speed and was now less than half a mile from the surface. As a final measure, after throwing away my coat, hat, and boots, I cut the car itself loose from the balloon, for it was no small weight. Clinging with both hands to the netting, I had barely time to see that the whole land, as far as I could see, was thickly scattered with tiny dwellings before I plunged headfirst into the center of a strange-looking city, among a vast crowd of ugly little people. Not one spoke a word or made the slightest effort to help me; they stood like fools, grinning absurdly and looking sideways at me and my balloon, their arms planted on their hips.”

I now come to my own story. There is little to tell of the early part of my life, and I will be brief; but I must linger somewhat over my childhood, so that it may be understood how, when one hope failed, all life became empty; and how, when the only affection I was allowed to cherish was destroyed, my existence died with it.

I have said that my aunt was very unlike my father. I believe that, without the slightest trace of malice, she possessed the coldest heart ever held in a human breast: it was wholly incapable of affection. She took me into her care because she considered it her duty; but she had lived too long alone, undisturbed by the noise and chatter of children, to permit me to disturb her peace. She had never married, and for the previous five years had lived entirely alone on an estate inherited through her mother, on the shores of Loch Lomond in Scotland. In his letters, my father had wished her to live with me at his family mansion, set in beautiful countryside near Richmond in Yorkshire. She refused this proposal; but as soon as she had settled the affairs that her brother’s departure had placed in her hands, she left England and took me with her to her Scottish estate.

My care as a baby, and later until I reached my eighth year, fell to one of my mother’s servants, who had accompanied us into retirement for that purpose. I was kept in a distant part of the house and saw my aunt only at fixed times. These came twice each day: around noon she visited my nursery, and after dinner I was brought to her. She never embraced me, and throughout my stay in the room seemed afraid that some childish prank would irritate her. My good nurse always instructed me most carefully before she dared take me into the parlour—and the awe inspired by my aunt’s cold looks and few forced words was so great that I rarely disgraced those lessons or departed from the exemplary silence I had been taught to maintain during these brief visits.

Under my good nurse’s care, I ran freely through our park and the neighbouring fields. Born of the deepest love, I showed from my earliest years the greatest sensitivity of feeling. I cannot express the passion with which I loved everything, even the lifeless objects around me.

And if he questioned why I desired it, and why I imagined I had any claim to it, I would tell him, though he cared little for such humble dreams, that I had loved Estella deeply and for a long time, and that, though I had lost her and must lead a desolate life, all that related to her remained closer and more precious to me than anything else in the world. Never had I seen two men regard one another more strangely than Mr. Jaggers and Wemmick did after this address. At first I feared that Wemmick would be dismissed from his post on the spot; but the fear passed when I saw Mr. Jaggers soften into something resembling a smile, and Wemmick grow more confident.

“What is all this?” said Mr. Jaggers. “You with an old father, and you with agreeable and playful habits?”

“Well!” replied Wemmick. “If I don’t bring them here, what difference does it make?”

“Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, putting his hand on my arm and smiling freely, “this man must be the cleverest impostor in all London.”

“Nothing of the sort,” returned Wemmick, becoming bolder still. “I think you are another.”

Again they gave each other those same strange looks, each seeming still suspicious that the other was deceiving him.

“_You_ with an agreeable home?” said Mr. Jaggers.

“So long as it does not interfere with business,” Wemmick replied, “let it stand. Now that I look at you, sir, I should not be surprised if _you_ were planning and arranging to have an agreeable home of your own some day, when you are weary of all this work.”

Mr. Jaggers nodded reflectively two or three times, and actually sighed. “Pip,” he said, “we will not speak of ‘poor dreams’; you know more of such matters than I do, having far more recent experience of that kind. He paused until I declared that I fully understood he had expressly said he admitted nothing.

Dear me, she was a prodigious talker. It would hardly do for me to hint that it was very late, and that I was weary and desperately sleepy. I wished I had retired when I had the opportunity. But now I had to endure it; there was no escape. So she chattered on and on, through the deep, spectral silence of the sleeping castle, until presently there rose, as though from far beneath our feet, a distant sound like a smothered cry--with such agony in it that my flesh crept. The queen paused, and her eyes kindled with delight; she cocked her lovely head as a bird does when listening. Once more the sound forced its way upward through the quiet.

“What is that?” I asked.

“It is a most stubborn soul, and endureth greatly. It hath been many hours now.”

“Endureth what?”

“The rack. Come--ye shall behold a merry sight. If he yield not his secret now, ye shall see him rent apart.”

What a sleek, smooth fiend she was; so calm and tranquil, while every cord in my legs seemed to ache in fellow-feeling with that man's torment. Escorted by armored guards carrying blazing torches, we marched through resounding corridors and down wet, dripping stone stairs, reeking of mould and the ages of captive night--a cold, eerie journey, and a long one, made neither briefer nor more pleasant by the sorceress's discourse concerning this victim and his offense. An unnamed informer had charged him with killing a stag in the royal preserves. I said:

“Anonymous evidence is scarcely the proper thing, your Highness. It would be more just to bring the accuser face to face with the accused.”

“I had not considered that, it being of little moment. Yet if I wished it, I could not do it, for the accuser came masked in the night, told the forester, and immediately departed again; thus the forester knoweth him not.”

“Then this Unknown is the sole person who saw the stag slain?”

“Marry, no man saw the deed, but this Unknown saw this sturdy wretch near the place where the stag lay, and with most loyal zeal went and betrayed him to the forester.”

“So the Unknown was near the dead stag as well? Is it not possible that he killed it himself? His loyal zeal--while masked--seems a trifle suspicious. But what does your highness hope to gain by racking the prisoner?”

“He will not confess otherwise, and then his soul would be lost. By law his life is forfeit for his crime--and assuredly I shall see that he pays it!--but it would endanger my own soul to permit him to die unconfessed and unabsolved.”

I tell it lightly, but it was no light matter to me. I cannot properly convey the pain it caused me to think that Estella should show any favour to a contemptible, awkward, sullen fool, so far beneath even the ordinary standard. Even now, I believe it was some pure flame of generosity and selflessness in my love for her that made me unable to bear the thought of her lowering herself to that brute. Certainly I should have been miserable whoever she favoured; but someone more worthy would have caused me a different kind and measure of suffering.

It was easy for me to discover, and I soon did discover, that Drummle had begun to pursue her closely, and that she permitted it. Before long he was always after her, and he and I encountered each other every day. He persisted in his dull, steady way, and Estella kept him going: sometimes encouraging him, sometimes discouraging him, sometimes nearly flattering him, sometimes openly despising him, sometimes knowing him very well, sometimes scarcely recalling who he was.

The Spider, as Mr. Jaggers had called him, was accustomed to lying in wait, however, and possessed the patience of his kind. Besides that, he had a fool’s confidence in his money and his family importance, which occasionally served him well—almost replacing focus and firm purpose. And she commonly began without a preface and ended without a conclusion. Thus interruptions only made matters worse; yet I had to interrupt, and rather often, too, to save my life; a man would perish if he let her monotony drip over him all day long.

“Oh, nearly anywhere.”

“Why, is it buried everywhere?”

“No, it surely isn’t. It’s buried in very special places, Huck—sometimes on islands, sometimes in decayed chests beneath the end of a branch on an old dead tree, exactly where the shadow lies at midnight; but most often beneath the floors of ha’nted houses.”

“My dear Victor,

“You have probably been waiting anxiously for a letter that would set the date of your return to us. At first I was tempted to write only a few lines, simply telling you the day I expected you. But that would be a cruel mercy, and I cannot do it. How shocked would you be, my son, if you expected a joyful welcome and instead found tears and misery? And how, Victor, can I tell you of our misfortune? Your absence cannot have made you indifferent to our happiness and sorrow; how can I bring pain to my son, who has been away so long? I want to prepare you for this dreadful news, but I know it is impossible; even now your eyes must be racing over the page, searching for the words that will bring you these terrible tidings.

“William is dead!—that sweet child, whose smiles brought warmth and joy to my heart, who was so gentle and yet so lively! Victor, he has been murdered!

“I will not try to comfort you, but will simply tell you what happened.

“Last Thursday, May 7th, I, my niece, and your two brothers went for a walk in Plainpalais. The evening was warm and calm, and we walked farther than usual. It was already growing dark when we thought of returning, and then we realized that William and Ernest, who had gone ahead, were nowhere to be found. We sat down on a bench to wait for them. Soon Ernest came and asked whether we had seen his brother. He said they had been playing together, that William had run off to hide, and that he had searched for him without success. He had then waited a long time, but William had not returned.

“This worried us, and we kept looking for him until night came. Then Elizabeth guessed that he might have gone back to the house. But he was not there. We went out again with torches, for I could not rest while I thought of my sweet boy lost and exposed to the cold dampness and dew of the night. Elizabeth too was in terrible distress. At about five in the morning, I found my lovely boy, whom I had seen the night before healthy, bright, and active, lying on the grass, pale and still; the mark of the murderer’s fingers was on his neck.

“He was carried home, and the grief on my face revealed the truth to Elizabeth. She begged urgently to see the body. At first I tried to stop her, but she insisted. Entering the room where it lay, she quickly examined the victim’s neck and, clasping her hands, cried, ‘O God!’

My imagination was strong, and my ability to analyze and act was equally powerful; together, these qualities led me to imagine and create a man. Even now, I cannot remember my dreams while the work was unfinished without deep emotion. In my thoughts I walked in heaven, sometimes rejoicing in my power, sometimes burning with thoughts of what it might accomplish. According to recent reports from Rotterdam, that city appears to be in a lofty fever of philosophical agitation. In truth, occurrences have taken place there so wholly unforeseen—so altogether unprecedented—so completely opposed to settled notions—as to convince me that, long before now, all Europe must be in commotion, all physics in turmoil, and reason and astronomy at open war.

It seems that upon the—— day of—— (of the precise date I am uncertain), an immense concourse of persons, for ends not distinctly stated, had gathered in the great Exchange square of the prosperous city of Rotterdam. The weather was warm—extraordinarily warm for the time of year—scarcely a breath was moving; and the crowd were not ill pleased to be occasionally sprinkled by brief, kindly showers, falling from great white cloud-masses that mottled, in a capricious fashion, the blue arch of heaven. Yet, near noon, a faint but singular disturbance showed itself among the gathering: the chatter of ten thousand tongues followed; and, a moment later, ten thousand countenances were raised heavenward, ten thousand pipes dropped together from the corners of ten thousand mouths, and a cry—comparable only with the thunder of Niagara—rang long, loud, and fiercely throughout the whole neighborhood of Rotterdam.

The source of the uproar was soon plain enough. From behind the enormous body of one of those sharply outlined cloud-masses already described, there slowly issued into a clear expanse of blue sky a strange, motley, yet seemingly solid object, so fantastically formed, so whimsically contrived, that the sturdy burghers standing below, mouths agape, could neither understand it in the least nor admire it sufficiently. What might it be? In the name of every vrow and devil in Rotterdam, what could it possibly signify? Nobody knew; nobody could conceive; nobody—not even the burgomaster, Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk—possessed the slightest clue for solving the enigma; and thus, since nothing more sensible suggested itself, every man carefully restored his pipe to the corner of his mouth and, lifting his right eye toward the apparition, puffed, paused, waddled to and fro, and grunted with significance—then waddled back, grunted, paused, and at last—puffed once more.

Meanwhile, however, the object of such curiosity, and occasion of so much smoke, descended lower and lower toward the worthy city. Within a few minutes it had come near enough to be plainly distinguished. It seemed to be—yes! it was unquestionably a kind of balloon; yet surely Rotterdam had never before beheld such a balloon.

“February 1st.

“MY DEAR ANNE,

You must be far too happy to concern yourself with Uppercross, which, as you know very well, supplies little worth writing of.
