They were bringing along a very fine-looking old gentleman, and a fine-looking younger one with his right arm in a sling. My souls, how the people shouted and laughed, and kept it up. But I couldn’t see anything funny in it, and I figured it would be hard for the duke and king to see any joke either. I expected them to turn pale. But no, they didn’t turn pale one bit. The duke never showed that he suspected what was happening; he just went around looking pleased and contented, like a jug bubbling out buttermilk. And the king only stared sadly at the newcomers, as if it gave his very heart a stomachache to think there could be such cheats and scoundrels in the world. Oh, he played it wonderfully. Many of the leading people gathered around the king, to show him they were on his side. The old gentleman who had just arrived looked completely puzzled. Soon he began to speak, and I saw at once that he pronounced words like an Englishman—not the king’s way, though the king’s was a pretty good imitation. I can’t repeat the old gentleman’s exact words, nor can I copy his accent; but he turned to the crowd and said something like this:

“This is a surprise I wasn’t expecting; and I’ll admit, openly and honestly, that I’m not very well prepared to face it or answer it. My brother and I have had bad luck: he has broken his arm, and our baggage was mistakenly put off at a town above here last night. I am Peter Wilks’ brother Harvey, and this is his brother William, who can neither hear nor speak—and now he can hardly even make signs, since he has only one hand to make them with. We are who we say we are, and in a day or two, when I get the baggage, I can prove it. But until then I won’t say anything more. I’ll go to the hotel and wait.”

Then he and the new dummy started away. The king laughed and blurted out:

“Broke his arm—very likely, ain’t it? And very convenient, too, for a fraud who has to make signs and hasn’t learned how. Lost their baggage! That’s mighty good—and mighty clever—under the circumstances!”

Then he laughed again, and so did everybody else, except three or four, maybe half a dozen. One was the doctor; another was a sharp-looking gentleman with an old-fashioned carpetbag made of carpet material. He had just come off the steamboat and was speaking quietly with the doctor, glancing toward the king now and then while they nodded their heads. It was Levi Bell, the lawyer who had gone up to Louisville. Another was a big, rough, powerful man who had come along and listened to everything the old gentleman said, and was listening to the king now.

It was well after noon when he woke. His valet had slipped several times, on tiptoe, into the room to discover whether he was moving, and had marvelled at his young master’s sleeping so late. At last his bell rang, and Victor entered quietly carrying a cup of tea and a heap of letters on a little tray of old Sèvres china, then drew aside the olive-satin curtains, lined with gleaming blue, before the three high windows.

“Monsieur has slept well this morning,” he said with a smile.

“What time is it, Victor?” Dorian Gray asked sleepily.

“A quarter past one, Monsieur.”

How late it was! He raised himself and, after drinking a little tea, looked through his letters. One was from Lord Henry and had been delivered by hand that morning. He paused a moment, then laid it aside. The rest he opened without interest. They held the customary assortment of cards, dinner invitations, tickets for private views, programmes for charitable concerts, and such things as are poured each morning in the season upon fashionable young men. There was a fairly substantial account for a chased silver Louis-Quinze toilet-set, which he had not yet dared forward to his guardians. They were exceedingly old-fashioned people, unable to understand that we live in an age in which superfluous things alone are necessary. There were also several most politely phrased letters from Jermyn Street money-lenders, offering to provide any amount at a moment’s notice and on the most reasonable terms of interest.

After some ten minutes, he rose and, putting on an elaborate dressing-gown of silk-embroidered cashmere wool, went into the bathroom paved with onyx. The cold water revived him after his long sleep. He appeared to have forgotten everything he had endured. Once or twice a vague feeling that he had played a part in some odd tragedy came over him, but it possessed the unreality of a dream.

When he was dressed, he went into the library and seated himself before a light French breakfast arranged on a small round table near the open window. It was a lovely day. The warm air seemed heavy with spices. A bee came flying in and hummed about the blue-dragon bowl, filled with sulphur-yellow roses, that stood before him. He felt entirely happy.

All at once his gaze rested on the screen he had set before the portrait, and he gave a start.

“Is Monsieur too cold?” asked his valet, as he placed an omelette on the table. “Shall I close the window?”

Dorian shook his head. “I am not cold,” he murmured.

My heart beat fast, and, though I knew not why, I was afraid. I sent away the servant, locked my door, and sat down to read my father’s letter. These were its contents.

“My dear Child

“I have violated your trust; I have sought to corrupt your mind, and have made your innocent heart familiar with the looks and speech of unlawful, monstrous passion. I must atone for these offences, and strive, in some measure, to make my punishment answer to my guilt. You are, I doubt not, prepared for what I am about to tell you; we must part and be separated for ever.

“I take from you your parent and sole friend. You are thrown, without shelter, upon the world: your hopes are ruined; the tranquillity and safety of your pure mind are destroyed; memory will present you with dreadful images of guilt, and the torment of innocent love deceived. Yet I, who bring all this wretchedness upon you; I, who drive you forth and pitilessly have stamped distrust and anguish upon the heart and brow of my own child, who with fiendish thoughtlessness have tried to rob her of her loveliness and put in its place the hideous deformity of sin; I, in the overflowing misery of my heart, beg you to forgive me.

“I do not seek your pity; you must, and do, loathe me: but forgive me, Mathilda, and do not let your thoughts pursue me in my exile with implacable anger. I must never again see you; never again hear your voice; yet the gentle murmurs of your forgiveness will reach me and soothe the burning of my disordered brain and heart; I am certain I should feel them even in my grave. And I dare support this plea by telling you how miserably I was ensnared in this web of fiery anguish, and of every struggle I made to free myself: indeed, were your soul less pure and radiant, I would not try to excuse myself before you; I should fear that, if I caused you to regard me with less horror, you might hate vice less. But in speaking to you, I feel as though I appealed to an angelic judge. I cannot leave without your forgiveness, and I must attempt to win it, or else despair. I implore you, therefore, to hear my words; and if guilt may in any degree be softened by keen agony and remorse that tears the brain like madness, perhaps you may believe—though I dare not—that I have some claim upon your compassion.

“I beg you to remember our first happy life upon the shores of Loch Lomond. I had returned from a weary wandering of sixteen years, in which, though I had endured many perils and misfortunes, my affections had remained a complete blank.

“I must point out, Sir Walter,” said Mr Shepherd one morning at Kellynch Hall, setting down the newspaper, “that the present moment is very much in our favour. This peace will bring all our wealthy naval officers ashore. They will all be looking for homes. There could not be a better time, Sir Walter, to have a choice of tenants—very reliable tenants. Many great fortunes have been made during the war. If a rich admiral should come our way, Sir Walter—”

“He would be a very fortunate man, Shepherd,” Sir Walter replied. “That is all I have to say. Kellynch Hall would indeed be a prize for him—the greatest prize of all, even if he had captured ever so many before. Eh, Shepherd?”

Mr Shepherd laughed, as he knew he was expected to do, at this joke, and then continued—

“I venture to say, Sir Walter, that in business matters naval gentlemen are good people to deal with. I have had some small acquaintance with their way of conducting business, and I freely admit that they have very generous ideas and are as likely to make desirable tenants as any group of people one might encounter. Therefore, Sir Walter, what I would suggest is this: if any rumours should spread about your intentions—which must be considered possible, because we know how difficult it is to keep the actions and plans of one part of the world from the notice and curiosity of another; consequence has its price. I, John Shepherd, could hide any family affairs I chose, because no one would think me worth watching; but Sir Walter Elliot has eyes upon him that may be very hard to evade. So I will venture this much: it would not greatly surprise me if, despite all our caution, some rumour of the truth got abroad. And in that case, as I was about to say, since applications will certainly follow, I think any from our wealthy naval commanders would be especially worth considering; and I beg to add that I can be here within two hours at any time, to spare you the trouble of answering them.”

Sir Walter merely nodded. But shortly afterward, getting up and walking about the room, he remarked sarcastically—

“There are few among the gentlemen of the navy, I imagine, who would not be astonished to find themselves in a house of this kind.”

“They would certainly look about them and bless their good fortune,” said Mrs Clay, who was present. Her father had driven her over, since nothing was so beneficial to Mrs Clay’s health as a drive to Kellynch. “But I entirely agree with my father that a sailor might make a very desirable tenant.”

There was something strange in all this that drew me in and enchanted me. It was as though he had awakened from a long, dreamlike sleep, and felt rather like one of the seven sleepers, or Nourjahad in that charming imitation of an eastern tale: Diana was gone; his friends had changed or died; and, when he awoke, I was all he had left to love on earth.

How dear the waters, mountains, and woods of Loch Lomond became to me, now that I had such a beloved companion on my walks. With my father, I visited every lovely place, whether on the islands or beside the waterfalls shaded by trees; every dark path and every little valley tangled with brushwood and ferns. His conversation broadened my thoughts. I felt remade, surrounded by the freshness and energy of a new life. Since his arrival, it seemed as if I had been carried from a small patch of earth into a universe without limits to imagination or understanding. Before, my life had been like a pleasant country stream, never meant to leave its native fields, but quietly to disappear when its work was done, leaving no mark behind. Now it seemed like a broad river flowing through a rich and beautiful landscape, always changing and always lovely. Alas! I did not know the desert it was soon to reach, the rocks that would tear its waters, or the dreadful scene that would be reflected, more horribly distorted, in its waves. Life was bright then; I was beginning to learn hope—and what brings more bitter despair to the heart than hope destroyed?

Is it not strange that grief should so quickly follow such heavenly happiness? I drank from an enchanted cup, but bitterness lay at the bottom of its long sweetness. My heart was filled with deep affection, yet it was calm because that feeling was so deep and full. I had never imagined that misery could come from love, and the lesson that everyone must eventually learn was taught to me in a way few are forced to endure. I mourn now, and always will mourn, those few short months of paradise. I broke no command, I ate no apple, yet I was cruelly driven from it. Alas! My companion did, and I was cast down with him in his fall. But I stray from my story—let sorrow come at its proper time; at this point, I may still speak of happiness.

Three months passed in this delightful companionship when my aunt became ill. I spent a whole month in her room nursing her, but her illness was fatal, and she died, leaving me inconsolable for a time. Death is so terrible to those who remain alive; the bonds of habit are so strong, even when affection does not bind them, that the heart must suffer when they are broken.

“Do you often come back?”

“I have not been here since.”

“Nor have I.”

The moon began to rise, and I thought of the peaceful face turned toward the white ceiling, now gone forever. The moon began to rise, and I remembered the pressure on my hand when I spoke the last words he heard on earth.

Estella was the first to break the silence between us.

“I have often hoped and meant to come back, but many things prevented me. Poor, poor old place!”

The first moonbeams touched the silver mist, and also the tears that fell from her eyes. Not knowing that I saw them, she tried to master them and said quietly,—

“Were you wondering, as you walked along, how it came to be left like this?”

“Yes, Estella.”

“The land belongs to me. It is the only thing I have not given up. Everything else has been taken from me, little by little, but I have kept this. It was the one thing I firmly resisted through all those miserable years.”

“Is it going to be built on?”

“At last, it is. I came here to say goodbye before it changes. And you,” she said, with tender concern for a wanderer, “do you still live abroad?”

“Still.”

“And you do well, I am sure?”

“I work fairly hard to earn enough to live on, and so—yes, I do well.”

“I have often thought of you,” Estella said.

“Have you?”

“Lately, very often. For a long, hard time, I kept away the memory of what I had thrown aside when I did not understand its value. But since my duty no longer prevents me from admitting that memory, I have given it a place in my heart.”

“You have always had your place in my heart,” I answered.

We were silent again until she spoke.

“I never thought,” Estella said, “that in saying goodbye to this place, I would also be saying goodbye to you. I am very glad that I can.”

“Glad to part again, Estella? To me, parting is painful. The memory of our last parting has always been sad and painful to me.”

“But you said to me,” Estella replied very earnestly, “‘God bless you, God forgive you!’ If you could say that to me then, you will not hesitate to say it now—now that suffering has taught me more strongly than anything else could, and has taught me to understand what your heart once was. I have been bent and broken, but—I hope—into a better form.”

On Saturday nights in our village there was a pleasant feeling of tidying up and taking a peaceful halt before beginning life anew, and this encouraged Joe to venture on remaining out half an hour later on Saturdays than on other evenings. When the half-hour and the rum-and-water came to an end together, Joe rose to leave and took my hand.

“Wait just a moment, Mr. Gargery,” said the stranger. “I believe I have a shining new shilling somewhere in my pocket, and, if I do, the boy shall have it.”

He picked it from a handful of loose coins, wrapped it in a bit of rumpled paper, and handed it to me. “Yours!” he said. “Remember! Your very own.”

I thanked him, gazing at him much longer than good manners allowed, while clutching Joe tightly. He bade Joe good-night, and bade Mr. Wopsle good-night too, for Mr. Wopsle left with us; but to me he gave only a look from his aiming eye—or rather, not a look, since he closed it, though an eye can work wonders by being hidden.

On our way home, had I felt inclined to speak, all the conversation would have had to come from me, because Mr. Wopsle left us at the Jolly Bargemen door, and Joe walked home with his mouth open as wide as possible, rinsing the rum away with air. But the reappearance of my former wrongdoing and old acquaintance had left me almost stunned, and I could think of nothing else.

My sister was not in an especially bad temper when we came into the kitchen, and that uncommon fact gave Joe courage to tell her of the bright shilling. “A bad one, I’ll wager,” said Mrs. Joe in triumph, “or he’d never have given it to the boy! Let us see it.”

I unwrapped it, and found it was a good shilling. “But what is this?” cried Mrs. Joe, dropping the shilling and snatching up the paper. “Two one-pound notes?”

They were nothing less than two plump, sweaty one-pound notes, which appeared to have enjoyed the closest acquaintance with every cattle-market in the county. Joe seized his hat again and hurried with them to the Jolly Bargemen to return them to their owner. While he was away, I sat on my usual stool, staring blankly at my sister, quite certain that the man would not be there.

Before long Joe returned, saying that the man had gone, though he, Joe, had left a message at the Three Jolly Bargemen about the notes.

Summer moved onward, and, wearing the sun’s powerful beams as a crown, plague hurled her certain arrows across the earth. The nations under her sway bent their heads and perished. The corn that had risen in abundance lay rotting upon the ground in autumn, while the mournful man who had gone forth to seek bread for his children lay rigid and plague-smitten in the furrow. The green forests lifted their branches in majesty, while the dying lay scattered beneath their shade, replying to the grave music with discordant cries. Bright-plumaged birds darted among the shadows; heedless deer rested unharmed upon the fern—the oxen and horses wandered from their unwatched stalls and fed amid the wheat, for death descended upon man alone.

As summer and death increased, so did our terrors. My poor beloved and I gazed at one another, and at our children.—“We will preserve them, Idris,” I said, “I will preserve them. In years to come we shall tell them of these fears, which will then have vanished with their cause. Though they alone remained upon the earth, yet they shall live; their cheeks shall not grow pale, nor their dear voices fail.” Our eldest partly understood the scenes around him, and sometimes, with a grave countenance, asked me why such immense desolation existed. But he was only ten; and youthful gaiety soon drove unreasoning anxiety from his brow. Evelyn, a merry cherub, a playful child, knowing nothing of grief or pain, would toss his light curls back from his eyes and make the halls ring with laughter, drawing our notice in a thousand innocent fashions to his games. Clara, our beautiful, gentle Clara, was our support, our comfort, our joy. She made it her duty to tend the sick, console the afflicted, aid the old, and share the amusements and stir the cheerfulness of the young. She passed through the rooms like a beneficent spirit sent from the heavenly realm to brighten our dark hour with unearthly splendour. Thankfulness and blessing followed the traces of her steps. Yet when she stood before us in modest simplicity, playing with our children, or diligently rendering small services to Idris with girlish care, one marvelled in what lovely feature of her pure beauty, in what gentle note of her moving voice, such heroism, wisdom, and active goodness could dwell.

The summer wore away slowly, for we hoped that winter would at least restrain the disease. To hope it would disappear entirely was too precious—too deeply felt—to be spoken. Whenever such a thought was carelessly voiced, those who heard it, in a burst of tears and impassioned sobbing, showed how profound their fears were and how slight their hopes.

At last, we agreed to live together during my stay in the city. Since my finances were somewhat less troubled than his, I was allowed to pay for renting and furnishing a house suited to the strangely gloomy taste we shared: an old, grotesque mansion, long abandoned because of superstitions we did not investigate, and nearly falling down in a secluded, desolate part of the Faubourg St. Germain.

Had the world known how we lived there, it would have considered us madmen—though perhaps harmless ones. Our isolation was complete. We received no visitors. In fact, the location of our retreat had been carefully hidden even from my former acquaintances; and Dupin had long since ceased either to know anyone in Paris or to be known by them. We lived entirely within ourselves.

My friend had a whim—what else can I call it?—of loving the night for its own sake. I quietly joined him in this oddity, as I did in all his others, surrendering myself completely to his wild preferences. The dark goddess could not live with us always, but we could imitate her presence. At the first light of morning, we shut every grimy shutter in the old house and lit two heavily scented candles, which gave off only the weakest, most ghostly light. With their help, we occupied ourselves in dreams—reading, writing, or talking—until the clock announced the coming of real Darkness. Then we went out into the streets arm in arm, continuing the subjects of the day or wandering far and wide until late, seeking among the wild lights and shadows of the crowded city that endless mental excitement which quiet observation can provide.

At such times, I could not help noticing and admiring in Dupin a remarkable power of analysis, though his rich imagination had led me to expect it. He also seemed to take keen pleasure in using it—if not precisely in showing it off—and readily admitted the enjoyment it gave him. With a low, chuckling laugh, he would boast that most men wore windows in their chests when facing him, and he often supported such claims with direct, startling proofs of how intimately he knew my own thoughts. At these moments his manner was cold and distant; his eyes looked blank, while his voice, usually a rich tenor, rose to a high pitch that would have sounded peevish if not for the careful slowness and perfect clarity with which he spoke.

At least, he believed so. But who could know? ... No. There had been nothing else. Out of vanity, he had spared her. In hypocrisy, he had put on the mask of goodness. Out of curiosity, he had attempted self-denial. He saw that now.

But would this murder haunt him for the rest of his life? Must he always carry the weight of his past? Was he truly going to confess? Never. Only one piece of evidence remained against him. The picture itself—that was the evidence. He would destroy it. Why had he kept it for so long? Once, he had taken pleasure in watching it change and grow old. Lately, it had given him no pleasure at all. It had kept him awake at night. Whenever he was away, he had been terrified that other eyes might see it. It had cast melancholy over his passions. The mere memory of it had spoiled many joyful moments. It had been like a conscience to him. Yes, it had been his conscience. He would destroy it.

He looked around and saw the knife that had stabbed Basil Hallward. He had cleaned it again and again until no trace of stain remained. It was bright and gleaming. Just as it had killed the painter, it would kill the painter’s work, and everything it represented. It would kill the past, and once the past was dead, he would be free. It would kill this monstrous life of the soul, and without its hideous warnings, he would be at peace. He seized it and drove it into the picture.

What was that disgusting red moisture, shining wetly on one of the hands, as if the canvas had sweated blood? How terrible it was! For a moment, it seemed even more terrible than the silent thing he knew lay stretched across the table—the thing whose strange, twisted shadow on the stained carpet showed that it had not moved, but was still there as he had left it.

Ten minutes later, his face pale with terror and his eyes wild with grief, Lord Arthur Savile rushed out of Bentinck House. He forced his way through the crowd of fur-coated footmen gathered around the large striped awning, seeming neither to see nor hear anything. The night was bitterly cold, and the gas lamps around the square flared and flickered in the sharp wind; but his hands were feverishly hot, and his forehead burned like fire. He went on and on, walking almost like a drunken man. A policeman watched him curiously as he passed, and a beggar who came out from an archway to ask for money drew back in fear, seeing suffering greater than his own. Once, Lord Arthur stopped beneath a lamp and looked at his hands. He thought he could already see bloodstains on them, and a faint cry escaped his shaking lips.

Murder! That was what the cheiromantist had seen in his hand. Murder! The night itself seemed to know it, and the lonely wind seemed to howl it in his ear. It filled the dark corners of the streets. It grinned down at him from the rooftops.

At first he came to the Park, whose dark woods seemed to draw him in. He leaned wearily against the railings, pressing his brow to the cold wet metal and listening to the trembling silence of the trees. “Murder! Murder!” he kept saying, as if repeating the word might lessen its horror. The sound of his own voice made him shiver, yet he almost hoped Echo would hear him and wake the sleeping city from its dreams. He felt a mad urge to stop some passing stranger and tell him everything.

Then he wandered across Oxford Street into narrow, wretched alleys. Two women with painted faces laughed at him as he passed. From a dark courtyard came the sounds of curses and blows, followed by sharp screams; and on a damp doorstep he saw the bent forms of poverty and old age huddled together. A strange pity came over him. Were these children of sin and misery destined for their fate, as he was for his? Were they, like him, only puppets in some monstrous show?

Yet it was not the mystery of suffering that struck him, but its absurdity: its complete uselessness, its grotesque lack of meaning. Everything seemed so confused! So without harmony! He was astonished by the gap between the shallow optimism of the day and the real facts of life. He was still very young.

After a while, he found himself before Marylebone Church. The silent road looked like a long ribbon of polished silver, marked here and there by the dark, curling patterns of moving shadows.

She was no longer the cheerful being who, in the days of our early youth, had roamed with me beside the lake and spoken rapturously of our hopes for the future. The first of those afflictions sent to detach us from the world had come upon her, and its shadow had extinguished her sweetest smiles.

“When I consider, my dear cousin,” she said, “the dreadful death of Justine Moritz, the world and all that is done in it no longer seem to me as they once did. Formerly, the stories of wickedness and injustice that I found in books or heard from others appeared like accounts from former ages or imagined misfortunes; at any rate, they were distant, and appealed more to reason than imagination. But now suffering has reached my own home, and men seem to me like monsters eager for one another’s blood. Yet I am surely unjust. Everyone believed that poor girl guilty; and had she been capable of the crime for which she died, she must indeed have been among the most depraved of human beings. For a handful of jewels, to murder the child of her benefactor and friend—a child she had cared for from birth, and seemed to love as though it were her own! I could never have agreed to the death of any person, yet I should certainly have considered such a being unfit to remain among mankind. But she was innocent. Only a few hours had passed, yet a great revolution had taken place in my life—the natural work of years had been accomplished since morning. My father was as dead to me, and for a moment I felt as though he, with his white hair, lay in his coffin, while I—my youth gone, nearing age—wept over his timely death. But it was not so. I was still young—oh, far too young—and he was not dead to others; but I, most miserable, must never see or speak to him again. I must flee from him more eagerly than from my greatest enemy: whether alone or among cities, I must never look upon him again. That thought left me breathless with anguish, and so possessed my imagination that for a time I could follow no further course of thought. From then on, I thought, I would live in the bleakest seclusion. I would withdraw to the Continent and become a nun—not for religion, since I was not Catholic, but so that I might be shut out from the world forever. There I would find solitude in which to weep, and the voices of life would never reach me.

But my father—my beloved and most wretched father? Would he die? Would he never overcome the fierce passion that now ruled him without pity? Might he not, many years from now, when age had extinguished the burning feelings he now endured, become a father to me again? This thought smoothed my brow, and I felt—and wept to feel it—a half-melancholy smile draw my lips away from their expression of suffering. I dared to entertain better hopes for my future life. Years must pass, but they would fly lightly on the wings of hope; or, if they passed heavily, still they would pass, and I had not lost my father forever. Let him spend another sixteen years wandering desolately. Let him once more speak his wild complaints to vast forests and terrible cataracts in another land. Let him again endure dreadful danger and hardships that crush the soul. Let the hot southern sun again burn his passion-worn cheeks, and cold night rains fall upon him and chill his blood.

To this life, miserable father, I devote you! Go! Let your days be spent among savages, and your nights beneath the open sky! Let your limbs be worn down and your heart grow cold, and let all youth die within you!

The mental powers called analytical are, in themselves, not easily analyzed. We recognize them only by their effects. Among other things, we know that, when someone possesses them in unusual strength, they give that person the keenest pleasure. Just as a strong man takes pride in his bodily power and enjoys exercises that put his muscles to work, the analyst delights in the mental activity that untangles things. He finds pleasure even in the smallest tasks that call his talent into use. He enjoys riddles, puzzles, and hieroglyphics, and in solving them shows a sharpness that seems almost supernatural to ordinary minds. His conclusions, reached through the very spirit and substance of method, truly have the appearance of intuition.

The power of resolving problems may be greatly strengthened by mathematical study, especially by its highest branch, which has unfairly been called analysis simply because it works backward. Yet calculating is not, by itself, analyzing. A chess player, for instance, may do the former without making any effort at the latter. It follows that chess is greatly misunderstood in its effect on the mind. I am not writing a formal essay, but only introducing a rather unusual story with a few scattered remarks; so I will say that the higher powers of reflective thought are tested more clearly and more usefully by the quiet game of draughts than by all the elaborate triviality of chess. In chess, where the pieces move in different and strange ways and have various changing values, mere complexity is mistaken, as often happens, for depth. Attention is strongly demanded. If it weakens for a moment, an error is made that brings loss or defeat. Since the possible moves are not only numerous but tangled, such errors become more likely; and nine times out of ten, the player with better concentration rather than greater sharpness wins. In draughts, by contrast, where the moves are fixed and vary little, the chance of carelessness is reduced. Since simple attention is comparatively less needed, any advantage gained by either player comes from superior insight. To make this less abstract, imagine a game of draughts reduced to four kings, where, naturally, no oversight is expected. It is clear that victory, if the players are otherwise equal, can be decided only by some subtle move resulting from a strong effort of the intellect.

Moralists, generally, had treated it as a warning, had attributed to it a certain ethical influence in shaping character, and had commended it as that which taught us what to pursue and indicated what to shun. His abrupt, wild love for Sibyl Vane was a psychological occurrence of considerable interest. Curiosity had undoubtedly played a large part in it—curiosity and the craving for fresh experiences—yet it was not a simple passion, but an exceedingly complicated one. Whatever in it belonged to the merely sensuous instinct of boyhood had been altered through imagination, made into something that appeared to the young man himself far removed from the senses, and was therefore all the more perilous. Whist has long been remarked for its effect upon what is called the calculating faculty; and men of the loftiest intellect have been known to find in it a seemingly inexplicable pleasure, while dismissing chess as frivolous. Certainly nothing of the same kind so severely exercises the power of analysis. The finest chess-player in Christendom may be scarcely more than the finest player of chess; but skill at whist denotes an ability to succeed in all those graver contests in which mind is matched against mind. By skill, I mean that perfection in the game which embraces an understanding of all the sources from which lawful advantage can be drawn. These sources are not merely numerous, but various in kind, and often lie in recesses of thought wholly beyond the reach of ordinary comprehension. To observe closely is to remember clearly; and thus far the concentrated chess-player will acquit himself well at whist, while the rules of Hoyle—being founded upon the mere mechanism of the game—are sufficiently easy to grasp in general. Hence a retentive memory and adherence to “the book” are commonly considered the whole of good play. Yet it is in concerns lying outside the bounds of bare rule that the analyst's ability reveals itself. Silently, he forms a multitude of observations and deductions. His companions may do likewise; but the difference in the amount of information gained lies less in the soundness of the inference than in the character of the observation. The essential knowledge is knowing what to observe. Our player limits himself in no way; nor, because the game is his object, does he refuse conclusions drawn from matters outside it. He studies his partner's face, carefully comparing it with those of each opponent. He watches the manner in which the cards are arranged in every hand, often reckoning trump after trump and honor after honor from the glances their possessors cast upon them. He marks every change of countenance as play advances, collecting material for reflection from expressions of confidence, surprise, triumph, or vexation. From the way a trick is gathered up, he decides whether its winner can take another in that suit. He detects what is played as a feint by the fashion in which it is laid upon the table. A chance or careless word; the accidental fall or exposure of a card, together with the anxiety or indifference shown in concealing it; the counting of tricks and the order in which they are placed; confusion, hesitation, eagerness, or alarm—all furnish his seemingly instinctive perception with signs of the true condition of affairs.

Still, what I could see was strange and exciting. Northward from that vast rim already mentioned—which, with slight qualification, may be called the limit of human discovery in these regions—there stretched one unbroken, or nearly unbroken, sheet of ice. In its first few degrees, the surface was noticeably flattened; farther on it sank into a level plane; and finally, becoming somewhat concave, it ended at the Pole itself in a sharply defined circular center. Its apparent diameter made an angle of about sixty-five seconds as seen from the balloon. Its dark color, varying in strength, was always darker than any other spot on the visible hemisphere, and sometimes deepened into complete, impenetrable blackness. Beyond this, little could be learned. By twelve o’clock the circular center had greatly decreased in size, and by seven P.M. The Tiber, that highway laid out by nature herself through her continent, lay before me, and many boats were moored along its banks. With a few books, some provisions, and my dog, I would enter one of them and drift with the river’s current to the sea; then, keeping close to shore, I would follow the lovely coasts and sunlit headlands of the blue Mediterranean, pass Naples, skirt Calabria, and venture through the double dangers of Scylla and Charybdis; afterwards, with resolute purpose—for what had I left to lose?—glide over the ocean towards Malta and the remoter Cyclades. I would shun Constantinople, whose familiar towers and bays belonged to a different condition of life than that which was now mine; I would sail along Asia Minor and Syria, and, beyond the seven-mouthed Nile, turn northward once more, until, leaving forgotten Carthage and desolate Lybia behind, I reached the pillars of Hercules. And then—wherever it might be—the slimy caverns and noiseless abysses of the sea might become my home before I completed this protracted voyage; or disease might strike my heart while I floated alone upon the heaving Mediterranean; or, at some place where I landed, I might discover what I sought—a companion. Or, should that be denied me—through endless years, feeble and grey-haired, my youth already buried with those whom I loved—the solitary wanderer would yet spread his sail and grasp the tiller; and, ever yielding to heaven’s winds, would pass for ever round one headland after another, cast anchor in bay after bay, and still cleave the barren sea, leaving the green land of native Europe behind, descending the tawny coast of Africa, and, having endured the violent waters of the Cape, might fasten my weathered skiff in some inlet shadowed by fragrant groves upon the scented islands of the distant Indian Ocean.

I am already far to the north of London, and, as I pass through the streets of Petersburgh, a chill northern wind touches my cheeks, strengthening my spirits and filling me with pleasure. Do you comprehend this sensation? This breeze, having come from the regions toward which I am bound, gives me a foretaste of those frozen lands. Animated by this promising wind, my waking dreams grow warmer and more distinct. In vain do I attempt to convince myself that the pole is a place of frost and barrenness; to my fancy it always appears a country of loveliness and delight. There, Margaret, the sun is ever in sight, its wide orb merely grazing the horizon and shedding an unceasing radiance. There—for, with your permission, sister, I shall place some faith in earlier navigators—snow and ice are driven away; and, borne across a tranquil sea, we may arrive at a land exceeding in marvel and beauty every region yet found upon the inhabited globe. Its products and aspect may be unparalleled, just as the appearances of the heavenly bodies surely are in those unknown wastes. What might one not hope for in a land of perpetual light? There I may discover the extraordinary force that draws the needle, and may arrange a thousand celestial observations which need only this voyage to make their apparent irregularities harmonious for ever. I shall satisfy my eager curiosity by beholding a portion of the world never previously visited, and perhaps set foot upon ground never marked by human tread. Such are my inducements, and they suffice to overcome every dread of peril or death, and to make me begin this arduous voyage with the delight a child experiences when he sets out in a small boat with his holiday companions upon a voyage of discovery up his native stream. Yet, even if all these suppositions prove mistaken, you cannot deny the priceless advantage I shall bestow upon all mankind, to the final generation, by finding a passage near the pole to those lands which now require so many months to reach; or by determining the mystery of the magnet, which, if it can be determined at all, can only be accomplished through an undertaking like my own.

These thoughts have banished the uneasiness with which I commenced my letter, and I feel my heart burn with an enthusiasm that raises me toward heaven; for nothing so greatly calms the mind as a fixed purpose—a point upon which the soul may rest its intellectual gaze.

“Well, I never!” said Joe, amazed. “I wonder how she came to know Pip!”

“Noodle!” exclaimed my sister. “Who said she knew him?”

“—Which somebody,” Joe again courteously suggested, “said that she wanted him to go and play there.”

“And mightn’t she ask Uncle Pumblechook whether he knew of a boy to go and play there? Isn’t it barely possible that Uncle Pumblechook is one of her tenants, and that he may now and then—we won’t say quarterly or half-yearly, because that would be expecting too much of you—but now and then—go there to pay his rent? And mightn’t she ask Uncle Pumblechook whether he knew of a boy to go and play there? And mightn’t Uncle Pumblechook, always so mindful and considerate of us—though perhaps you don’t think so, Joseph,” she added in the most reproachful tone, as though he were the hardest-hearted of nephews, “then name this boy, standing Prancing here”—which I solemnly affirm I was not—“for whom I have always been a willing slave?”

“Good again!” cried Uncle Pumblechook. “Well said! Neatly put! Very good indeed! Now, Joseph, you understand the case.”

“No, Joseph,” said my sister, maintaining her reproachful manner, while Joe apologetically passed the back of his hand repeatedly across his nose, “you do not yet—though you may suppose you do—understand the case. You may imagine that you do, but you do not, Joseph. For you do not know that Uncle Pumblechook, realizing that, for anything we can say, this boy’s fortune may be made by going to Miss Havisham’s, has offered to carry him into town to-night in his own chaise-cart, to keep him there to-night, and to bring him with his own hands to Miss Havisham’s to-morrow morning. And Lor-a-mussy me!” cried my sister, flinging off her bonnet in sudden despair, “here am I talking to mere Mooncalfs, while Uncle Pumblechook waits, and the mare takes cold at the door, and the boy is begrimed with crock and dirt from the crown of his head to the sole of his foot!”

And I summon you, spirits of the departed, and you, roving agents of vengeance, to assist and guide me in my undertaking. Let the accursed, infernal monster drain the cup of suffering; let him know the despair that now afflicts me.”

I had commenced my invocation with a solemnity and dread that nearly persuaded me the ghosts of my murdered friends listened to and sanctioned my devotion; but as I ended, the furies took hold of me, and fury strangled my voice.

The silence of the night returned me a loud, demoniacal laugh. It sounded in my ears, prolonged and oppressive; the mountains repeated it, and I seemed encompassed by all hell, jeering and laughing at me. In that instant I surely would have yielded to madness and ended my wretched life, had not my oath been heard and I been preserved for revenge. The laughter faded, and then a familiar, detested voice, seeming to speak beside my ear, said in an audible whisper, “I am content, unhappy wretch! You have resolved to live, and I am content.”

I sprang toward the place whence the sound had come, but the fiend slipped beyond my reach. At once the wide orb of the moon rose and cast its full light upon his hideous, misshapen form as he fled with speed beyond that of man.

I chased him, and for many months this has been my occupation. Led by a faint trace, I followed the course of the Rhone, though without success. The blue Mediterranean came into view, and, by a singular accident, I saw the fiend enter at night and conceal himself aboard a ship sailing for the Black Sea. I secured passage on that same vessel, but he escaped me, by what means I cannot tell.

Through the wastes of Tartary and Russia, though he continued to avoid me, I have always pursued his trail. At times peasants, terrified by that dreadful apparition, told me which way he had gone; at others he himself, fearing that, if I lost every sign of him, I would despair and perish, left some token to direct me. Snow fell upon my head, and I beheld the impression of his enormous foot upon the white expanse. How can you, just entering life, to whom anxiety is unfamiliar and anguish unknown, comprehend what I have endured and yet endure? Cold, hunger, and weariness were the smallest sufferings appointed to me; some devil had cursed me, and I bore my everlasting hell within me. Yet a benevolent spirit still attended and led my steps, and, when I complained most bitterly, would suddenly free me from difficulties that appeared impossible to overcome. Sometimes, when nature, subdued by hunger, gave way beneath exhaustion, a meal was set before me in the wilderness, restoring my strength and courage.

But enough of this. I will begin my story: it is my final task, and I hope I have strength enough to complete it. I record no crimes; my errors may readily be forgiven, for they arose not from evil intent but from poor judgment. I believe few could claim that, through different conduct and greater wisdom, they might have escaped the misfortunes of which I am the victim. My fate has been ruled by necessity—a dreadful necessity. It demanded hands stronger than mine; stronger, I believe, than any human power, to break the thick, unyielding chain that has bound me—me, once alive only to joy, always filled with warm love and delight in goodness—to a misery that could end only, and is now about to end, in death. But I forget myself; my story remains untold. I will pause for a few moments, dry my dim eyes, and try to lose the present, vague yet crushing sense of unhappiness in the sharper emotions of the past.

I was born in England. My father was a man of rank. He lost his own father early and was raised by a weak mother, with all the indulgence she believed was owed to a wealthy nobleman. He was sent to Eton and afterward to college, and from childhood was permitted the free use of large sums of money. Thus, from his earliest youth, he enjoyed the independence that a boy with such advantages invariably gains at a public school.

Under these conditions, his passions found rich ground in which to take root and flourish, as either flowers or weeds according to their nature. Because he had always been allowed to act for himself, his character became strongly and early defined, showing a varied surface upon which a keen observer might see the seeds of both virtues and misfortunes. His careless extravagance, which led him to waste immense sums satisfying passing whims—whims he elevated to the name of passions because of their apparent force—often appeared as limitless generosity. Yet while he devoted himself earnestly to the needs of others, his own desires were satisfied to the fullest degree. He gave money, but sacrificed none of his own wishes in giving it; he gave time, which he did not value, and affection, which he was pleased to have called into action in any way.

I do not say that, if his own desires had been set against those of others, he would have shown excessive selfishness; but he was never put to that test. He was raised in prosperity and surrounded by all its advantages; everyone loved him and wished to please him.

I was born in a small island land surrounded by sea and shadowed by clouds. When I think of the globe, with its endless ocean and unknown continents, it seems no more than a tiny speck in that vast whole. Yet, measured by the power of the mind, it outweighed countries far larger and more populous. This proves that the human mind alone created all that was good and great for mankind, while Nature was only its first servant. England, lying far north in the troubled sea, now appears in my dreams as a great, well-crewed ship, mastering the winds and riding proudly over the waves. In my childhood, she was the whole universe to me. When I stood on my native hills and saw plains and mountains reaching to the edge of sight, dotted with my countrymen’s homes and made fertile by their labour, the centre of the earth itself seemed fixed in that place. The rest of the world was like a fable, and forgetting it would have cost neither my imagination nor my understanding any effort.

From the first, my life has shown how greatly change can rule the course of a man’s existence. In my case, this seemed almost inherited. My father was one of those men on whom nature had lavishly bestowed the admired gifts of wit and imagination, then sent his little vessel of life onward under those winds without giving him reason for a rudder or judgment for a pilot. His family background was obscure, but circumstances brought him early to public attention, and his small inheritance was soon spent in the brilliant world of fashion and luxury in which he played a part. During the brief years of careless youth, he was adored by the fashionable idlers of the day, especially by the young king, who escaped the schemes of political parties and the hard duties of ruling to find constant amusement and high spirits in my father’s company. My father’s impulses, never under his own control, continually led him into troubles from which only his cleverness could free him. His growing debts, both of honour and trade, would have crushed any other man, but he carried them with a light heart and untamed cheerfulness. His presence was so necessary at the dinners and gatherings of the rich that his faults were forgiven, and he himself was welcomed with intoxicating praise.

Such popularity, like all popularity, soon fades. The troubles of every kind that he had to face grew at a terrifying rate, while his limited means of escaping them did not grow with them.

Dupin spoke those last words very softly and calmly. Just as calmly, he walked to the door, locked it, and put the key in his pocket. Then he drew a pistol from his coat and, without the slightest agitation, laid it on the table.

The sailor’s face reddened as though he were fighting for breath. He sprang to his feet and seized his club, but the next instant sank back into his chair, trembling violently, with the face of a dead man. He said nothing. I pitied him from the depths of my heart.

“My friend,” said Dupin kindly, “you are frightening yourself without cause—you truly are. We mean you no harm at all. To look at a star indirectly—to see it from the corner of the eye, by turning toward it the outer parts of the retina (which are more sensitive to faint impressions of light than the center)—is to see the star clearly, to appreciate its brilliance most fully. That brilliance fades in exact proportion as we direct our gaze fully upon it. In the latter case, more rays actually strike the eye; but in the former, the capacity for perception is finer. Excessive depth confuses and weakens thought; and it is possible to make Venus herself disappear from the sky by examining her too steadily, too intently, or too directly.

The woman’s words and manner had touched Rose Maylie’s heart; and, joined with her love for her young charge, and scarcely less strong in its sincerity and warmth, was her earnest wish to bring the outcast back to repentance and hope.

They intended to remain in London for only three days before leaving for several weeks at a distant part of the coast. It was now midnight on the first day. What action could she decide upon that might be carried out within forty-eight hours? Or how could she delay the journey without arousing suspicion?

Mr. Losberne was staying with them and would remain for the next two days; but Rose knew the excellent gentleman’s impulsive nature too well, and saw too clearly the anger with which, in his first burst of indignation, he would view the person responsible for Oliver’s recapture, to entrust him with the secret when no experienced person could support her pleas on the girl’s behalf. These were all reasons for the utmost caution and discretion in telling Mrs. Maylie, whose first impulse would certainly be to consult the worthy doctor about it. As for seeking legal advice, even if she had known how, that was scarcely possible for the same reason. Troubled by these conflicting thoughts, leaning first toward one course and then another, then shrinking from them all as each new consideration came to mind, Rose spent a sleepless, anxious night. After further reflection the next day, she came to the desperate decision to consult Harry.

“If it is painful for him,” she thought, “to return here, how painful it will be for me! But perhaps he will not come; he may write, or he may come himself and carefully avoid meeting me—he did so when he left. I scarcely expected that he would, but it was better for us both.” Here Rose laid down her pen and turned away, as if even the paper that was to carry her message must not see her weep.

It was after two o’clock when, by a sudden turning, I found myself near the lake, beside a cove where a small skiff lay moored—It was close to our house, and I perceived my father and aunt walking upon the lawn. I sprang into the boat and, practised in such exploits, thrust it from the shore and used all my strength to row rapidly across. As I came on, clad in white, covered only by my tartan _rachan_, with my hair floating over my shoulders, and darting forward with a swiftness beyond what my boat seemed capable of, my father has often said that I appeared more a spirit than a mortal girl. I reached the bank; my father caught the boat, I sprang lightly ashore, and the next instant was in his embrace.

Then indeed I began to live. Everything about me changed from dreary sameness into the most brilliant prospect of pleasure and delight. The happiness I found in my father’s society surpassed even my eager expectations. We were continually together, and our conversation supplied us with endless subjects. He had spent the sixteen years of his absence among countries almost unknown to Europe; he had travelled through Persia, Arabia, and northern India, and had entered the dwellings of the natives with a liberty granted to few Europeans. His accounts of their customs, his anecdotes, and his descriptions of scenery beguiled delicious hours, when we had exhausted discussion of our own designs for the future.

The language of affection was so strange to me that I listened with rapture when he spoke of what he had felt for me through those long years of seeming neglect. “At first,” he said, “I could not endure to think of my poor little girl; but later, when grief had softened and hope returned to visit me, my thoughts could turn only to her, and amid cities and deserts her little fairy shape, as I pictured it, was ever passing before me. The northern wind, when it refreshed me, seemed sweeter and gentler, because it appeared to bear with it some portion of your spirit. I often imagined that I would return at once and carry you away with me to some fruitful island, where we might dwell in peace for ever. As I came back, my ardent hopes were checked by so many fears; my impatience grew painfully intense. I dared not imagine that the sun might shine and the moon rise, not upon your living form, but upon your grave. But no—it is otherwise; I possess my Mathilda, my comfort and my hope.”—

It seemed to be a cluster of back lanes, ditches, and small gardens, with the look of a rather quiet, dull retreat. Wemmick’s house was a little wooden cottage among garden plots, with its roof cut and painted to resemble a gun battery.

“My own work,” said Wemmick. “Looks nice, doesn’t it?”

I praised it warmly. I think it was the smallest house I had ever seen, with the strangest Gothic windows—most of them false—and a Gothic door almost too small to enter.

“That’s a real flagstaff, you see,” said Wemmick, “and on Sundays I fly a real flag. Now look. Once I’ve crossed this bridge, I raise it—like this—and cut off all communication.”

The bridge was a plank across a gap about four feet wide and two feet deep. Still, it was very pleasant to see the pride with which he lifted and secured it, smiling with genuine enjoyment rather than doing it merely by habit.

“At nine every night, Greenwich time,” said Wemmick, “the gun goes off. There it is, you see! And when you hear it fire, I think you’ll call it a Stinger.”

The cannon he meant stood in a separate fort made of latticework. An ingenious little tarpaulin arrangement, like an umbrella, protected it from the weather.

“Then, at the back,” said Wemmick, “out of sight, so it doesn’t spoil the idea of the fortifications—for it’s a rule of mine that, if you have an idea, you should carry it through and keep it up—I don’t know whether you agree—”

I said that I certainly did.

“—At the back, there’s a pig, and fowls and rabbits. Then I put together my own little frame, you see, and grow cucumbers; and at supper you’ll judge what kind of salad I can produce. So, sir,” said Wemmick, smiling again, though seriously as well, while shaking his head, “if you can imagine this little place under siege, it could hold out a devilishly long time for provisions.”

Then he led me to a bower about twelve yards away, though the path wound about so cleverly that it took a long time to reach it. In this retreat, our glasses had already been set out. “Charles Evrémonde, known as Darnay,” was finally brought to trial.

His judges sat on the Bench wearing feathered hats, though rough red caps and tricoloured cockades were the usual dress elsewhere. Looking at the Jury and the wild crowd, he might have believed that the natural order had been turned upside down, and that criminals were judging honest men. The lowest, most cruel, and worst part of the city’s population—though every city has some such people—controlled the scene. They shouted comments, approval, and disapproval, guessed at the verdict, and pushed it forward without restraint. Most of the men carried weapons of one kind or another. Some women wore knives or daggers; some ate and drank while they watched; many knitted. Among the knitters was a woman working with an extra piece of knitting tucked beneath her arm. She sat in the front row beside a man Darnay had not seen since arriving at the Barrier, but whom he immediately recognized as Defarge. Once or twice she whispered in his ear, and she appeared to be his wife. Yet what Darnay noticed most was that, though they sat as near to him as possible, neither of them ever looked at him. They seemed to be waiting stubbornly for something, watching the Jury and nothing else. Below the President sat Doctor Manette, dressed as quietly as usual. As far as the prisoner could tell, he and Mr. Lorry were the only men there unconnected with the Tribunal who still wore their ordinary clothes instead of the rough Carmagnole dress.

Charles Evrémonde, called Darnay, was charged by the public prosecutor as an emigrant whose life was owed to the Republic under the decree that banished all emigrants under penalty of death. It did not matter that the decree had been dated after his return to France. He was there, and so was the decree; he had been arrested in France, and the crowd demanded his head.

“Take off his head!” cried the audience. “An enemy of the Republic!”

The President rang his bell to silence them and asked the prisoner whether it was not true that he had lived in England for many years.

It certainly was true.

Then was he not an emigrant? What else could he call himself?

He hoped he was not an emigrant in the meaning and spirit of the law.

Why not? the President asked.

Because he had willingly given up a title he disliked and a position he disliked, and had left his country—before, he submitted, the word emigrant had acquired the meaning now used by the Tribunal—to earn his own living in England rather than live on the labour of the overburdened people of France.

My heart was pounding, and I felt afraid without knowing why. I sent the servant away, locked my door, and sat down to read my father’s letter. These were its words.

“My dear Child,

“I have betrayed your trust. I have tried to corrupt your mind and have made your innocent heart aware of the looks and words of forbidden, monstrous passion. I must pay for these crimes and try, in some measure, to make my punishment fit my guilt. You are, I do not doubt, prepared for what I am about to tell you: we must part and be separated forever.

“I take from you your parent and only friend. You are thrown out into the world without shelter; your hopes are ruined; the peace and safety of your pure mind are destroyed. Memory will bring you terrible images of guilt and the pain of innocent love betrayed. Yet I, who bring all this misery upon you; I, who cast you out and cruelly set the mark of distrust and agony upon the heart and face of my own child; I, who with devilish carelessness tried to steal away her beauty and replace it with the ugly deformity of sin—I, in the overflowing anguish of my heart, beg you to forgive me.

“I do not ask for your pity; you must, and do, hate me. But forgive me, Mathilda, and do not let your thoughts follow me into exile with unending anger. I must never see you again, never hear your voice again; but the gentle whisper of your forgiveness will reach me and cool the burning of my troubled mind and heart. I am sure I would feel it even in my grave. And I dare support this request by telling you how miserably I was drawn into this trap of fiery anguish, and of all my struggles to escape it. Indeed, if your soul were less pure and bright, I would not try to excuse myself to you. I would fear that, if I led you to regard me with less horror, you might hate vice less. But when I speak to you, I feel as though I appeal to an angelic judge. I cannot leave without your forgiveness, and I must try to win it, or I must despair. I beg you, therefore, to listen to my words; and if guilt can in any degree be softened by severe suffering and remorse that tears the mind like madness, perhaps you may think—though I do not dare—that I have some claim upon your compassion.

“I beg you to remember our first happy life on the shores of Loch Lomond. I had returned from sixteen years of weary wandering, during which, though I had faced many dangers and misfortunes, my affections had remained entirely blank.

“Oh, your father may let you stay, of course, if your mother can spare you. Daughters are never as important to a father. And if you stay another full month, I could take one of you as far as London, since I am going there for a week early in June. Dawson does not mind riding on the barouche-box, so there would be plenty of room for one of you. Indeed, if the weather is cool, I should not mind taking both of you, since neither of you is large.”

“You are very kind, madam, but I think we must keep to our original plan.”

Lady Catherine appeared to accept this. “Mrs. Collins, you must send a servant with them. Lady Catherine had many more questions about their journey; and because she did not answer all of them herself, Elizabeth had to pay attention. Elizabeth thought this fortunate, for with her mind so occupied, she might otherwise have forgotten where she was. She had to save reflection for the hours when she was alone. Whenever she was by herself, she gave herself up to it as her greatest comfort; and not a day passed without a solitary walk, when she could enjoy all the pleasure of painful memories.

She was soon on the way to knowing Mr. Darcy’s letter by heart. She examined every sentence, and her feelings toward its writer often changed greatly. When she remembered the manner in which he had spoken to her, she was still filled with anger; but when she considered how unfairly she had judged and reproached him, her anger turned against herself, and his disappointed feelings became an object of compassion.

“Why, you can’t mean—” my sister began.

“Yes, I do, Mum,” said Pumblechook; “but hold on a moment. Go on, Joseph. That’s it! Go on!”

“What would the present company say,” Joe continued, “to twenty pounds?”

“Handsome would be the word,” my sister replied.

“Well then,” said Joe, “it’s more than twenty pounds.”

That miserable hypocrite Pumblechook nodded again and said, with a patronizing laugh, “It’s more than that, Mum. Good again! Keep after her, Joseph!”

“Then, to finish it,” said Joe, delightedly handing the bag to my sister, “it’s twenty-five pounds.”

“It’s twenty-five pounds, Mum,” echoed that lowest of swindlers, Pumblechook, getting up to shake hands with her; “and it’s no more than you deserve—as I said when I was asked my opinion—and I wish you joy of the money!”

Had the villain stopped there, his conduct would have been bad enough; but he deepened his guilt by taking me into custody, with an air of authority that made all his earlier crimes seem insignificant.

“Now you see, Joseph and wife,” said Pumblechook, taking me by the arm above the elbow, “I’m one of those who always carry through whatever they begin. This boy must be bound at once. That’s my way. Bound at once.”

“Goodness knows, Uncle Pumblechook,” said my sister, clutching the money, “we’re deeply grateful to you.”

“Never mind me, Mum,” replied that devilish corn merchant. “A pleasure is a pleasure, wherever you are. But this boy, you see—we must have him bound. I said I’d attend to it, to tell you the truth.”

The mental qualities spoken of as analytical are, in themselves, scarcely open to analysis. We estimate them only through their effects. We know, among other things, that, when possessed in excess, they are ever to their owner a source of the keenest pleasure. As the powerful man rejoices in his bodily strength, taking delight in exercises that summon his muscles to action, so does the analyst glory in that moral activity which _unravels._ He finds enjoyment even in the most insignificant pursuits that bring his faculty into exercise. He delights in riddles, conundrums, and hieroglyphics; displaying in his answers to each a degree of _acumen_ that seems to ordinary understanding præternatural. His conclusions, produced by the very spirit and essence of method, possess, indeed, all the appearance of intuition.

The power of re-solution may perhaps be greatly strengthened by mathematical study, and particularly by that loftiest division of it which, unjustly, and solely because of its backward operations, has been termed, as though _par excellence_, analysis. But calculation is not, of itself, analysis. A chess-player, for instance, performs the former without striving after the latter. Hence the influence of chess upon mental character is seriously misconceived. I am not composing a treatise, but merely introducing a somewhat singular narrative with observations thrown out at random; I shall therefore venture to maintain that the higher faculties of the reflective mind are more distinctly and more profitably exercised by the unobtrusive game of draughts than by all the elaborate trifling of chess. In the latter game, where the pieces move in differing and _bizarre_ ways, and bear diverse and shifting values, mere complexity is mistaken—an error by no means uncommon—for profundity. The _attention_ is there strongly summoned into action. Should it falter for a moment, an oversight occurs, bringing loss or defeat. Since the possible moves are not merely numerous but involute, the opportunities for such errors are increased; and in nine instances out of ten, it is the player of greater concentration, rather than greater acuteness, who prevails. In draughts, by contrast, where the moves are _unique_ and admit little variation, the likelihood of inadvertence is reduced; and, attention being comparatively unoccupied, whatever advantages either player gains are gained through superior _acumen_. To make this less abstract, suppose a game of draughts in which the pieces have been reduced to four kings, and in which, naturally, no oversight need be anticipated. It is plain that victory here can be determined, the players being at all equal, only by some _recherché_ move, born of a vigorous exertion of intellect.

‘We have not chosen to live there ourselves,’ said Lord Canterville, ‘ever since my grandaunt, the Dowager Duchess of Bolton, was frightened into a fit, from which she never wholly recovered, when two skeleton hands were laid upon her shoulders as she dressed for dinner; and I feel obliged to inform you, Mr. Otis, that the ghost has been seen by several living members of my family, and also by the rector of the parish, the Rev. Augustus Dampier, a Fellow of King’s College, Cambridge. After the Duchess’s unhappy accident, none of our younger servants would remain with us, and Lady Canterville frequently had scarcely any sleep at night because of the strange sounds that issued from the corridor and the library.’

‘My Lord,’ replied the Minister, ‘I shall take the furniture and the ghost at a valuation. I come from a modern country, where we possess everything money can purchase; and with all our lively young fellows painting the Old World red, and carrying away your finest actresses and prima-donnas, I reckon that, if such a thing as a ghost existed in Europe, we should have one at home very soon, either in one of our public museums or travelling the roads as a show.’

‘I am afraid the ghost does exist,’ said Lord Canterville, smiling, ‘although it may have resisted the offers of your enterprising impresarios. It has been known for three centuries—since 1584, in fact—and invariably appears before the death of any member of our family.’

‘Well, the family doctor does that too, Lord Canterville. But there is no such thing, sir, as a ghost, and I suppose the laws of Nature are not likely to be suspended for the British aristocracy.’

‘You are certainly very natural in America,’ returned Lord Canterville, who did not entirely grasp Mr. Otis’s final remark, ‘and if a ghost in the house does not trouble you, it is all right. Only remember that I warned you.’

Yet those who argued for such a boundary seemed to have overlooked one circumstance. Though it did not positively disprove their belief, it seemed to me a matter deserving serious investigation. When the intervals between Encke’s comet’s successive returns to perihelion are compared, after allowing as exactly as possible for every disturbance caused by the planets’ attraction, the periods appear gradually to shorten. That is, the major axis of the comet’s ellipse is becoming shorter in a slow but perfectly regular way. This is exactly what should happen if the comet met resistance from an extremely thin ethereal medium spread through the regions of its orbit. Such a medium, by slowing the comet’s motion, must increase its centripetal force by weakening its centrifugal force. In other words, the sun’s attraction would steadily gain power, and the comet would be drawn nearer with every revolution. Indeed, there is no other way to explain this variation. Again, the actual diameter of the same comet’s nebulosity is seen to shrink rapidly as it approaches the sun, and to expand equally rapidly as it travels toward its aphelion. Was I not justified, with M. Valz, in supposing that this apparent shrinking in volume came from the compression of the same ethereal medium I have mentioned, which becomes denser only in proportion to its nearness to the sun? The lens-shaped phenomenon called the zodiacal light also deserved attention. This glow, so visible in the tropics and not to be mistaken for any meteoric light, stretches diagonally upward from the horizon and generally follows the direction of the sun’s equator. It seemed clearly to me to be a thin atmosphere extending outward from the sun, at least beyond Venus’s orbit, and, I believed, indefinitely farther. Indeed, I could not suppose this medium was confined either to the comet’s elliptical path or to the sun’s immediate neighborhood.

The Tiber, the road laid out by nature herself across her continent, lay at my feet, and many boats were tied along its banks. With a few books, provisions, and my dog, I would board one of them and drift down the river into the sea. Then, keeping close to shore, I would follow the beautiful coasts and sunny headlands of the blue Mediterranean, pass Naples, sail along Calabria, and dare the twin dangers of Scylla and Charybdis. Then, with a fearless purpose—for what had I to lose?—I would skim over the sea toward Malta and the farther Cyclades. I would avoid Constantinople, for the sight of its familiar towers and inlets belonged to another life, not my present one. I would sail along Asia Minor and Syria, pass the seven mouths of the Nile, and turn north again until, leaving forgotten Carthage and deserted Libya behind, I reached the Pillars of Hercules. And then—wherever it might be—the muddy caves and silent depths of the ocean might become my home before I completed this long voyage; or disease might strike my heart as I floated alone on the rough Mediterranean. Or, at some place where I landed, I might find what I sought: a companion. Or, if that could not be, then through endless years, weak and grey-haired—my youth already buried with those I loved—the lonely wanderer would still raise his sail and grasp the tiller. Still obeying heaven’s winds, forever passing one headland after another, anchoring in one bay after another, still cutting through the barren sea, leaving green native Europe behind, following Africa’s tawny coast, surviving the fierce seas around the Cape, I might moor my worn little boat in a creek shaded by the spice groves of the fragrant islands of the distant Indian Ocean.

These are wild dreams. Yet ever since they came to me a week ago, as I stood on the height of St. Peter’s, they have ruled my imagination. I have chosen my boat and gathered my small supplies. I have selected a few books, chiefly Homer and Shakespeare—but the libraries of the world lie open to me, and in any port I can replace them.
