“You need not trouble yourself. The moral will be entirely proper. Lady Catherine’s unwarrantable attempts to part us were what removed all my doubts. I do not owe my present happiness to your anxious wish to offer your thanks. I was not disposed to wait for an opportunity from you. My aunt’s information had given me hope, and I resolved to learn everything at once.”

“Lady Catherine has been of endless service, which ought to please her, since she delights in being useful. But tell me, what brought you down to Netherfield? Was it only to ride to Longbourn and be embarrassed? or had you planned consequences of a more serious kind?”

“My true object was to see _you_, and to discover, if I could, whether I might ever hope to make you love me. My declared object—or rather, the one I declared to myself—was to learn whether your sister still cared for Bingley, and, if she did, to make to him the confession I have since made.”

“Will you ever have the courage to tell Lady Catherine what is to happen to her?”

“I am more likely to need time than courage, Elizabeth. But it should be done; and if you will give me a sheet of paper, it shall be done immediately.”

“And if I had no letter of my own to write, I might sit beside you and admire the regularity of your hand, as another young lady once did. But I too have an aunt, who must not be neglected any longer.”

Unwilling to admit how greatly her intimacy with Mr. Darcy had been exaggerated, Elizabeth had not yet replied to Mrs. Gardiner’s long letter; but now, having _that_ to tell her which she knew would be most welcome, she was nearly ashamed to think that her uncle and aunt had already been deprived of three days’ happiness, and she immediately wrote as follows:--

“I ought to have thanked you sooner, my dear aunt, for your long, kind, and satisfactory account of every particular; but, to speak honestly, I was too out of humour to write. You imagined more than truly existed. But _now_ imagine as much as you please; let your fancy run free, indulge your imagination in every flight the subject can permit, and unless you suppose me actually married, you cannot be very far wrong.”

“These thoughts soothed me, and that afternoon I fell into a deep sleep; but the fever in my blood would not permit peaceful dreams. The terrible scene of the day before played endlessly before my eyes: the women fleeing, and the furious Felix dragging me away from his father’s feet. I woke exhausted, and, finding that night had already fallen, crept from my hiding place to search for food.

“When I had satisfied my hunger, I made my way along the familiar path leading to the cottage. Everything there was quiet. I slipped into my hovel and waited silently for the usual hour when the family rose. That hour passed; the sun climbed high in the sky, yet the cottagers did not appear. I shook violently, fearing some dreadful disaster. The cottage was dark within, and I heard no movement; I cannot describe the torment of that suspense.

“Soon two countrymen passed by, but they stopped near the cottage and began talking with violent gestures. I could not understand them, for they spoke the language of the country, which differed from that of my protectors. Shortly afterward, however, Felix came toward them with another man. I was astonished, since I knew he had not left the cottage that morning, and I listened anxiously, hoping his words would explain these strange events.

“‘Have you considered,’ his companion said to him, ‘that you will have to pay three months’ rent and lose the produce of your garden? I do not wish to take unfair advantage of you, and so I ask that you take a few days to consider your decision.’

“‘It is completely useless,’ Felix replied. ‘We can never live in your cottage again. My father’s life is in the greatest danger because of the dreadful event I have told you about. My wife and sister will never recover from their horror. I beg you, do not argue with me any longer. Take possession of your house, and let me flee this place.’

“Felix trembled violently as he spoke. He and his companion entered the cottage, remained there a few minutes, and then left. I never saw any member of the De Lacey family again.

“For the rest of the day, I remained in my hovel in a state of blank, senseless despair. My protectors had gone, breaking the only bond that connected me to the world. For the first time, revenge and hatred filled my heart, and I made no effort to restrain them. Letting myself be carried along by that current, I turned my thoughts toward harm and death.”

It is only four o’clock, but it is winter, and the sun has already gone down. No clouds cross the clear, frosty sky to catch its slanting rays; yet the air itself is faintly rose-coloured, and that colour is reflected on the snow covering the ground. I live in an isolated cottage on a broad, lonely heath: no sound of life reaches me. Before me lies the desolate plain, white except for a few black patches made by the midday sun on the tops of those sharp hillocks, where the snow, slipping as it fell, settled less deeply than on the level ground. A few birds peck at the hard ice over the pools—for the frost has lasted long.

I am in a strange state of mind. I am alone—entirely alone—in the world. Misfortune has passed over me like a blight and left me withered. I know I am about to die, and I feel happy—joyful. I feel my pulse; it beats quickly. I lay my thin hand against my cheek; it burns. A slight, swift spirit remains within me, now giving off its final sparks. I will never see the snows of another winter. I truly believe I will never again feel the life-giving warmth of a summer sun; and in that belief I begin to write my tragic history. Perhaps a history like mine should die with me, but some feeling I cannot name urges me onward, and I am too weak in body and mind to resist even the smallest impulse. While life was strong in me, I believed there was a sacred horror in my story that made it unfit to be spoken; now, near death, I profane its mysterious terrors. It is like the grove of the Eumenides: none but the dying may enter it; and Oedipus is about to die.

What am I writing? I must gather my thoughts. I do not know whether anyone will read these pages except you, my friend, who will receive them when I die. I do not address them to you alone, because I would take pleasure in lingering over our friendship in a manner that would be unnecessary if you were the only reader of what I write. Therefore I will tell my story as though I were writing for strangers. You have often asked why I live so alone; why I weep; and, above all, why my silence is so impenetrable and unkind. In life I did not dare; in death I reveal the mystery. Others may turn these pages over carelessly. But to you, Woodville—kind, loving friend—they will be dear: precious remains of a heartbroken girl who, even as she dies, is still warmed by gratitude toward you. Your tears will fall upon the words that record my misfortunes; I know they will. And while I still live, I thank you for your sympathy.

One day, while I was occupied with my books and Mr. Pocket, a note came to me by post, and the very address upon it put me in a great agitation; for although I had never before seen the handwriting, I guessed at once whose hand had written it. It began with no formal salutation—no Dear Mr. Pip, Dear Pip, Dear Sir, or Dear Anything—but was as follows:—

“I am coming to London by the midday coach the day after to-morrow. I believe it was arranged that you were to meet me? In any case, Miss Havisham understands it so, and I write in compliance with that understanding. She sends her regards.

“Yours, ESTELLA.”

Had there been time, I would doubtless have ordered several new suits for the occasion; but there was none, and I had to make do with what I possessed. My appetite disappeared at once, and I had neither quiet nor repose until the day came. Nor did its coming give me either; for I was then more unsettled than before, and began prowling about the coach-office in Wood Street, Cheapside, before the coach had even departed the Blue Boar in our town. Though I knew this quite well, I nevertheless felt it unsafe to allow the coach-office out of my view for more than five minutes together; and, in this unreasonable state, I had completed the first half-hour of a watch that was to last four or five hours when Wemmick encountered me.

“Halloa, Mr. Pip,” he said; “how are you? I should scarcely have supposed this to be _your_ beat.”

I told him that I was waiting to meet someone arriving by coach, and asked after the Castle and the Aged.

“Both flourishing, thankye,” said Wemmick, “and the Aged especially. He’s in wonderful feather. He’ll be eighty-two on his next birthday. I’m thinking of firing eighty-two shots, provided the neighbourhood doesn’t object, and that cannon of mine proves able to bear the strain. But this isn’t London talk. Where do you suppose I’m bound for?”

“To the office?” I said, since he was walking that way.

“The next thing to it,” Wemmick replied. “I’m going to Newgate. We’re engaged in a banker’s-parcel case at present, and I’ve been down the road to take a look at the scene of action, and must now have a word or two with our client.”

“Did your client do the robbery?” I asked.

“Bless your soul and body, no,” Wemmick answered, very dryly. “But he’s charged with it. You or I might be charged with it too. Either of us might be accused of it, you know.”

It was well past noon when he woke. His valet had quietly entered the room several times on tiptoe to see whether he was moving, and had wondered why his young master was sleeping so late. At last the bell rang, and Victor came in softly with a cup of tea and a stack of letters on a small tray of old Sèvres china. He drew back the olive-satin curtains, lined with shining blue silk, that covered the three tall windows.

“Monsieur has slept well this morning,” he said with a smile.

“What time is it, Victor?” Dorian Gray asked sleepily.

“A quarter past one, Monsieur.”

How late it was! He sat up, sipped some tea, and looked through his letters. One was from Lord Henry and had been delivered by hand that morning. He paused for a moment, then set it aside. He opened the others without much interest. They contained the usual cards, dinner invitations, tickets to private exhibitions, charity-concert programmes, and similar things that fashionable young men received every morning during the season. There was a fairly large bill for an engraved silver Louis-Quinze toilet set, which he had not yet dared send to his guardians. They were very old-fashioned people and did not understand that, in this age, useless things are our only necessities. There were also several politely written letters from Jermyn Street moneylenders, offering to lend him any amount at once and at the most reasonable interest rates.

After about ten minutes, he rose and put on an elaborate dressing-gown of cashmere wool embroidered with silk. Then he went into the bathroom, whose floor was paved with onyx. The cool water refreshed him after his long sleep. He seemed to have forgotten everything he had been through. Once or twice, a faint feeling came over him that he had played a part in some strange tragedy, but it had the unreal quality of a dream.

As soon as he was dressed, he went into the library and sat down to a light French breakfast laid out on a small round table near the open window. It was a beautiful day. The warm air seemed full of spice. A bee flew in and buzzed around the blue dragon bowl, filled with sulphur-yellow roses, that stood before him. He felt completely happy.

Then his eyes fell on the screen he had placed before the portrait, and he started.

“Is Monsieur too cold?” his valet asked, setting an omelette on the table. “Shall I close the window?”

Dorian shook his head. “I am not cold,” he murmured.

I uncovered it, and a mild breeze soon blew it into flame. I noticed this too, and fashioned a fan from branches, which stirred the embers whenever they were almost dead. When night returned, I discovered with delight that the fire afforded light as well as warmth, and that this element was of use in preparing my food; for I found that some offals left by the travellers had been roasted, and were far more savoury than the berries I plucked from the trees. I therefore attempted to prepare my food in the same way, laying it upon the glowing embers. The berries, I found, were ruined by the process, while the nuts and roots were greatly improved.

“Food, nevertheless, grew scarce, and I frequently spent an entire day seeking fruitlessly for a few acorns to relieve the pains of hunger. When I perceived this, I determined to leave the place I had until then inhabited, and search for another where the few wants I felt might be more readily supplied. In this removal I deeply regretted losing the fire I had gained by chance and did not know how to renew. I devoted several hours to earnest reflection on this difficulty, but was compelled to abandon every effort to replace it; and, wrapping my cloak about me, I crossed the wood in the direction of the setting sun. I wandered thus for three days, and at last came upon open country. A heavy snow had fallen during the preceding night, and the fields lay in a single expanse of white; the prospect was dreary, and my feet were numbed by the cold, wet substance covering the earth.

“It was near seven in the morning, and I eagerly desired food and shelter. At last I saw a little hut upon rising ground, doubtless erected for the use of some shepherd. It was a sight unfamiliar to me, and I inspected its construction with intense curiosity. Seeing the door open, I went inside. An old man sat there beside a fire, over which he was making his breakfast. At the sound I made, he turned; on seeing me, he gave a loud cry and, leaving the hut, fled across the fields with a swiftness his feeble body scarcely seemed able to possess. His appearance, unlike any I had previously beheld, and his flight, surprised me somewhat. Yet I was charmed by the hut itself: snow and rain could not enter there; the floor was dry; and at that moment it seemed to me as exquisite and heavenly a refuge as Pandæmonium had appeared to the dæmons of hell after their torments in the lake of fire.

While these events were taking place in the country workhouse, Mr. Fagin sat in the old den—the very one from which the girl had taken Oliver—brooding beside a dim, smoky fire. A pair of bellows lay across his knee, and he had apparently been trying to stir the fire into a brighter blaze; but he had sunk into deep thought. With his arms folded over them and his chin resting on his thumbs, he stared absently at the rusty grate.

At a table behind him sat the Artful Dodger, Master Charles Bates, and Mr. Chitling, all absorbed in a game of whist. The Artful played dummy against Master Bates and Mr. Chitling. That gentleman’s face, always unusually sharp and intelligent, gained fresh interest from the close attention he gave the game and the careful study he made of Mr. Chitling’s hand. From time to time, whenever opportunity allowed, he cast it a number of earnest looks, wisely adjusting his own play according to what he observed in his neighbour’s cards. Since it was a cold night, the Dodger wore his hat, as he often did indoors. He also kept a clay pipe between his teeth, removing it only briefly when he thought it necessary to refresh himself from the quart pot on the table, filled and ready with gin and water for the company’s use.

Master Bates, too, watched the game closely; but being more excitable than his accomplished friend, he turned more often to the gin and water, and also gave way to many jokes and irrelevant comments, all quite unsuitable to a serious rubber. Indeed, the Artful, relying on their close friendship, more than once solemnly lectured his companion on these improprieties. Master Bates took every rebuke in excellent humour, merely asking his friend to be “blowed,” or to put his head in a sack, or answering with some other neatly phrased joke of the same sort, whose aptness greatly impressed Mr. Chitling. It was remarkable that Mr. Chitling and his partner always lost; and that, instead of irritating Master Bates, this seemed to amuse him enormously. At the end of every deal he laughed uproariously and declared he had never seen such a jolly game in all his life.

“That’s two doubles and the rub,” said Mr. Chitling, looking very miserable as he pulled a half-crown from his waistcoat pocket. “I never saw such a fellow as you, Jack; you win everything.”

Madame and Mademoiselle L’Espanaye were not killed by spirits. Their killers were physical beings, and they escaped by physical means. But how? Fortunately, there is only one way to reason about this question, and it must bring us to a clear answer. Let us consider, one by one, every possible way out. Clearly, when the group came up the stairs, the murderers were in the room where Mademoiselle L’Espanaye was found, or at least in the adjoining room. Therefore, we need look for exits only from these two rooms. The police had stripped open the floors, ceilings, and wall masonry in every direction. No hidden passage could have escaped their attention. Still, I did not rely on their eyes alone, and examined them myself. There were no hidden exits. Both doors from the rooms into the passage were firmly locked, with the keys on the inside. Let us consider the chimneys. Though they were of normal width for eight or ten feet above the fireplaces, they would not allow the body of even a large cat to pass through their full length. Since escape by the means already mentioned is absolutely impossible, we are left with the windows. No one could have escaped through those in the front room without being seen by the crowd in the street. The murderers must therefore have gone through the windows of the back room. Having reached this conclusion so clearly, we must not reject it merely because it seems impossible. We need only prove that these seeming impossibilities are not truly impossible.

“There are two windows in the chamber. One is not blocked by furniture and can be seen completely. The lower part of the other is hidden by the headboard of the heavy bed, which has been pushed close against it. The first was found securely fastened from within. It resisted every effort to raise it. A large hole had been bored into its frame on the left, and a very strong nail had been driven into it almost to the head. On examining the other window, a similar nail was found in the same way; and a forceful attempt to raise that sash also failed. The police were then fully convinced that no escape had occurred through these windows. Therefore, they considered it unnecessary to remove the nails and open them.

“My own examination was more careful, for the reason I have just stated: I knew that here all apparent impossibilities had to be shown not to be impossible in fact.

Wake up after a while, and look around to find what caused it, and maybe spot a steamboat puffing up-stream, so far over toward the other shore you couldn’t make out anything about her except whether she was stern-wheel or side-wheel; then for maybe an hour there wouldn’t be a sound nor a sight—nothing but downright lonesomeness. By-and-by you’d see a raft drifting past, way off yonder, and perhaps some galoot aboard chopping wood, because they’re nearly always at it on a raft; you’d watch the axe gleam and fall—you don’t hear a thing; you see that axe rise again, and when it gets above the man’s head you hear the _k’chunk!_—it had taken all that while to travel across the water. That was how we spent the day, loafing about and hearkening to the quiet. Once there came a heavy fog, and the rafts and such things passing by were banging tin pans so the steamboats wouldn’t run them down. A scow or raft passed so near that we could hear them talking, swearing, and laughing—hear them clear enough; but we couldn’t see the least sign of them; it gave you a creepy feeling; it was like spirits making merry in the air. Jim said he reckoned they were spirits; but I said:

“No; spirits wouldn’t say, ‘Dern this dern fog.’”

As soon as night came on, we shoved off; once we had her about midstream, we left her be and let her drift wherever the current chose to carry her; then we lighted our pipes, hung our legs in the water, and talked of every sort of thing—we went naked all the time, day and night, whenever the mosquitoes allowed it—the new clothes Buck’s people had made me were too fine to feel easy in, and anyhow I never cared much for clothes.

Sometimes we had that whole river to ourselves for a mighty long spell. There were the banks and islands yonder, across the water; and maybe a spark—which was a candle shining in a cabin window; and sometimes you could see one or two sparks out on the water—on a raft or scow, you know; and perhaps hear a fiddle or a song floating over from one of those crafts. It is lovely living on a raft. Above us was the sky, all sprinkled with stars, and we used to lie on our backs looking at them, and argue whether they had been made or had merely happened. Jim allowed they were made, but I allowed they happened; I reckoned it would have taken too long to _make_ so many.

And I call upon you, spirits of the dead, and you, wandering agents of vengeance, to help and guide me in my task. Let the cursed monster from hell drink deeply of suffering; let him know the despair that now tortures me.”

I began this appeal with such solemnity and awe that I almost believed the spirits of my murdered friends heard and approved my devotion. But as I finished, fury took hold of me, and rage choked off my words.

The silence of the night was answered by a loud, devilish laugh. It sounded in my ears, long and heavy; the mountains echoed it, and I felt as though all hell had surrounded me with scorn and laughter. Surely, at that moment, I would have gone mad and destroyed my wretched life, if my vow had not been heard and I had not been kept alive for vengeance. The laughter faded, and then a familiar, hated voice, seeming to speak close beside my ear, whispered clearly, “I am satisfied, miserable wretch! You have chosen to live, and I am satisfied.”

I rushed toward the place where the sound had come from, but the devil escaped my grasp. Suddenly, the broad moon rose and shone fully on his ghastly, twisted form as he fled with speed beyond that of any human being.

I chased him, and for many months this has been my work. Following a faint clue, I traced the winding course of the Rhone, but without success. Then the blue Mediterranean came into view, and by strange chance I saw the fiend enter a ship at night and hide aboard it; it was bound for the Black Sea. I booked passage on the same vessel, but he escaped, though I do not know how.

Through the wild regions of Tartary and Russia, though he continued to avoid me, I have always followed his trail. Sometimes peasants, frightened by this horrible figure, told me which way he had gone. At other times he himself, fearing that I would lose every trace of him, despair, and die, left some sign to lead me onward. Snow fell upon my head, and I saw the marks of his enormous footsteps across the white plain. You, just beginning life, for whom worry is new and suffering unknown—how can you understand what I have felt, and still feel? Cold, hunger, and exhaustion were the smallest pains I was meant to endure. Some devil had cursed me, and I carried my own eternal hell within me. Yet a good spirit still followed and guided my steps, and when I complained most bitterly, it would suddenly free me from difficulties that seemed impossible to overcome. Sometimes, when hunger had overcome nature and I collapsed from exhaustion, a meal was prepared for me in the wilderness, restoring my strength and courage.

But in that bitter attack on Chantilly, published in yesterday’s ‘Musée,’ the satirist made some shameful references to the cobbler’s change of name when he became an actor, and quoted a Latin line we had often discussed. I mean the line

Perdidit antiquum litera prima sonum.

“I had told you that it referred to Orion, once spelled Urion; and because of certain pointed details connected with that explanation, I knew you could not have forgotten it. It was clear, then, that you would connect the two ideas of Orion and Chantilly. I saw that you had done so by the kind of smile that crossed your lips. You thought of the poor cobbler’s sacrifice. Until then, you had been walking with a stoop; but now I saw you straighten yourself to your full height. I was then certain that you were thinking of Chantilly’s small size. At that moment I broke into your thoughts by saying that, since Chantilly was in fact such a little fellow, he would be better suited to the Théâtre des Variétés.”

Not long afterward, we were reading an evening edition of the “Gazette des Tribunaux” when the following paragraphs caught our attention.

“Extraordinary Murders.—This morning, at about three o’clock, the residents of the Quartier St. Roch were awakened by a series of terrible screams, apparently coming from the fourth floor of a house in the Rue Morgue. The house was known to be occupied only by Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, Mademoiselle Camille L’Espanaye. After some delay, caused by an unsuccessful attempt to gain entry in the usual way, the gate was forced open with a crowbar, and eight or ten neighbors entered with two gendarmes. By then the cries had stopped; but as the group rushed up the first flight of stairs, they heard two or more harsh voices arguing angrily, apparently from the upper part of the house. When they reached the second landing, these sounds had also stopped, and all was completely quiet. The group separated and hurried from room to room. On reaching a large rear chamber on the fourth floor—the door was locked, with the key inside, and had to be forced open—they found a sight that filled everyone present with both horror and astonishment.

“The room was in complete disorder. Furniture had been broken and scattered in every direction. There was only one bedstead, and its bed had been removed and thrown into the middle of the floor. On a chair lay a razor, smeared with blood.

Raymond paced angrily up and down the room. I stood prepared to hear and answer his accusations. Adrian leaned against the wall. “This is utterly absurd,” he cried. “If you were schoolboys, you could not behave more foolishly.”

“You do not understand,” said Raymond. “This is only one part of a system—a plan of tyranny to which I will never submit. Because I am Protector of England, must I be the only slave in its empire? Is my privacy to be invaded, my actions criticized, my friends insulted? But I will cast off the whole thing at once.—Be my witnesses.” He took the star, the badge of his office, from his breast and threw it onto the table. “I give up my office; I surrender my power—let whoever wishes take it!”

“Let him take it,” exclaimed Adrian, “who can call himself, or whom the world can call, your superior. No man in England has such arrogance. Know yourself, Raymond, and your anger will fade; your confidence will return. A few months ago, whenever we prayed for the prosperity of our country or ourselves, we also prayed for the life and welfare of the Protector, knowing it was inseparably joined to our own. Your time was devoted to our good; your ambition was to win our praise. You adorned our towns with buildings, gave us useful institutions, and made the land richly fertile. The powerful and unjust trembled before your court, while the poor and oppressed rose like flowers awakened by morning beneath the sunshine of your protection.

“Can you wonder that we are shocked and grieve when this seems to have changed? But come, this bitter mood has already passed. Resume your duties; your supporters will welcome you, your enemies will be silenced, and our love, honour, and duty will again be shown to you. Master yourself, Raymond, and the world is subject to you.”

“All this would be very sensible if you said it to someone else,” Raymond replied gloomily. “Learn the lesson yourself, and you, the first peer of the land, may become its ruler. You—the good, wise, and just—may govern every heart. But I see, too soon for my own happiness and too late for England’s good, that I took on a task beyond my strength. I cannot govern myself. My passions rule me; my smallest impulse is my tyrant. Do you think I gave up the Protectorate—and I have given it up—in a moment of anger? By the living God, I swear I will never take up that trinket again; never again burden myself with the weight of care and misery of which it is the visible sign.”

The next day, the ghost was very weak and exhausted. The terrible strain of the past four weeks was beginning to tell on him. His nerves were completely shattered, and he jumped at the slightest sound. For five days he stayed in his room, and finally decided to abandon the matter of the bloodstain on the library floor. If the Otis family did not want it, they plainly did not deserve it. They were clearly people on a low, material level of existence, quite unable to appreciate the symbolic value of sensory phenomena. The matter of ghostly appearances and the development of astral bodies was, of course, entirely different, and not really under his control. It was his solemn duty to appear in the corridor once a week, and to gibber from the large oriel window on the first and third Wednesday of every month, and he could not see how he could honorably avoid these obligations. It was true that he had led a very wicked life, but on the other hand, he was extremely conscientious in everything connected with the supernatural. For the next three Saturdays, therefore, he walked the corridor as usual between midnight and three o’clock, taking every possible care not to be heard or seen. He took off his boots, stepped as lightly as he could over the old worm-eaten boards, wore a large black velvet cloak, and made sure to use the Rising Sun Lubricator to oil his chains. I must admit that he found it rather difficult to bring himself to adopt this final precaution. Still, one night, while the family was at dinner, he slipped into Mr. Otis’s bedroom and took the bottle. At first he felt somewhat humiliated, but afterward he was sensible enough to recognize that the invention had much to recommend it and, to some extent, served his purpose. Yet despite everything, he was not left alone. Strings were constantly stretched across the corridor, and he tripped over them in the dark; and on one occasion, dressed as ‘Black Isaac, or the Huntsman of Hogley Woods,’ he fell badly after stepping on a butter-slide the twins had built from the entrance of the Tapestry Chamber to the top of the oak staircase. This final insult enraged him so much that he resolved to make one last effort to assert his dignity and social standing. The following night, he decided to visit the insolent young Etonians in his famous role of ‘Reckless Rupert, or the Headless Earl.’

He had not appeared in that costume for more than seventy years—indeed, not since he had frightened pretty Lady Barbara Modish so badly with it that she abruptly ended her engagement to the present Lord Canterville’s grandfather and ran away to Gretna Green with handsome Jack Castleton. She declared that nothing in the world could persuade her to marry into a family that allowed such a dreadful phantom to pace up and down the terrace at twilight.

Well, three or four months passed by, and it was deep winter now. I had gone to school nearly all the time and could spell, read, and write a little, and could recite the multiplication table as far as six times seven is thirty-five, and I don’t reckon I could ever get beyond that if I lived forever. I don’t put much faith in mathematics, anyhow.

At first I hated school, but after a while I got where I could bear it. Whenever I got especially tired of it I played hookey, and the whipping I got the next day did me good and brightened me up. So the longer I attended school, the easier it became. I was getting somewhat accustomed to the widow’s ways, too, and they weren’t so hard on me. Living in a house and sleeping in a bed cramped me pretty badly most of the time, but before cold weather came I used to slip out and sleep in the woods now and then, and that rested me. I liked the old ways best, but I was beginning to like the new ones too, a little. The widow said I was improving slowly but surely, and doing very satisfactory. She said she wasn’t ashamed of me.

One morning at breakfast I happened to upset the salt-cellar. I grabbed for some salt as fast as I could, to toss over my left shoulder and ward off the bad luck, but Miss Watson got there before me and stopped me. She says, “Take your hands away, Huckleberry; what a mess you are forever making!” The widow spoke up kindly for me, but that wasn’t going to turn away the bad luck; I knew that well enough. After breakfast I set out feeling troubled and unsteady, wondering where it would strike me and what it would be. There are ways to prevent certain kinds of bad luck, but this wasn’t one of those kinds; so I didn’t try anything, but merely went along low in spirits and keeping watch.

By skill, I mean perfection in the game, including an understanding of every source from which a fair advantage may be gained. These sources are not merely numerous but varied, and often lie in corners of thought entirely beyond the reach of ordinary understanding. Silently, he makes countless observations and deductions. His companions may do the same; yet the difference in the amount of information gained lies less in whether their deductions are sound than in the quality of what they observe. The essential knowledge is knowing what to observe. Our player limits himself in no way; nor, simply because the game is his object, does he reject conclusions drawn from things outside the game. He studies his partner's face, carefully comparing it with those of each opponent. He watches how the cards are arranged in every hand, often counting trump after trump and honor after honor from the glances their holders give them. He notices every change of expression as play continues, gathering material for thought from signs of certainty, surprise, triumph, or disappointment. From the way a trick is gathered up, he judges whether the person who takes it can win another in that suit. He recognizes a card played as a feint by the manner in which it is thrown onto the table. I told him my brother and I had been over on Spanish Island hunting yesterday afternoon, and had camped on a bit of raft we found; and about midnight he must have kicked his gun in his sleep, because it went off and shot him in the leg. We wanted him to come over and mend it, and not say anything about it or let anybody know, because we meant to get home this evening and surprise the folks.

“Who are your folks?” he says.

“The Phelpses, down yonder.”

“Oh,” he says. Then, after a minute, he says:

“How did you say he got shot?”

“He dreamed,” I says, “and it shot him.”

“An uncommon dream,” he says.

Then he lit his lantern, took up his saddle-bags, and we set out. But when he saw the canoe he didn’t fancy the looks of her—said she was large enough for one, but not very safe-looking for two. I says:

“Oh, you needn’t be scared, sir; she carried all three of us easy enough.”

“What three?”

“Why, me and Sid, and—and—and the guns; that’s what I mean.”

“Oh,” he says.

But he put his foot on the gunnel and rocked her, shook his head, and said he reckoned he would look about for a larger one. But every one was locked and chained; so he took my canoe, and told me to wait until he came back, or hunt around some more, or perhaps I had better go down home and get things ready for the surprise, if I wanted. But I said I didn’t; so I told him exactly how to find the raft, and off he went.

Pretty soon an idea came to me. I says to myself, s’pose he can’t mend that leg in three shakes of a sheep’s tail, as the saying goes? S’pose it takes three or four days? What are we going to do—hang around there until he lets the cat out of the bag? No, sir; I know what I’ll do. I’ll wait, and when he comes back, if he says he has to go again, I’ll get down there too, if I have to swim; and we’ll tie him up, keep him, and push off down the river. And when Tom is through with him, we’ll give him what it’s worth, or everything we have, and then let him go ashore.

So I crawled into a lumber-pile to sleep; and the next time I woke, the sun was high over my head! I jumped out and hurried to the doctor’s house, but they said he had gone away sometime in the night, and hadn’t come back yet.

Emma Woodhouse—beautiful, intelligent, and wealthy, with a comfortable home and a cheerful nature—seemed to possess many of life’s greatest advantages. She had lived almost twenty-one years with very little to trouble or annoy her.

She was the younger of two daughters of a deeply affectionate, indulgent father, and, after her sister married, had become the mistress of his household at a very early age. Her mother had died too long before for Emma to remember more than vaguely her affection; her place had been filled by an excellent governess, whose love had come very close to that of a mother.

Miss Taylor had been with Mr. Woodhouse’s family for sixteen years, more as a friend than a governess. She was very fond of both daughters, but especially of Emma. Their relationship was more like that of sisters. Even before Miss Taylor gave up the formal position of governess, her gentle nature had scarcely permitted her to exercise restraint; and now that even the appearance of authority had long disappeared, they lived together as devoted friends. Emma did exactly as she pleased, valuing Miss Taylor’s judgment greatly, but guided chiefly by her own.

The true drawbacks of Emma’s position were that she had rather too much her own way and was inclined to think a little too highly of herself. These were the faults that threatened to spoil her many pleasures. Yet the danger was so unnoticed at present that she did not consider them misfortunes at all.

Sorrow came—a mild sorrow, but not in the form of any unpleasant self-awareness. Miss Taylor married. It was the loss of Miss Taylor that first brought Emma grief. On the wedding day of this beloved friend, Emma first sat in lasting sadness. Once the wedding was over and the bridal party had gone, she and her father were left to dine alone, with no third person to brighten the long evening ahead. As usual, her father settled himself to sleep after dinner, and she had nothing to do but sit and think about what she had lost.

The marriage promised every happiness for her friend. Mr. Weston was a man of flawless character, comfortable means, suitable age, and agreeable manners. Emma found some comfort in remembering the selfless, generous friendship with which she had always wished for and encouraged the match; but for her it was a dark day’s work. She would feel Miss Taylor’s absence every hour of every day. She remembered all her past kindness—sixteen years of kindness and affection—how Miss Taylor had taught her and played with her since she was five years old, devoted all her abilities to winning and entertaining her when she was well, and nursed her through the many illnesses of childhood.

“That’s how I am, every time,” I said. “But maybe his claim isn’t worth any more than that, if he’ll sell it so cheap. Maybe something’s not right about it.”

“But it is, though—straight as a string. I saw the handbill myself. It tells all about him exactly—describes him like a picture, and names the plantation he came from, below New Orleans. No sir, there’s no trouble with that deal, you can bet on it. Say, give me a chew of tobacco, will you?”

I didn’t have any, so he left. I went to the raft and sat down in the wigwam to think. But I couldn’t come up with anything. I thought until my head ached, but I couldn’t see any way out of the trouble. After that long journey, and after all we’d done for those scoundrels, it had all come to nothing—everything smashed up and ruined—because they could bring themselves to play such a trick on Jim, making him a slave again for the rest of his life, among strangers too, for forty filthy dollars.

At one point I told myself it would be a thousand times better for Jim to be a slave at home, where his family was, if he had to be a slave at all; so I ought to write Tom Sawyer and tell him to tell Miss Watson where Jim was. But I soon gave up that idea for two reasons: she’d be angry and disgusted at his wickedness and ingratitude in running away from her, and she’d sell him straight down the river again; and if she didn’t, everybody naturally despises an ungrateful Black man, and they’d make Jim feel it all the time, so he’d feel miserable and disgraced. And then there was me! Word would get around that Huck Finn had helped a Black man get his freedom; and if I ever saw anybody from that town again, I’d be ready to kneel down and lick his boots from shame. That’s how it is: a person does something low-down, then doesn’t want to face the consequences. He thinks that as long as he can hide it, it isn’t disgraceful. That was exactly my situation. The more I thought about it, the more my conscience ground away at me, and the more wicked, low-down, and miserable I felt.

“But when I beheld you become the object of another’s love; when I conceived that you might be loved in any manner save as a sacred emblem and image of beauty and virtue; or that you might love another with an affection more fervent than that which you felt for me, then the fiend within me stirred; I sent away your lover; and from that hour I have known no tranquillity. I have vainly pursued sleep and repose; my eyelids would not shut, and my blood was ever in commotion. I rose into a new existence, as one dying in hope might awaken in Hell. I will not stain your fancy by relating my struggles, my wrath against myself, and my despair. Let a curtain fall over the inconceivable feelings of a guilty father; the mysteries of a heart so tortured must not be made common. All was tumult, crime, remorse, and hatred, yet still the most tender love; and what first roused me to the fixed purpose of mastering my passion and restoring her father to my child was the sight of your sorrowful and compassionate grief. This brought me hither: I believed that, if I could revive in my heart the sorrow I had endured at your mother’s loss, and the many associations of her memory that had slept for seventeen years, all love for her child would perish. In a moment of heroism I resolved to depart alone; to leave you, the life of my life, and not behold you again until I could do so without guilt. But it could not be: I had valued my strength too highly, or my love too lightly. I must surely have died had you not come swiftly to me. Would that I had truly been extinguished!

The sight of this house, these fields and woods where my first love dwelt appears to have increased it: in my madness I ventured to tell myself—Diana died in giving her birth; her mother’s spirit passed into her form, and she should be Diana to me. With every endeavour to reject it, this love fastens itself more closely, this guilty love, more unnatural than hatred, which blights your hopes and ruins me for ever.

Better to have loved despair, & safer to have kissed her.

Neither time nor distance can rend from my soul that which is a portion of it. Since I came here, I have not for one instant ceased to feel the hell of passion planted within me, to burn until all is cold, and rigid, and dead.

I now turn to my own history. Of the first years of my life there is little to tell, and I shall be short; yet I must be permitted to linger somewhat over my childhood, that it may be seen how, when one hope was lost, all life became a void; and how, when the sole affection I was allowed to cherish was destroyed, my being perished with it.

I have said that my aunt differed greatly from my father. I think that, without the least stain of an evil heart, she possessed the coldest heart that ever inhabited a human breast: it was wholly incapable of affection. She received me into her care because she deemed it her duty; but she had lived too long alone, untroubled by the clamour and chatter of children, to permit me to interrupt her repose. She had never married; and during the preceding five years had lived entirely alone upon an estate which had come to her through her mother, on the banks of Loch Lomond in Scotland. In his letters my father had wished that she would live with me at his family seat, situated in a lovely district near Richmond in Yorkshire. She refused this proposal; but, as soon as she had settled the matters which her brother’s departure had left in her charge, she left England and carried me with her to her Scottish estate.

The charge of me in infancy, and afterwards until I had completed my eighth year, fell upon one of my mother’s servants, who had accompanied us into retirement for that end. I was lodged in a distant part of the house, and saw my aunt only at appointed times. These came twice each day: about noon she visited my nursery, and after dinner I was brought to her. She never fondled me, and throughout my stay in the room appeared afraid that some childish prank might vex her. My kind nurse always instructed me most carefully before she dared enter the parlour—and the dread inspired by my aunt’s chilly looks and few forced words was so strong that I rarely dishonoured her teaching, or departed from the model quietness I had been taught to maintain during these brief calls.

Beneath my good nurse’s care I roamed freely through our park and the adjoining fields. The child of the deepest love, I showed from my earliest years the greatest tenderness of feeling. I cannot describe the ardour with which I loved everything, even the lifeless things around me.

Elizabeth was sorrowful and hopeless; she no longer found pleasure in her usual activities. Any enjoyment seemed to her a betrayal of the dead; she believed that endless grief and tears were the proper tribute she owed to innocence so cruelly ruined and destroyed. She was no longer the happy girl who, in our younger days, had walked with me along the lake shore and spoken with delight of our hopes for the future. The first of those sorrows that come to detach us from the world had fallen upon her, and its shadow had extinguished her sweetest smiles.

“When I think, my dear cousin,” she said, “of the terrible death of Justine Moritz, I can no longer see the world and all that happens in it as I once did. Before, the stories of vice and injustice I read in books or heard from others seemed like accounts from ancient times or imagined evils; at least, they were distant, and more familiar to reason than to imagination. But now misery has come into my own home, and people seem to me like monsters thirsting for one another’s blood. Yet I am surely being unfair. Everyone believed that poor girl guilty; and if she had truly committed the crime for which she suffered, she would certainly have been among the most depraved of human beings. For the sake of a few jewels, to murder the son of her benefactor and friend—a child she had cared for from birth, and seemed to love as though he were her own! I could never agree to the death of any human being, but I would certainly have thought such a person unfit to remain among mankind. But she was innocent. I know it; I feel that she was innocent. You believe so too, and that strengthens my conviction. Alas, Victor, when lies can resemble truth so closely, who can be certain of happiness? I feel as though I am walking along the edge of a precipice, while thousands press around me, trying to force me into the abyss. William and Justine were murdered, and the murderer escapes; he walks freely through the world, perhaps even respected. But even if I were sentenced to suffer on the scaffold for the same crimes, I would not exchange places with such a wretch.”

I listened to her words in the deepest agony. Though not by my own hand, I was in truth the real murderer. Elizabeth saw my anguish in my face and, gently taking my hand, said, “My dearest friend, you must compose yourself. These events have affected me—God knows how deeply—but I am not as miserable as you are.”

“Mark my words; I have mastered the language of despair: I know it all by heart, for I am Despair; and a strange creature am I, glad, victorious Despair. Yet those words are untrue, for though the wave may be dark, it is not bitter. We lie down and shut our eyes with a quiet good night, and when we awaken, we are free. Come then, delay no longer, thou lingering one! See the welcome draught! Behold, I am a spirit of good, not a human maiden who invites thee, and in persuasive tones, (oh, that they might persuade thee!) cries, Come and drink.”

While I spoke, I kept my gaze upon his face; and his perfect beauty, the divine compassion shining from his eyes, his mild but earnest expression of remonstrance and astonishment, even before he answered, changed my overwrought feelings, stripping away all the harshness of despair and leaving me only the gentlest sorrow. I saw that his eyes too were moist as he took both my hands in his; then, seating himself beside me, he said:

“This is a mournful act to which you would draw me, dearest friend, and your misery must truly be profound to have filled you with such unhappy thoughts. You desire death, yet fear it, and would have me share it with you. But I possess less courage than you, and even with such companionship I do not dare to die. Hear me, and then consider whether you should seek to win me to your design, even if, by the commanding eloquence of despair, you could render black death so alluring that bright heaven itself would seem dark. Listen, I beseech you, to one who has himself cherished desperate thoughts and yearned impatiently for death, but who at last has trodden the phantom beneath his feet and broken its sting. Come; as you have acted Despair toward me, I will perform Una’s part toward you, and lead you unharmed from his gloomy cave. Listen to me, and let yourself be moved by words in which no selfish passion remains.

“We do not know the meaning of this vast world, with its strange mingling of good and evil. Yet we have been set here and commanded to live and hope. I do not know for what we are to hope; but some good lies beyond us which we must pursue, and that is our task on earth. If misfortune assails us, we must struggle against her; we must thrust her away, and still proceed to discover that which our nature bids us desire. Whether this promise of future good prepares us for another life, I cannot tell; or whether it is only that we, as labourers in God’s vineyard, must help to make the path smoother for those who come after us.

Even now, I had not drained the bitter cup to its dregs; I was not yet convinced of my loss. I did not yet feel, in every heartbeat, every nerve, every thought, that I alone remained of my kind—that I was the LAST MAN.

The day grew overcast, and a fine rain began at sunset. Even the everlasting heavens weep, I thought; is there any shame, then, in mortal man pouring himself out in tears? I recalled the old fables in which people are said to melt away through weeping, becoming fountains that flow forever. Ah, if only it were so; then my fate would in some way resemble the watery deaths of Adrian and Clara. Oh, grief is fantastical; it spins a web upon which it traces the story of its suffering from every shape and alteration around it. It joins itself to all living nature; it draws nourishment from every object. Like light, it fills everything, and, like light, gives all things its own colors.

In my search I had wandered some distance from the place where I had been thrown ashore, and reached one of those watchtowers that stand at regular intervals along the Italian coast. I welcomed the shelter, welcomed finding something made by human hands after looking so long upon nature's bleak emptiness. I went inside and climbed the rough, winding stairs to the guardroom. Fate had been kind enough that no painful trace of its former occupants remained. A few boards laid across two iron trestles and scattered with dried Indian-corn leaves formed the bed offered to me; and an open chest containing several half-molded biscuits stirred an appetite that may have existed before, though I had not noticed it until then. Thirst, too—fierce and burning, caused by the seawater I had drunk and by my body's exhaustion—tormented me. Kind nature had made the satisfying of such needs pleasurable, so that I—even I—felt restored and soothed as I ate this miserable food and drank a little sour wine from a flask left half full in the deserted dwelling. Then I lay down upon the bed, which no shipwrecked sufferer could reject. The earthy scent of the dry leaves was balm to me after the hateful smell of seaweed. I forgot my loneliness. I looked neither behind nor ahead; my senses sank into rest. I fell asleep and dreamed of beloved inland scenes: haymakers; a shepherd whistling to his dog when he called for help driving the flock into the fold; sights and sounds belonging to my mountain childhood, long forgotten.

We were raised together, with less than a year between our ages. It hardly needs saying that we knew no quarrels or disagreements. Harmony was the heart of our companionship, and the differences in our characters only brought us closer. Elizabeth was calmer and more thoughtful; but though I was passionate, I could apply myself more intensely and was more deeply driven by a thirst for knowledge. She occupied herself with the airy creations of poets, and in the grand and wonderful scenes around our Swiss home—the towering mountains, the changing seasons, storm and calm, winter's silence, and the life and wildness of our Alpine summers—she found endless cause for admiration and pleasure. While my companion looked upon these magnificent sights with a serious and contented mind, I delighted in seeking their causes. The world seemed to me a secret I longed to understand. Curiosity, eager study of nature's hidden laws, and joy almost like rapture when they were revealed to me are among my earliest memories.

When my second brother was born, seven years younger than I, my parents gave up their wandering life entirely and settled in their native country. We had a house in Geneva and a country home at Belrive, on the eastern shore of the lake, a little more than a league from the city. We lived mainly at the latter, and my parents led fairly secluded lives. By nature, I avoided crowds and attached myself deeply to a few people. I therefore cared little for most of my schoolmates, but formed the closest friendship with one of them. Henry Clerval was the son of a Geneva merchant. He was a boy of unusual talent and imagination. He loved bold undertakings, hardship, and even danger for their own sake. He had read deeply in tales of chivalry and romance. He wrote heroic songs and began many stories of magic and knightly adventure. He tried to persuade us to perform plays and take part in masquerades, with characters drawn from the heroes of Roncesvalles, King Arthur's Round Table, and the chivalrous company who shed their blood to free the holy sepulchre from the hands of the infidels.

No one could have had a happier childhood than I did. My parents were filled with kindness and indulgence. We felt they were not tyrants who ruled our lives according to their whims, but the makers and providers of all the many pleasures we enjoyed.

With this in mind, I saw no reason to burden myself with provisions for more than forty days.

“There was, however, another difficulty that caused me some concern. It has been observed that when balloons rise to great heights, people suffer not only pain in breathing, but severe discomfort in the head and body, often with nosebleeds and other alarming symptoms. These grow worse as the altitude increases. This thought was somewhat frightening. Was it not likely that such symptoms would continue to increase, perhaps ending only in death? In the end, I decided they would not. They arose from the gradual loss of the usual atmospheric pressure on the body’s surface, which caused the small blood vessels to swell—not from any actual breakdown of the body, as happens when breathing becomes difficult because the air is too thin to properly renew the blood in a chamber of the heart. Except for the lack of this renewal, I could see no reason why life could not continue even in a vacuum. The expansion and contraction of the chest, commonly called breathing, is purely a muscular action; it is the cause, not the effect, of respiration. In short, I believed that as the body grew accustomed to the absence of atmospheric pressure, the painful sensations would gradually lessen. While they lasted, I trusted confidently in the iron strength of my constitution.

So that was the story of Dorian Gray’s parents. Though it had been told to him bluntly, it stirred him with the idea of a strange, almost modern romance. A beautiful woman risking everything for a reckless passion. A few wild weeks of happiness ended by a horrible, treacherous crime. Months of silent suffering, and then a child born in pain. The mother taken by death, the boy left alone under the rule of an old man without love. Yes, it was an interesting history. It gave the lad a pose, made him seem more perfect. Behind every beautiful thing, there was something tragic. Worlds had to suffer in labour before even the smallest flower could bloom.... And how charming he had been at dinner the night before, sitting opposite him at the club with startled eyes and lips parted in frightened delight, while the red candle shades deepened the awakening wonder in his face to a richer rose. Talking with him was like playing a fine violin. He responded to every touch and movement of the bow.... There was something deeply captivating in the use of influence. No other activity was like it. To send one’s soul into some graceful form and let it remain there for a moment; to hear one’s own ideas returned with the added music of passion and youth; to pour one’s temperament into another person as if it were a subtle liquid or strange perfume: there was real pleasure in that—perhaps the greatest pleasure left to us in an age as narrow and vulgar as ours, an age crude in its pleasures and crude in its ambitions.... This lad was a marvellous type, too, whom he had met by such a curious chance in Basil’s studio—or who could at least be shaped into one.

As it ran down an alley behind the Rue Morgue, the fugitive noticed a light shining from the open window of Madame L’Espanaye’s fourth-floor chamber. It rushed to the house, saw the lightning rod, and climbed it with unbelievable agility. Grasping the shutter, which stood fully open against the wall, it used it to swing itself directly onto the bed’s headboard. The entire feat took less than a minute. As the Ourang-Outang entered the room, it kicked the shutter open again.

Meanwhile, the sailor was both relieved and confused. He strongly hoped he could now recapture the beast, since it could hardly escape the trap it had entered except by the rod, where he might catch it as it climbed down. But he also had great reason to fear what it might do inside the house. That fear drove him to continue after it. A sailor can climb a lightning rod without much trouble; yet when he reached the height of the window, far to his left, he could go no farther. All he could do was stretch out far enough to glimpse the room inside. At that sight, horror nearly made him lose his grip. Then the terrible screams rose into the night, waking the residents of the Rue Morgue. It stood open, with its contents scattered on the floor beside it. The victims must have been seated with their backs to the window; and, judging by the time between the beast’s entrance and their screams, they probably did not notice it at once. They would naturally have thought the shutter’s closing was caused by the wind.

As the sailor looked in, the huge animal had seized Madame L’Espanaye by her hair, loose because she had been combing it, and was waving the razor around her face, copying the movements of a barber.

Lady Catherine appeared resigned. “Mrs. Collins, you must send a servant with them. Lady Catherine had many more questions about their journey; and because she did not answer all of them herself, attention was required—which Elizabeth thought fortunate for her. Otherwise, with her mind so occupied, she might have forgotten where she was. Reflection had to be saved for hours of solitude: whenever she was alone, she gave herself up to it as her greatest relief; and not a day passed without a solitary walk, during which she could indulge in the full pleasure of painful memories.

He went quickly towards Portland Place, glancing back from time to time as if afraid of pursuit. At the corner of Rich Street, two men were studying a little notice pasted on a hoarding. A strange curiosity seized him, and he crossed the road. As he approached, the word ‘Murder,’ in heavy black type, caught his eye. He recoiled, a dark flush rising in his face. It was a notice offering a reward for information that might lead to the capture of a man of middling height, aged between thirty and forty, dressed in a billy-cock hat, black coat, and checked trousers, and bearing a scar on his right cheek. Again and again he read it, wondering whether the miserable fellow would be taken, and how he had received the scar. Perhaps one day his own name would be posted upon the walls of London. Perhaps, too, a reward would be offered for his head.

The idea turned him faint with terror. He wheeled round and pressed onward through the night.

He scarcely knew where he went. He retained only a vague recollection of roaming amid a maze of shabby houses, of losing himself in an immense network of gloomy streets; and when at last he reached Piccadilly Circus, the dawn was clear and bright. Walking homeward towards Belgrave Square, he encountered the great waggons bound for Covent Garden. The carters in white smocks, their cheerful, sun-browned faces framed by rough curling hair, marched sturdily along, snapping their whips and occasionally shouting to one another; perched on the back of a vast grey horse, leader of a clattering team, was a plump boy with primroses tucked into his battered hat, clutching the mane in his small hands and laughing; while the enormous heaps of vegetables seemed like jade against the morning sky, like green jade set against the pink petals of some wonderful rose. Lord Arthur was oddly moved, though he could not say why. In the fragile beauty of the dawn there was something unspeakably pathetic to him, and he reflected on all the days that open in loveliness and close in storm. And these country people, with their hearty rough voices and careless manner—what a singular London they must behold! A London untouched by the night’s sin or the day’s smoke: a wan, spectral city, a deserted town of graves! He wondered what they made of it, and whether they knew anything of its glory and disgrace, its fierce joys of flaming colour and its dreadful hunger, of all that it creates and destroys from morning until evening.

Becky’s face turned pale, but she thought she could.

Becky burst into tears and cries. Tom did what he could to comfort her, but it helped little. At last Becky said:

“Tom!”

The frightened look on Becky’s face brought Tom to his senses, and he saw he had made a mistake. Becky was not supposed to go home that night! The children fell silent and thoughtful. A moment later, Becky’s fresh burst of grief showed Tom that she had thought of it too—that Sunday morning might be half over before Mrs. Thatcher discovered Becky was not at Mrs. Harper’s.

The children stared at their small piece of candle and watched it slowly, cruelly melt away. At last only half an inch of wick remained. They saw the weak flame rise and fall, climb the thin column of smoke, pause at its top for a moment, and then—the horror of complete darkness took over!

Neither could say how long afterward Becky slowly realized she was crying in Tom’s arms. All they knew was that, after what seemed like a very long time, both woke from a heavy, numb sleep and returned to their misery. Tom said it might be Sunday now—perhaps Monday. He tried to make Becky talk, but her grief was too great; all her hope was gone. Tom said they must have been missed long ago, and surely people were searching for them. He would shout, and perhaps someone would come. He tried, but the far-off echoes sounded so terrible in the darkness that he did not try again.

The hours dragged by, and hunger began to torture the prisoners again. Part of Tom’s half of the cake remained; they divided it and ate it. But they felt hungrier than before.

Woodville was forced to travel into the country and was delayed day after day, painfully separated from his lovely bride. He received a letter from her saying that she was slightly ill, yet urging him to hurry to her: she would find health in his eyes, and his company would be her surest medicine. He was held back three more days, then rushed to her. His heart, though he did not know why, foretold disaster; he had heard nothing further from her. He feared she had grown worse, and that fear made him impatient and restless until he could once again see her standing before him in health and beauty. For a dark voice seemed always to whisper, “You will never see her again as she was.”

When he reached her home, everything within was silent. He passed through several rooms; in one, he saw a servant weeping bitterly. Weak with fear, he could barely ask, “Is she dead?” He only heard the dreadful reply: “Not yet.” These shocking words struck him as less terrible than those he had expected; to learn that she still lived, and that he might still hope, brought him some relief. He remembered her letter and gave himself up to the wild thought that his kisses, warm with love and life, would breathe new spirit into her; that she could not die while he was beside her; that his presence was the talisman preserving her life.

He hurried to her sickroom. She lay there, her cheeks burning with fever, her eyes closed, apparently unconscious. He gathered her in his arms; he pressed breathless kisses upon her burning lips; in a voice restrained by anguish, he called her by the most tender names. “Come back, Elinor; I am with you—your life, your love. Come back, dearest one. You promised me this gift: that I would bring you health. Let your sweet spirit revive; you cannot die near me. What is death? Never to see you again? To be parted from one who is part of myself, without whom I have neither memory nor future?”

He also turned my mind from sorrow by comparing it to the despair he had felt when he lost my mother. Even then, I shuddered at the picture he gave of his emotions. He had a poet’s imagination, and when he described the storm that had torn through his feelings, he made his words so vivid that I believed him even as I trembled. I wondered how he had ever returned to the ordinary duties of life after such wild thoughts had seemed to connect him with things beyond this world. As he spoke, the ideas he expressed were so immense that the human heart seemed too limited to contain them. His feelings appeared more suited to a spirit living among earthquakes and volcanoes than to one enclosed in a mortal body with human features. But these were only memories; he had changed since then. Now he was all love and gentleness, and when I looked at him in wonder as he spoke, the smile on his lips showed that his heart was filled with the softest feelings.

Two months after my aunt’s death, we moved to London, where my father guided me toward more serious studies than I had known before. My progress delighted him. He stayed with me through all my studies and helped me, or joined me, in every lesson. We went often into society, and not a day passed without my father trying to brighten it with some new pleasure. His tender love for me, and the love and respect with which I returned it, gave every moment a special charm. The hours passed slowly because every minute was occupied. We lived more in one week than many people do in several months, and the variety and newness of our pleasures made each one more enjoyable.

We were always taking excursions together. Whether we went to see beautiful landscapes, fine paintings, or simply to seek whatever amusement might arise, I was always happy when I was near my father. I regretted it whenever a third person joined us; yet if I looked uneasily toward my father, his eyes, fixed on me and shining with tenderness, immediately brought joy back to my heart. O hours of deepest delight! Though you were brief, when I look back through the mist of grief that rose so soon afterward, as if to hide you from my sight, you seem as long to me as an entire life.

I could scarcely believe such good fortune had come to me, but when I was certain that my enemy had truly fled, I clapped my hands with joy and ran down to Clerval.

We went up to my room, and the servant soon brought breakfast; but I could not control myself. It was not joy alone that filled me; my skin tingled with extreme sensitivity, and my pulse raced. I could not stay still for a moment; I leapt over chairs, clapped my hands, and laughed aloud. At first Clerval thought my strange excitement came from joy at his arrival, but when he watched me more closely, he saw a wildness in my eyes that he could not explain, and my loud, uncontrolled, empty laughter frightened and amazed him.

“Do not ask me,” I cried, covering my eyes with my hands, because I thought I saw the dreaded ghost slip into the room. “He can tell you. Oh, save me! Save me!” I imagined the monster had seized me; I struggled wildly and fell down in a fit.

Perhaps this was the signal that freed everyone’s tongues. A chorus answered, “Good day!”

“It is bad weather, gentlemen,” said Defarge, shaking his head.

“My wife,” Defarge said loudly, speaking to Madame Defarge, “I have travelled several leagues with this good road-mender, called Jacques. I met him—by chance—a day and a half’s journey from Paris. This road-mender, called Jacques, is a good fellow. Give him something to drink, my wife!”

So I passed two years. Day after day, hundreds of them, went by; they brought no outward change, but a few slowly changed my mind as I drifted toward death. I began to study more, to feel more deeply the thoughts of others as they were expressed in books, to read history, and to lose my own identity among the crowds who had lived before me. Perhaps, as the feeling of immediate suffering faded, I became more human. Solitude too lost some of its appeal: I began again to long for sympathy. I was never tempted to seek a crowd, but I wished for one friend who would love me. Perhaps you will say that I was gradually becoming fit to return to society. I do not think so. The sympathy I wanted had to be so pure, so free from the influence of outward circumstances, that in the world I could not help being disappointed by the coarse elements that mix even with its best feelings. Believe me, I was then less fit for any connection with my fellow creatures than before. When I left them, they had tormented me, but in the way pain and illness torment: as something outside the mind that irritated it and that I wished to throw off. But now I would have wanted sympathy; I would have wished to join my soul to another's, and so prepared for myself deep disappointment and suffering. For I was as delicate as the sensitive plant, all nerves. I did not want sympathy and help in ambition or wisdom, but sweet, mutual affection: smiles to cheer me and gentle words of comfort. I wished for one heart into which I could pour my complaints without restraint, where, through the heavenly nature of the soil, blessed fruit might grow from such bad seed. Yet how could I find it? The love that is the soul of friendship is a gentle spirit, seldom found except when two kind creatures have been joined from early youth, or are bound by shared suffering and pursuits. It comes to some chosen people without being sought or expected; it falls like soft dew on favored places which, however barren before, become fertile under its kind influence with every sweet plant. But when it is desired, it flees; it mocks the prayers of those who worship it; it may give itself, but cannot be pursued.

I knew all this and did not go looking for sympathy; yet there, on my lonely heath, beneath my humble roof, with desert all around me, it came to me like a winter sunbeam, beautiful as it helps melt the piled snow. Alas, the sun shone on ruined fruit; I did not revive in its light, for I was too completely destroyed to feel its healing power.

He knew that fear and gloomy expectations greatly aided disease, and that despair and anxious brooding made people especially open to infection. So no shocking scenes were visible: most shops remained open, and the streets still held some passing crowds. Yet, though the look of an infected city had been concealed, London seemed greatly changed to me, who had not seen it since the plague began. There were no carriages, and grass had grown high in the streets; the houses looked deserted, most shutters were closed, and the people I met wore a pale, frightened expression, unlike the usual busy manner of Londoners. My lone carriage drew attention as it rattled toward the Protectoral Palace, and the fashionable streets leading there looked even sadder and more empty. I found Adrian’s antechamber crowded; it was the hour when he received visitors. Unwilling to interrupt his work, I waited and watched the petitioners enter and leave. They were people of the middle and lower classes, whose livelihoods had failed as trade stopped and the active pursuit of money, so common in our country, came to an end. The newcomers looked anxious, sometimes terrified, in sharp contrast to the calm, even satisfied faces of those who had seen him. I could see my friend’s influence in their quicker steps and brighter expressions. At two o’clock, no more were admitted. Those turned away left angrily or sadly, while I entered the audience chamber.

This morning, to my immense joy, at about nine o’clock, with the moon’s surface terrifyingly close and my fears at their height, the pump of my condenser finally showed clear signs of a change in the atmosphere. By ten, I had reason to think its density had increased considerably. By eleven, the apparatus required very little effort; and at twelve, though somewhat hesitant, I dared to unscrew the tourniquet. Finding that this caused no ill effects, I at last opened the gum-elastic chamber and removed it from around the car. As might have been expected, spasms and a violent headache immediately followed an experiment so rash and dangerous. But since these and the other difficulties of breathing were not severe enough to endanger my life, I resolved to bear them as best I could, knowing that I would leave them behind moment by moment as I approached the denser layers near the moon. This approach, however, remained exceedingly swift; and it soon became alarmingly clear that, although I had probably been right in expecting an atmosphere whose density corresponded to the satellite’s mass, I had been mistaken in believing that this density, even at the surface, would be sufficient to support the great weight in my balloon’s car. Yet it ought to have done so, and to the same degree as at the earth’s surface, the actual gravity of bodies on either planet being assumed to be in proportion to the condensation of the atmosphere. My rapid descent was proof enough that this was not so; why it was not so can only be explained by reference to those possible geological disturbances I mentioned before. In any event, I was now very near the planet and descending with dreadful force. I lost no time in throwing overboard first my ballast, then my water-kegs, then my condensing apparatus and gum-elastic chamber, and finally every object in the car. But it was useless. I continued to fall with horrible speed, and was now less than half a mile from the surface. As a final measure, after discarding my coat, hat, and boots, I cut the car itself loose from the balloon, for it was far from light. Then, clinging to the netting with both hands, I had barely time to notice that the entire country, as far as I could see, was thickly dotted with tiny dwellings before I plunged headfirst into the center of a fantastical-looking city, and into the midst of a vast crowd of ugly little people. Not one spoke a word or made the slightest effort to help me; they merely stood there like a pack of fools, grinning absurdly and staring sideways at me and my balloon, their arms planted on their hips.”

He had lived the refined, luxurious life of a young man with rank and wealth, a life wonderfully free from common worries, with the graceful carelessness of youth; and now, for the first time, he understood the dreadful mystery of Fate, the terrible meaning of Doom.

How insane and horrible it all seemed! Could it be that his hand bore, in signs he could not read but another person could, some dreadful secret of sin, some blood-red mark of crime? Was there no way to escape? Were people no more than chess pieces, moved by an unseen hand, like vessels shaped by a potter as he pleased, for honour or disgrace? His mind rebelled against the thought, yet he felt that some tragedy hung over him, and that he had suddenly been made to carry an unbearable burden. Actors are fortunate. They can choose whether to appear in tragedy or comedy, whether to suffer or be cheerful, to laugh or weep. Real life is different. Most men and women must play parts for which they are not suited. Our Guildensterns play Hamlet, while our Hamlets must joke like Prince Hal. The world is a stage, but the roles are badly assigned.
