Week after week passed, and I became ever more deeply absorbed in you. Then a fresh thing happened. I had painted you as Paris in delicate armour, and as Adonis in a hunter’s cloak, carrying a bright boar-spear. With great lotus-flowers crowning you, you had sat upon the prow of Adrian’s barge, looking out over the green, muddy Nile. You had bent above the quiet pool in some Greek forest and beheld, in the water’s mute silver, the wonder of your own face. And all this had been what art ought to be—unconscious, ideal, and distant. One day—a disastrous day, I sometimes believe—I resolved to paint a splendid portrait of you as you truly were, not in the dress of vanished centuries, but in your own clothes and your own age. Whether it was the realism of the treatment, or simply the marvel of your personality, so directly before me without cloud or covering, I cannot say. But I know that, while I worked, every touch and layer of colour appeared to disclose my secret. I became frightened that others might discover my worship of you. I felt, Dorian, that I had revealed too much, that I had placed too much of myself within it. It was then that I decided never to let the picture be exhibited. You were somewhat vexed; but you did not understand what it meant to me. Harry, when I spoke to him of it, laughed at me. Yet I did not care. When the portrait was complete, and I sat alone before it, I knew that I had been right.... Well, a few days later it left my studio, and once I was free of the unbearable fascination of its presence, I thought I had been foolish to imagine I saw anything there beyond the fact that you were remarkably handsome and that I knew how to paint. Even now I cannot help thinking it mistaken to suppose that the passion felt in creation is ever truly visible in the work created. Art is always more abstract than we imagine. Form and colour speak only of form and colour—that is all. It often seems to me that art hides the artist much more completely than it reveals him. So, when this offer came from Paris, I resolved that your portrait should be the chief work in my exhibition. It never entered my mind that you would object. I see now that you were right. The picture must not be displayed. You must not be angry with me, Dorian, for what I have said.

When Tom woke in the morning, he wondered where he was. He sat up, rubbed his eyes, and looked around. Then he understood. It was the cool gray dawn, and the deep calm and silence of the woods gave him a wonderful feeling of rest and peace. Not a leaf moved; no sound disturbed Nature’s quiet thoughts. Dewdrops shone on the leaves and grass. A white layer of ashes covered the fire, and a thin blue thread of smoke rose straight into the air. Joe and Huck were still asleep.

Far off in the woods, a bird called, and another answered. Soon a woodpecker could be heard tapping. Little by little, the cool, dim gray morning grew white, and more sounds appeared as life began to stir. The boy watched thoughtfully as Nature woke from sleep and went to work. A little green worm crawled over a wet leaf, raising two-thirds of its body into the air now and then and “sniffing around” before moving on again. It was measuring, Tom said. When the worm came toward him on its own, he sat as still as a stone. His hopes rose and fell as the creature kept coming closer or seemed ready to go another way. At last it paused for a painful moment, its curved body raised in the air, then came down firmly on Tom’s leg and began to travel over him. Tom’s heart filled with joy, for this meant he was going to have a new suit of clothes—without a doubt, a bright pirate uniform. Then a line of ants appeared from nowhere in particular and went about their work. One bravely struggled along carrying a dead spider five times bigger than itself, hauling it straight up a tree trunk. A brown-spotted ladybug climbed the dizzying height of a blade of grass. Tom bent close and said, “Ladybug, ladybug, fly away home, your house is on fire, your children’s alone,” and she spread her wings and flew off to check—which did not surprise him. He had long known that ladybugs believed such stories about fires, and he had fooled them more than once. Next came a tumblebug, pushing hard at its ball. Tom touched it to watch it pull in its legs and pretend to be dead. By now the birds were making a great noise. A catbird, the northern mocker, landed in a tree above Tom’s head and happily sang imitations of its neighbors. Fortunately, there is only one way to reason through this question, and it must bring us to a definite conclusion. Let us consider, one by one, every possible means of escape. Clearly, when the party came up the stairs, the murderers were in the room where Mademoiselle L’Espanaye was found, or at least in the adjoining room. Therefore, we need look for exits only from these two rooms. The police had stripped the floors, ceilings, and wall masonry in every direction. No secret passage could have escaped their attention. Let us consider the chimneys. Though they are of ordinary width for eight or ten feet above the hearths, they would not admit the body of a large cat for their entire length. Since escape by the means already mentioned is absolutely impossible, we are left with the windows. Many years ago, I became close friends with a Mr. William Legrand. He came from an old Huguenot family and had once been wealthy, but a series of misfortunes had left him poor. To escape the humiliation caused by his losses, he left New Orleans, the city of his ancestors, and settled on Sullivan’s Island, near Charleston, South Carolina.

This island is a very unusual place. It is made up of little but sea sand and is about three miles long. Nowhere is it more than a quarter of a mile wide. It is separated from the mainland by a barely visible creek that winds through a wilderness of reeds and mud, a favorite haunt of the marsh hen. As one might expect, the vegetation is sparse, or at least stunted. There are no trees of any great size. Near the western end, where Fort Moultrie stands, and where a few poor wooden buildings are occupied in summer by people fleeing Charleston’s dust and fever, one can find the rough palmetto. But the rest of the island, except for this western point and a strip of hard white beach along the sea, is covered with a thick growth of sweet myrtle, so valued by English gardeners. Here the shrub often grows fifteen or twenty feet high, forming an almost impassable thicket and filling the air with its scent.

Deep within this thicket, not far from the eastern, more distant end of the island, Legrand had built a small hut, where he lived when I first met him by chance. Our acquaintance soon became a friendship, for there was much in this recluse to inspire both interest and respect. I found him well educated and gifted with unusual intelligence, but troubled by a dislike of mankind and by strange shifts between excitement and sadness. He had many books, though he rarely used them. His chief pleasures were hunting and fishing, or wandering along the beach and through the myrtles in search of shells or insect specimens; his collection of the latter might have been envied by a Swammerdamm. On these outings he was usually accompanied by an old negro named Jupiter, who had been freed before the family’s misfortunes. Yet neither threats nor promises could persuade him to give up what he saw as his right to follow his young “Massa Will.” It is possible that Legrand’s relatives, believing his mind somewhat unsteady, had encouraged this stubborn devotion in Jupiter so that he might watch over and protect the wanderer.

All at once Mrs. Otis noticed a faded red mark on the floor near the fireplace and, having no idea what it truly meant, remarked to Mrs. Umney, ‘I fear something has been spilled there.’

‘Yes, madam,’ said the elderly housekeeper softly, ‘blood was spilled upon that place.’

‘How dreadful!’ exclaimed Mrs. Otis. ‘I have no liking whatever for blood-stains in a sitting-room. It must be taken away immediately.’

The old woman smiled and replied in the same hushed, mysterious tone, ‘It is the blood of Lady Eleanore de Canterville, murdered on that very spot by her own husband, Sir Simon de Canterville, in 1575. Sir Simon outlived her by nine years, then vanished suddenly in circumstances of great mystery. His body has never been found, though his guilty spirit still haunts the Chase. The blood-stain has been greatly admired by tourists and others, and it cannot be removed.’

‘That is utter nonsense,’ cried Washington Otis. ‘Pinkerton’s Champion Stain Remover and Paragon Detergent will have it clean in no time’; and, before the frightened housekeeper could stop him, he was on his knees, briskly rubbing the floor with a little stick resembling a black cosmetic. Within a few moments, every sign of the blood-stain had vanished.

‘I knew Pinkerton would manage it,’ he declared triumphantly, looking about at his admiring family; but scarcely had he spoken when a dreadful flash of lightning illuminated the gloomy room, a terrible crash of thunder sent them all to their feet, and Mrs. Umney fainted.

At the usual vespertide hour, she led him to the chapel; and though she trembled and wept for him, she played without a flaw in rhythm or a wrong note the hymn composed to celebrate the creation of the beautiful earth, which would soon become her tomb.

We seemed to her like visitors from heaven itself; at the sight of relief, her fiercely summoned courage and barely sustained composure gave way. With a cry, she rushed toward us, clasped Adrian’s knees, and, saying only, “Oh, save my father!” opened the long-closed floodgates of her grief in sobs and hysterical cries.

Poor girl! She and her father now lie side by side beneath the tall walnut tree where her lover rests, and which she had pointed out to us in her final moments. At last aware of his daughter’s danger, unable to see the changes in her beloved face, her father stubbornly held her hand until it grew cold and rigid in death. Even then he neither moved nor spoke, until, twelve hours later, kind death carried him to his unbroken rest. They lie beneath the turf, the tree their monument. The sacred place remains clear in my memory, enclosed by the rocky Jura and the distant, immeasurable Alps; the spire of the church they attended still rises from the sheltering trees; and though her hand is cold, I still think the divine music they loved drifts there, comforting their gentle ghosts.

When Tom woke in the morning, he wondered where he was. He sat up, rubbed his eyes, and looked around. Then he understood. It was the cool gray dawn, and a delicious feeling of rest and peace lay in the deep, all-pervading stillness of the woods. Not a leaf moved; no sound disturbed great Nature’s meditation. Beads of dew rested on the leaves and grass. A white blanket of ashes covered the fire, and a thin blue wisp of smoke rose straight into the air. Joe and Huck were still asleep.

Far off in the woods, a bird called; another answered; soon the tapping of a woodpecker could be heard. Gradually the cool, dim gray of morning turned white, and just as gradually sounds increased and life began to show itself. The wonder of Nature waking from sleep and setting to work unfolded before the thoughtful boy. A little green worm crawled across a dewy leaf, now and then raising two-thirds of its body into the air and “sniffing around,” then moving on again—for it was measuring, Tom said; and when the worm came toward him of its own accord, he sat as motionless as a stone, his hopes rising and falling by turns as the creature continued toward him or seemed likely to go another way. At last it paused for an agonizing moment, its curved body lifted in the air, then came down decisively on Tom’s leg and began traveling over him. His heart was full of joy, for that meant he was going to have a new suit of clothes—without a shadow of doubt, a bright pirate uniform. Then a procession of ants appeared from nowhere in particular and went about their work. One struggled bravely along carrying a dead spider five times its own size, and hauled it straight up a tree trunk. A brown-spotted ladybug climbed the dizzy height of a blade of grass, and Tom bent close and said, “Ladybug, ladybug, fly away home, your house is on fire, your children are alone,” and she spread her wings and flew off to see about it. This did not surprise the boy, for he had long known that this insect was gullible about fires, and he had taken advantage of its simplicity more than once. Next came a tumblebug, pushing sturdily at its ball, and Tom touched it to watch it draw its legs against its body and pretend to be dead. By now the birds were in full uproar. A catbird, the northern mocker, landed in a tree above Tom’s head and poured out imitations of its neighbors in delighted excitement. Then a shrill jay swooped down like a flash of blue flame and stopped on a twig almost within the boy’s reach, tilted its head to one side, and stared at the strangers with intense curiosity. A gray squirrel and a large fox squirrel came scurrying along, sitting up now and then to inspect the boys and chatter at them, for the wild creatures had probably never seen human beings before and scarcely knew whether they should be afraid.

You will be glad to hear that no misfortune has attended the beginning of an enterprise you viewed with such dark forebodings. I arrived here yesterday, and my first duty is to assure my dear sister that I am well and increasingly confident in the success of my undertaking.

I am already far north of London, and as I walk through the streets of Petersburg, I feel a cold northern breeze on my cheeks, strengthening my nerves and filling me with delight. Do you understand this feeling? This breeze, which has travelled from the regions toward which I am advancing, gives me a taste in advance of those icy climates. Encouraged by this promising wind, my dreams grow more intense and vivid. I try in vain to convince myself that the pole is a place of frost and desolation; in my imagination, it always appears as a region of beauty and delight. There, Margaret, the sun is forever visible, its broad disk merely skimming the horizon and spreading an unending radiance. There—for, with your permission, my sister, I will place some faith in earlier navigators—snow and frost are banished; and, sailing across a calm sea, we may be carried to a land surpassing in wonder and beauty every region yet discovered on the habitable globe. Its natural productions and features may be unparalleled, just as the phenomena of the heavenly bodies surely are in those unexplored solitudes. What might not be expected in a country of eternal light? There I may discover the marvelous force that draws the needle, and may settle a thousand celestial observations that need only this voyage to make their apparent irregularities forever consistent. I shall satisfy my burning curiosity by seeing a part of the world never before visited, and may set foot on land never before marked by human feet. These are my temptations, and they are enough to overcome every fear of danger or death and lead me to begin this arduous voyage with the joy a child feels when he sets out in a small boat with his holiday companions on a voyage of discovery up his native river. But even if all these conjectures prove false, you cannot deny the priceless benefit I shall grant all humanity, to the last generation, by discovering a passage near the pole to those countries that now require so many months to reach, or by determining the secret of the magnet, which, if it can be determined at all, can only be achieved by an undertaking like mine.

These thoughts have driven away the uneasiness with which I began this letter, and I feel my heart burn with an enthusiasm that lifts me toward heaven; for nothing brings such peace to the mind as a fixed purpose—a point upon which the soul may rest its intellectual gaze.

A gentleman of limited means, living near his family seat, had three beautiful daughters. The eldest was by far the loveliest; yet her beauty merely heightened her other merits—her mind was lucid and vigorous, her temper sweetly angelic. She and my father had played together from infancy: Diana, even as a child, had been a favourite with his mother; and this fondness increased as the beautiful, spirited girl grew older, so that during his holidays from school and college they were continually together. Novels, and all the means through which civilized youth are taught the existence of passions before they truly experience them, had greatly affected one so singularly open to every impression. At eleven, Diana was his dearest companion in play, yet he already spoke the language of love. Though she was nearly two years older, her education had left her more childlike, at least in her understanding and expression of emotion; she accepted his fervent declarations innocently, returning them without knowing their import. She had read no novels and knew only her younger sisters; how should she distinguish love from friendship? When her expanding mind revealed to her the real character of their intercourse, her heart was already given to her friend, and her sole fear was that new attractions or inconstancy might lead him to forsake his childish promises.

Yet their attachment grew daily more ardent and affectionate. It was a passion that had increased with his own growth, woven itself into every faculty and sentiment, and could end only with his life. No one knew of their love but their two hearts; and though, in every other matter—and even in this—he feared his companions' blame for loving one beneath him in fortune, nothing could for an instant alter his resolve to marry her as soon as he had gathered courage enough to confront the obstacles he meant to overcome.

Diana was entirely deserving of his profoundest love.

Winters at the latitude of Sullivan’s Island are rarely very harsh, and during the autumn it is indeed an uncommon occurrence for a fire to be thought needful. Near the middle of October, 18—, there came, however, a day of unusual cold. A little before sundown I made my way through the evergreens to the cottage of my friend, whom I had not called upon for some weeks—my home then being in Charleston, nine miles from the island, while the means of going and returning were greatly inferior to those of the present time. On arriving at the hut, I knocked, according to my habit, and, receiving no answer, looked for the key in the place where I knew it was hidden, opened the door, and entered. A cheerful fire burned on the hearth. It was something novel, and far from unwelcome. I cast aside my overcoat, seated myself in an arm-chair beside the snapping logs, and waited patiently for my hosts to return.

Not long after nightfall they came in and welcomed me with great warmth. Jupiter, grinning broadly, hurried about preparing several marsh-hens for supper. Will the reader grow weary, should I describe in detail our tedious journey from Paris to Geneva? Were I, day after day, to set down in journal form the crowded miseries of our condition, could my hand endure to write, or speech supply expressions for the manifoldness of our grief; for the jostling and pressing of one miserable occurrence upon the heels of another? Have patience, O reader! whoever thou mayest be, wherever thou livest, whether of spiritual race, or descended from some surviving pair, thy nature shall be human, and the earth thy dwelling; here thou wilt read the actions of an extinct race, and wonder whether those who endured what thou findest written were fashioned of frail flesh and tender organization like thine own. Most certainly they were—weep, then; for surely, lonely being, thou wilt possess a gentle nature; let compassionate tears fall; yet meanwhile give heed to the narrative, and learn the acts and sufferings of thy forebears.

Still, the final occurrences that attended our passage through France were so charged with unusual terror and dark misery that I dare not linger over them in my account. If I dissected every incident, each slight portion of a second would yield a dreadful history, whose smallest phrase might chill the blood within thy youthful veins. It is fitting that I raise, for thy instruction, this memorial of the departed race; but not that I should lead thee through the wards of a hospital, or into the hidden rooms of the charnel-house.

That afternoon Becky Thatcher found herself wandering sadly around the deserted schoolyard. But she found nothing there to comfort her. She said to herself:

“Oh, if only I had that brass andiron knob again! But I don’t have anything now to remember him by.” And she swallowed back a small sob.

Presently she stopped and said to herself:

“It was right here. Oh, if I could do it over, I wouldn’t say that—I wouldn’t say it for all the world. But he’s gone now; I’ll never, never, never see him again.”

The thought overwhelmed her, and she wandered away with tears running down her cheeks. Then a whole group of boys and girls—Tom’s and Joe’s playmates—came along and stood looking over the picket fence, speaking in hushed, reverent voices about how Tom had done this or that the last time they saw him, and how Joe had said some little thing or other (full of dreadful prophecy, as they could plainly see now!). Each speaker pointed out the exact place where the lost boys had stood, then added something like, “And I was standing just so—just as I am now—and if you were him, I was this close—and he smiled like this—and then something came over me, sort of awful, you know—and of course I never thought what it meant, but I can see it now!”

Then they argued over who had seen the dead boys last while they were alive. Many claimed that gloomy honor and offered evidence, more or less altered by the witness. When it was finally decided who really had seen the departed boys last and exchanged the last words with them, the fortunate ones assumed a kind of sacred importance, and everyone else stared at them and envied them. One poor boy, with no other distinction to offer, said with fairly obvious pride at the memory:

“Well, Tom Sawyer beat me up once.”

But that attempt at glory failed. Most of the boys could say the same, and that made the distinction too cheap. The group drifted away, still recalling memories of the lost heroes in awestruck voices.

Her shyness was not affected; it came from a fear that she would not be properly valued, and from the slight regard she had for the world's neglect—feelings that also marked Raymond. Yet Perdita thought of others more constantly than he did; part of her reserve came from a desire not to make those around her feel inferior, though such a thought never entered her own mind. Because of her birth and education, Idris would have been better suited to the forms of ceremony; but the ease with which habit made them natural to her also made them tiresome. He scarcely knew what to do with his newly gained power; his mind was crowded with plans, though he had chosen none. Elizabeth was sad and hopeless; she no longer found pleasure in her usual activities. Any enjoyment seemed like disrespect toward the dead; she believed that endless grief and tears were the proper tribute she owed to innocence so cruelly ruined and destroyed. She was no longer the cheerful girl who, in our younger days, walked with me beside the lake and spoke excitedly of our hopes for the future. The first of those sorrows that draw us away from the world had come to her, and its shadow had extinguished her sweetest smiles.

“When I think, my dear cousin,” she said, “of the terrible death of Justine Moritz, I can no longer see the world and its people as I once did. Before, the stories of wickedness and injustice that I read in books or heard from others seemed like events from ancient times or imagined evils. At least they were far away, easier to understand with reason than to picture in the mind. But now suffering has come close to home, and people seem to me like monsters thirsty for one another’s blood. Yet perhaps I am being unfair. Everyone believed that poor girl was guilty; and if she had committed the crime for which she died, she would surely have been one of the most corrupt human beings. For a few jewels, to murder the son of her benefactor and friend—a child she had cared for since his birth and seemed to love as her own! I could never agree to the death of any person, but I would certainly have thought such a creature unfit to live among other people. But she was innocent. I know it; I feel that she was innocent. You think so too, and that strengthens my belief. Alas, Victor, when lies can look so much like truth, who can be sure of happiness? I feel as though I am walking along the edge of a cliff, while thousands press around me and try to force me into the abyss. William and Justine were murdered, while the murderer escapes. He walks freely through the world, perhaps even respected. But even if I were condemned to die on the scaffold for the same crimes, I would not trade places with such a wretch.”

I listened to her words in the deepest agony. Though not by my own hand, I was in truth the murderer. Elizabeth saw my suffering in my face and, gently taking my hand, said, “My dearest friend, you must calm yourself. These events have affected me deeply, God knows; but I am not as miserable as you are.”

After sharing in the general distress over the terrible outcome of this event, which Elizabeth thought almost certain and Miss Bennet could not say was entirely impossible, Elizabeth continued, “But tell me everything I have not already heard. Give me more details. What did Colonel Forster say? Had they suspected anything before the elopement? They must have seen the two of them together constantly.”

“Colonel Forster admitted that he had often suspected some affection between them, especially on Lydia’s side, but nothing that gave him real alarm. I am so sorry for him. He was as attentive and kind as possible. He was already coming to see us, to assure us of his concern, before he had any idea that they might not have gone to Scotland. When that fear first became known, it made him hurry his journey.”

“And was Denny sure that Wickham would not marry her? Did he know they meant to run away? Had Colonel Forster seen Denny himself?”

“Yes; but when Colonel Forster questioned him, Denny denied knowing anything of their plan and would not give his true opinion of it. He did not repeat his belief that they would not marry, and that makes me hope he may have been misunderstood before.”

“And until Colonel Forster came himself, none of you doubted, I suppose, that they had really married?”

“How could such an idea have entered our minds? I felt a little uneasy—a little afraid for my sister’s happiness in marrying him, because I knew his behaviour had not always been quite right. “No, I do not think so.”

“I must admit that he did not speak as well of Wickham as he once had. He believed him careless and wasteful; and since this sad event, people say he left Meryton deeply in debt. But I hope that is untrue.”

Perhaps," said Sir Launcelot, "his cause is here today, and perhaps he is best loved by this lady of all who are here. For I can see that he strains and pushes himself to do great deeds. After providing immediate aid to the sick, Adrian’s chief effort had been to conceal the plague’s symptoms and advance from London’s inhabitants. He knew that fear and gloomy expectation were powerful allies of illness; that despair and anxious brooding made the human body especially vulnerable to infection. Thus no shocking scenes were visible: the shops were generally open, and some flow of pedestrians was maintained. Yet though the outward appearance of an infected city had been prevented, London seemed greatly altered to me, who had not seen it since the visitation began. There were no carriages, and grass had grown high in the streets; the houses looked abandoned; most shutters were closed; and the people I encountered wore a ghastly, frightened expression, utterly unlike Londoners’ usual businesslike manner. My lone carriage drew attention as it rattled toward the Protectoral Palace, and the fashionable streets leading there looked even more bleak and empty. I found Adrian’s antechamber crowded; it was the hour when he received visitors. Unwilling to interrupt his work, I waited and watched the petitioners enter and leave. They were people of the middle and lower classes, whose livelihoods had vanished with the halt in trade and in the money-making activity, in all its forms, so characteristic of our country. The arrivals bore an air of anxiety, sometimes terror, sharply contrasting with the resigned, even contented faces of those who had been received. In their brisker movements and cheerful expressions, I could see my friend’s influence. Two o’clock struck, after which no one else was admitted; those turned away departed sullenly or sadly, while I entered the audience chamber.

I was struck by the improvement in Adrian’s health. He was no longer bowed to the ground like an over-tended spring flower which, growing beyond its strength, is weighed down even by its own crown of blossoms. His eyes shone, his face was calm, and an air of focused energy filled his whole person, very unlike his former languor. He sat at a table with several secretaries, who were sorting petitions or recording notes from that day’s audience. Two or three petitioners still waited nearby. I admired his fairness and patience. Those able to live outside London, he urged to leave at once, providing them with the means to do so.

“Well, it surely does, Tom. And who will we rob?”

“Oh, almost anybody. We ambush people—that’s mostly how it’s done.”

“No, not always. We keep them in the cave until they raise a ransom.”

“What’s a ransom?”

“Money. You make them get all they can from their friends; and after you’ve kept them a year, if it hasn’t been raised by then, you kill them. That’s the usual way. Only you don’t kill women. You lock up the women, but you don’t kill them. They’re always beautiful and rich, and terribly frightened. You take their watches and things, but you always take off your hat and speak politely. Nobody is as polite as robbers—you’ll see that in any book. Then the women start loving you, and after they’ve been in the cave for a week or two, they stop crying, and after that you couldn’t make them leave. If you drove them out, they’d turn right around and come back. That’s how it is in all the books.”

“Why, that’s really great, Tom. I think it’s better than being a pirate.”

“Yes, it’s better in some ways, because it’s close to home, and circuses, and all that.”

This strengthened the desperate decision Charles Darnay had begun to form: he would go to Paris.

Yes. Like the sailor in the old tale, winds and currents had carried him within reach of the Loadstone Rock; it was pulling him toward itself, and he had to go. Every thought that came before him drove him onward, faster and more steadily, toward that terrible attraction. His hidden uneasiness had been that evil purposes were being carried out in his unhappy country by evil men, while he, who knew he was better than they were, was not there trying to prevent bloodshed and defend mercy and humanity. That uneasiness, half suppressed and half accusing him, had led him to compare himself with the brave old gentleman whose sense of duty was so strong. That comparison, unfavourable to himself, had immediately brought Monseigneur's mocking words to mind; they had wounded him deeply. Then came Stryver's sneers, which were especially crude and painful for old reasons. After them had come Gabelle's letter: the appeal of an innocent prisoner, in danger of death, to his justice, honour, and good name.

When Tom woke that morning, he wondered where he was. He raised himself, rubbed his eyes, and glanced about. Then he understood. It was the cool gray dawn, and a delightful feeling of rest and peace lay in the deep, all-pervading stillness of the woods. Not a leaf moved; no sound disturbed great Nature’s meditation. Dewdrops, like beads, rested on the leaves and grass. A white coating of ashes lay over the fire, and a slender blue wisp of smoke climbed straight upward. Joe and Huck were still asleep.

Far off in the forest a bird cried, and another replied; soon the tapping of a woodpecker could be heard. Little by little the cool, shadowy gray of morning turned white, and just as gradually sounds increased and life began to show itself. The wonder of Nature casting aside sleep and setting to work revealed itself before the thoughtful boy. A small green worm crawled across a wet leaf, now and then raising two-thirds of its body into the air and “sniffing around,” before moving on again—for it was measuring, Tom declared; and as the worm came toward him of its own accord, he remained as motionless as a stone, his hopes alternately rising and sinking as the creature advanced or appeared disposed to turn elsewhere. At last it paused for a trying instant, its curved body lifted in the air, then came down firmly upon Tom’s leg and began traveling over him. His heart was full of joy, for this signified that he would have a new suit of clothes—beyond all doubt, a showy pirate uniform. Next a line of ants emerged from no particular place and set about their business; one bravely struggled past carrying a dead spider five times its own size, and hauled it directly up a tree trunk. A brown, spotted ladybug climbed the dizzy summit of a blade of grass, and Tom bent close and said, “Lady-bug, lady-bug, fly away home, your house is on fire, your children’s alone,” whereupon she spread her wings and flew away to look into it. This did not surprise the boy, since he had long known the insect to be gullible concerning fires, and had taken advantage of its simplicity more than once. Then came a tumblebug, stoutly pushing at its ball, and Tom touched it to watch it draw its legs against its body and feign death. By now the birds were in full riot. A catbird, the Northern mocker, alighted in a tree above Tom’s head and poured out imitations of its neighbors in delighted ecstasy; then a sharp-voiced jay flashed down like blue fire and perched on a twig nearly within the boy’s reach, tilted its head aside, and studied the strangers with eager curiosity. Merlin was still burning smoke-powders, clawing at the air, and muttering gibberish as vigorously as ever, though he looked rather disheartened, since naturally he had not raised so much as a drop of sweat from that well. “How does it look by now, partner?”

“Behold, I am at this moment engaged in testing the mightiest enchantment known to the masters of occult arts in the Eastern lands; if it fail me, nothing can prevail. Peace, till I have done.”

“If any exertion of mortal power could break the spell that holds these waters, this which I have but now attempted would have done so. It has failed; and thereby I now know that what I feared is proven true: the token of this failure is that the most powerful spirit known to the magicians of the East, whose name none may speak and live, has cast his spell upon this well. “Perhaps.”

“That is what I mean.”

“Wherefore, ye mean also that when he says none can break the spell—”

“Yes, when he says that, he says something not necessarily true. There are circumstances in which an attempt to break it may have some chance—that is, some slight, some trifling chance—of succeeding.”

Whist has long been recognized for its effect on what is called the calculating faculty; and men of the highest intellect have been known to take an apparently inexplicable pleasure in it while dismissing chess as frivolous. Without question, nothing of a similar kind places such demands upon the power of analysis. The finest chess player in Christendom may be little more than the finest player of chess; but skill at whist suggests the capacity to succeed in all those more important contests in which mind struggles against mind. By skill, I mean that perfection in the game which includes an understanding of all the sources from which legitimate advantage may be drawn. These are not merely numerous but varied, and often lie in corners of thought wholly beyond the reach of ordinary understanding. To observe closely is to remember clearly; and in this respect the concentrated chess player will do well enough at whist, while Hoyle's rules—being founded on the mere mechanics of the game—are generally easy to understand. Thus, a retentive memory and adherence to “the book” are commonly considered the whole of good play. But it is in matters beyond the bounds of mere rule that the analyst's skill reveals itself. In silence, he makes a multitude of observations and inferences. Perhaps his companions do the same; yet the difference in the amount of information gained lies less in the soundness of the inference than in the quality of the observation. The essential knowledge is knowing what to observe. Our player limits himself in no way; nor, because the game is his object, does he reject conclusions drawn from matters outside it. He studies his partner's face, carefully comparing it with that of each opponent. He considers how the cards are arranged in every hand, often counting trump by trump and honor by honor from the glances their holders cast upon them. He notices every change of expression as play proceeds, gathering material for thought from signs of certainty, surprise, triumph, or disappointment. From the way a trick is gathered up, he judges whether the person who takes it can win another in that suit. He recognizes a feint by the manner in which a card is thrown upon the table. A casual or unintended word; the accidental dropping or turning of a card, together with the anxiety or carelessness shown in concealing it; the counting of tricks and the order in which they are arranged; embarrassment, hesitation, eagerness, or nervousness—all offer his seemingly intuitive perception signs of the true state of affairs.

You were a little annoyed, but you did not understand what it meant to me. Harry, when I spoke to him about it, laughed at me. But I did not care. When the portrait was finished and I sat alone with it, I felt I had been right.... Well, after a few days it left my studio, and once I was free of the unbearable fascination of having it there, I began to think I had been foolish to imagine I saw anything in it beyond the fact that you were very handsome and that I could paint. Even now, I cannot help thinking it is wrong to believe that the passion felt in creating something is ever truly visible in the work itself. Art is always more abstract than we think. Form and colour tell us only of form and colour—that is all. It often seems to me that art hides the artist much more completely than it reveals him. So, when I received this offer from Paris, I decided to make your portrait the main work in my exhibition. It never entered my mind that you would refuse. I see now that you were right. The picture cannot be shown. You must not be angry with me, Dorian, for what I have told you.

“I will, sir,” I replied. For as I had walked along, I had given careful thought to what I meant to say.

“Don’t commit yourself,” said Mr. Jaggers, “and don’t commit anyone else. You understand—anyone. Tell me nothing: I want to know nothing; I am not curious.”

Mr. Jaggers nodded. “But did you say ‘told’ or ‘informed’?” he asked, tilting his head and looking not at me, but at the floor as though listening to it. “Told would seem to suggest spoken communication. You cannot have spoken communication with a man in New South Wales, you know.”

“I will say informed, Mr. Jaggers.”

“Good.”

“I have been informed by a person named Abel Magwitch that he is the benefactor who was so long unknown to me.”

“That is the man,” said Mr. Jaggers, “in New South Wales.”

“And he alone?” I asked.

“And he alone,” said Mr. Jaggers.

“I am not so unreasonable, sir, as to hold you in any way responsible for my errors and mistaken conclusions; but I had always believed it was Miss Havisham.”

“As you say, Pip,” Mr. Jaggers replied, fixing his cool eyes on me and biting his forefinger, “I am not responsible for that at all.”

“And yet it seemed so much like it, sir,” I pleaded, my heart sinking.

“Not the smallest bit of evidence, Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, shaking his head and gathering up his coat-tails. “Judge nothing by appearances; judge everything by evidence. There is no better rule.”

“I have nothing more to say,” I said with a sigh, after standing silent for a while. “I have confirmed my information, and that is the end of it.”

“And Magwitch—in New South Wales—having finally revealed himself,” said Mr. Jaggers, “you will understand, Pip, how strictly, throughout all my dealings with you, I have kept to the exact line of fact. “Fully, sir.”

“I told Magwitch—in New South Wales—when he first wrote to me—from New South Wales—that he must not expect me ever to depart from the exact line of fact.”

I wandered for three days and at last came upon open country. A heavy snowfall had fallen the night before, and the fields lay in an unbroken sheet of white. The sight was bleak, and my feet were chilled by the cold, wet substance covering the ground.

“It was about seven in the morning, and I longed for food and shelter. At last I saw a small hut on rising ground, no doubt built for the use of some shepherd. It was a new sight to me, and I examined it with great curiosity. Finding the door open, I went inside. An old man sat near a fire, preparing his breakfast over it. He turned at the sound, and when he saw me, he gave a loud cry and fled the hut, running across the fields with a speed his weakened body scarcely seemed capable of. His appearance, unlike any I had ever seen, and his flight surprised me somewhat. But I was enchanted by the hut itself: snow and rain could not enter there; the ground was dry; and at that moment it seemed to me as exquisite and divine a refuge as Pandæmonium had seemed to the demons of hell after their suffering in the lake of fire.

We spent several mournful hours until eleven o’clock, the hour appointed for the trial to begin. As my father and the other members of the family were required to appear as witnesses, I went with them to the court. Throughout this miserable semblance of justice I endured a living agony. It was to be determined whether the fruit of my curiosity and unlawful contrivances would bring death upon two fellow creatures: one, a cheerful infant, rich in innocence and delight; the other, murdered still more horribly, amid every circumstance of disgrace that could render the deed unforgettable in its terror. Justine, too, was a girl of worth, endowed with qualities that seemed destined to make her happy; now all was to be swallowed up in a dishonoured grave—and I was the cause! A thousand times I would rather have declared myself guilty of the crime laid to Justine’s charge; but I had been absent when it occurred, and such an avowal would have been judged the delirium of a madman, nor would it have cleared her who suffered because of me.

Justine’s manner was composed. She wore mourning, and her face, ever pleasing, was made exquisitely lovely by the gravity of her emotions. Still, she seemed assured of her innocence and did not shake, though thousands watched and cursed her; for whatever sympathy her beauty might otherwise have awakened had been erased from the spectators’ minds by their conception of the monstrous crime imputed to her. She was serene, though her serenity was plainly forced; and since her earlier confusion had been cited as evidence of guilt, she summoned her thoughts into an outward show of courage. On entering the court, she cast her eyes about and soon found where we sat. A tear appeared to cloud her eye at the sight of us, but she promptly mastered herself, and an expression of mournful affection seemed to bear witness to her complete innocence.

The trial opened, and when the advocate opposing her had set forth the accusation, several witnesses were summoned. A number of unusual circumstances united against her, enough to unsettle anyone lacking the proof of her innocence that I possessed. She had been abroad throughout the night when the murder was committed, and near morning a market-woman had seen her not far from the place where the murdered child’s body was later discovered. The woman asked what she was doing there, but Justine looked strangely at her and gave only a bewildered, unintelligible reply. She came back to the house at about eight o’clock, and when asked where she had spent the night, answered that she had been searching for the child, urgently demanding whether any news of him had been received.

Other chances to make her observations were sure to arise. Anne had soon been in company with all four of them together often enough to form an opinion, though she was too sensible to admit it at home, where she knew it would have pleased neither husband nor wife. Though she thought Louisa rather the favourite, she could not help believing, so far as memory and experience allowed her to judge, that Captain Wentworth was in love with neither sister. They were more in love with him; yet even there it was not love. It was a slight fever of admiration, but it might—probably must—end in love for one of them. Charles Hayter seemed conscious of being neglected, while Henrietta sometimes appeared divided between the two men. Anne wished she had the power to show them all what they were doing, and to point out some of the dangers to which they were exposing themselves. She suspected no one of deceit. It gave her the greatest comfort to believe that Captain Wentworth was entirely unaware of the pain he caused. There was no triumph in his manner, no cruel triumph. He had probably never heard of, or considered, any claims Charles Hayter might have. His only fault was in accepting—for accepting was the word—the attentions of two young women at once.

After a brief struggle, however, Charles Hayter seemed to withdraw from the contest. Three days passed without his coming even once to Uppercross, a most marked change. He had even declined one of his usual dinner invitations; and when Mr. Musgrove found him on that occasion sitting before some large books, Mr. and Mrs. Musgrove were certain that something was wrong, and spoke gravely of his studying himself to death. Mary hoped and believed that Henrietta had given him a definite dismissal, while her husband constantly expected to see him tomorrow. Anne could only feel that Charles Hayter was wise.

The next morning, when the Otis family met for breakfast, they talked at length about the ghost. The United States Minister was naturally a little annoyed that his gift had not been accepted. ‘I have no desire,’ he said, ‘to harm the ghost personally, and I must say that, considering how long he has lived in this house, it is not at all polite to throw pillows at him’—a very fair remark, though, I am sorry to say, the twins burst out laughing. ‘On the other hand,’ he went on, ‘if he truly refuses to use the Rising Sun Lubricator, we shall have to take away his chains. It would be impossible to sleep with that noise outside the bedrooms.’

For the rest of the week, however, they were left alone. The only thing that drew attention was the blood-stain on the library floor, which kept appearing again. This was certainly very strange, since Mr. Otis always locked the door at night and kept the windows firmly barred. The stain’s changing colours also caused much discussion. Some mornings it was a dull, almost Indian red; then it would be vermilion, then a deep purple; and once, when they came downstairs for family prayers according to the simple customs of the Free American Reformed Episcopalian Church, they found it bright emerald-green. These shifting colours naturally amused the family greatly, and every evening they freely made bets about them. The only person who did not share the joke was little Virginia, who, for some unknown reason, was always deeply upset by the sight of the blood-stain and nearly cried on the morning it was emerald-green.

The ghost appeared for the second time on Sunday night. Soon after they had gone to bed, they were suddenly frightened by a terrible crash in the hall. They rushed downstairs and found that a large suit of old armour had come loose from its stand and fallen onto the stone floor. The Canterville ghost was sitting in a high-backed chair, rubbing his knees, with an expression of sharp pain on his face. The twins, who had brought their pea-shooters, immediately fired two pellets at him, with the accurate aim that can only come from long, careful practice on a writing-master. Meanwhile, the United States Minister pointed his revolver at him and, following Californian etiquette, ordered him to hold up his hands. The ghost leapt up with a wild shriek of anger and passed through them like mist, putting out Washington Otis’s candle as he went and leaving them all in complete darkness.

I have said that he was a poet. At twenty-three, he first published a poem, and the whole nation welcomed it with enthusiasm and delight. Fortune seemed always to favor him; never had a reputation been made so quickly, or become so universal. Ordinary people praised the same poems that amazed the scholar in his study: not a single voice disagreed.

It was then, at the height of his fame, that he met Elinor. She was a young heiress of extraordinary beauty, living under the care of her guardian. From the first time they were seen together, they seemed made for each other. Elinor did not possess Woodville's genius, but she was generous and noble. Her youth and the love she inspired had raised her above any knowledge except of virtue and excellence. She was lovely; her manner was open and simple; her deep blue eyes shone with a light that could come only from feeling joined with wisdom.

They were made for one another, and soon they loved. For the first time, Woodville knew the joy of love; and Elinor was delighted to possess the heart of one so handsome and admired among his fellow men. What could come from such a union except pure happiness?

Woodville was a poet. Every society sought him out, and when he appeared, all eyes turned to him alone. But he was the son of a poor clergyman, while Elinor was a rich heiress. Her guardian did not object to their love: Woodville's merit was too great for anyone to criticize him because of his lesser wealth. Yet her father's dying will forbade her to marry before she came of age, and her fortune depended on her obeying this command. She had just turned twenty, and she and her lover had to accept the delay. Still, they were always together, and their happiness seemed like Paradise. They studied together, made plans for their future work, and drank in love and joy from each other's eyes and words. They scarcely complained of the delay before their complete union. Woodville continued to rise in fame, and Elinor grew lovelier and wiser under the guidance of her accomplished lover.

In two months Elinor would be twenty-one, and everything was ready for their marriage. How can I tell of disaster after so much joy? Yet the earth would not be the earth it is, covered with suffering and sorrow, if such a pair of angelic beings had been allowed to live for one another. Search the world, and you will not find the perfect happiness their marriage would have given them. The order of things among us miserable people of earth would have needed to be changed to allow such complete joy.

Summer moved on, and, crowned by the sun’s fierce rays, the plague sent its unerring arrows across the earth. Nations under its power bowed their heads and died. The grain that had risen abundantly lay rotting on the ground in autumn, while the miserable man who had gone out to gather bread for his children lay rigid and plague-stricken in the furrow. The green woods majestically stirred their branches while the dying lay beneath their shade, answering their solemn music with discordant cries. Bright birds darted through the shadows; heedless deer rested unharmed among the ferns; oxen and horses wandered from their unguarded stalls and grazed amid the wheat, for death struck humankind alone.

As summer and death increased, so did our fears. My poor love and I looked at one another, and at our children. “We will save them, Idris,” I said. “I will save them. Years from now, we will tell them of these fears, which will have passed with their cause. Even if they alone remain upon the earth, they shall live; their cheeks shall not grow pale, nor their sweet voices fade.” Our eldest partly understood the scenes around him, and sometimes, with a grave expression, asked me why such vast desolation existed. But he was only ten, and the cheerfulness of youth soon drove such unnatural care from his brow. Evelyn, a laughing cherub, a playful child with no notion of pain or sorrow, would toss his light curls back from his eyes and make the halls ring with laughter, drawing our attention in a thousand innocent ways to his games. Clara, our lovely, gentle Clara, was our support, our comfort, our joy. She made it her duty to tend the sick, console the grieving, help the old, and share the games and stir the spirits of the young. She moved through the rooms like a benevolent spirit sent from heaven to brighten our dark hour with unearthly splendor. Gratitude and praise followed her footsteps. Yet when she stood before us in modest simplicity, playing with our children or diligently performing small kindnesses for Idris, one wondered in what beautiful feature of her pure loveliness, in what gentle note of her moving voice, such heroism, wisdom, and active goodness could dwell.

The summer passed slowly, for we trusted that winter would at least restrain the disease. To hope it would disappear entirely was too precious, too deeply felt, to be spoken aloud. Whenever such a thought was carelessly voiced, those who heard it answered with a rush of tears and passionate sobs, revealing how profound their fears were and how slight their hopes.

One day, while I was occupied with my books and Mr. Pocket, I received a note in the post. The sight of the envelope alone made me tremble with excitement; for although I had never seen the handwriting before, I guessed at once whose hand had written it. It had no formal opening—no Dear Mr. Pip, Dear Pip, Dear Sir, or Dear Anything—but simply said:—

“I am coming to London by the midday coach the day after to-morrow. I believe it was arranged that you should meet me? In any case, Miss Havisham thinks so, and I write because she wishes it. She sends you her regards.

“Yours, ESTELLA.”

If there had been time, I would probably have ordered several new suits for the occasion; but there was not, so I had to be satisfied with what I owned. My appetite disappeared at once, and I had no peace or rest until the day came. Its arrival did not bring either, for I was worse than before. I began hovering around the coach office in Wood Street, Cheapside, before the coach had even left the Blue Boar in our town. Though I knew this perfectly well, I still felt it was unsafe to let the coach office out of my sight for more than five minutes at a time. In this unreasonable state, I had completed the first half-hour of a watch that was to last four or five hours when Wemmick came upon me.

“Halloa, Mr. Pip,” he said. “How are you? I should hardly have thought this was your usual ground.”

I explained that I was waiting to meet someone arriving by coach, and asked after the Castle and the Aged.

“Both doing well, thankye,” said Wemmick, “especially the Aged. He’s in wonderful spirits. He’ll be eighty-two on his next birthday. I’m thinking of firing eighty-two shots, if the neighbours don’t object and my cannon can stand the strain. But this isn’t London talk. Where do you think I’m going?”

“To the office?” I said, since he was walking that way.

“The next thing to it,” Wemmick replied. “I’m going to Newgate. We have a banker’s-parcel case at present, and I’ve been down the road to take a look at the scene of action. Now I must have a word or two with our client.”

“Did your client commit the robbery?” I asked.

“Bless your soul and body, no,” Wemmick answered very dryly. “But he is accused of it. So might you or I be. Either of us could be accused of it, you know.”

How dreadful it was!—dreadful, for that instant, even more than the silent object he knew lay stretched across the table, the object whose grotesque, distorted shadow on the stained carpet told him it had not moved, but remained where he had left it.

He drew a long breath, opened the door a little farther, and, his eyes half shut and his head turned aside, went swiftly in, resolved not to glance even once at the dead man. Then, bending down to pick up the gold-and-purple drapery, he threw it directly over the picture.

Sir Walter Elliot of Kellynch Hall, in Somersetshire, was a man who, for his own entertainment, never opened any book but the Baronetage. In it he found something to occupy an idle hour and comfort in a troubled one; there his mind was stirred to admiration and respect by considering the few surviving patents of the earliest creation; there any unpleasant feelings caused by family matters naturally turned into pity and contempt as he turned through the nearly endless creations of the last century; and there, if every other page failed him, he could read his own history with an interest that never diminished. This was the page at which his favourite volume always opened:

“ELLIOT OF KELLYNCH HALL.

“Walter Elliot, born March 1, 1760, married, July 15, 1784, Elizabeth, daughter of James Stevenson, Esq. of South Park, in the county of Gloucester, by which lady (who died 1800) he has issue Elizabeth, born June 1, 1785; Anne, born August 9, 1787; a still-born son, November 5, 1789; Mary, born November 20, 1791.”

That was exactly how the paragraph had originally come from the printer; but Sir Walter had improved it by adding, for the benefit of himself and his family, these words after the date of Mary’s birth—“Married, December 16, 1810, Charles, son and heir of Charles Musgrove, Esq. of Uppercross, in the county of Somerset”—and by inserting, with great precision, the day of the month on which he had lost his wife.

Then came the history and advancement of the ancient and respectable family, in the customary language: how it had first settled in Cheshire; how it was mentioned in Dugdale; its service as high sheriff, its representation of a borough in three successive parliaments, its acts of loyalty, and its baronetcy in the first year of Charles II, along with all the Marys and Elizabeths they had married. It filled two handsome duodecimo pages and ended with the arms and motto:—“Principal seat, Kellynch Hall, in the county of Somerset,” followed once more by Sir Walter’s handwriting:

“Heir presumptive, William Walter Elliot, Esq., great grandson of the second Sir Walter.”

Vanity was the beginning and end of Sir Walter Elliot’s character: vanity about his appearance and his position. He had been remarkably handsome when young and, at fifty-four, was still a very fine-looking man. Few women thought more about their appearance than he did, nor could the valet of any newly made lord take greater pleasure in his place in society. He regarded the gift of beauty as second only to the gift of a baronetcy; and Sir Walter Elliot, possessing both, was the constant object of his deepest respect and devotion.

His looks and rank had one legitimate claim on his affection, since he must have owed to them a wife of far superior character to anything he himself deserved.

Sir Walter Elliot, of Kellynch Hall, in Somersetshire, was a man who, for his private amusement, never opened any book except the Baronetage; in it he found employment for an idle hour and comfort for a troubled one; there his powers were stirred to admiration and esteem by viewing the scant remains of the earliest patents; there every disagreeable feeling produced by family concerns was naturally transformed into pity and contempt as he turned the nearly innumerable creations of the last century; and there, should all other pages fail, he could read his own history with an interest that never disappointed him. It was at this page that the cherished volume invariably opened:

“ELLIOT OF KELLYNCH HALL.

“Walter Elliot, born March 1, 1760, married, July 15, 1784, Elizabeth, daughter of James Stevenson, Esq. of South Park, in the county of Gloucester, by which lady (who died 1800) he has issue Elizabeth, born June 1, 1785; Anne, born August 9, 1787; a still-born son, November 5, 1789; Mary, born November 20, 1791.”

The paragraph had originally appeared exactly thus from the printer; but Sir Walter had enhanced it by appending, for his own and his family’s information, these words after the date of Mary’s birth—“Married, December 16, 1810, Charles, son and heir of Charles Musgrove, Esq. of Uppercross, in the county of Somerset,”—and by recording with the greatest precision the day of the month on which he had lost his wife.

After this came the account of the rise and history of the ancient, respectable family, in the customary language: how it had first established itself in Cheshire; how it was noticed in Dugdale, held the office of high sheriff, represented a borough in three consecutive parliaments, displayed loyalty, and received the dignity of baronet in the first year of Charles II, together with all the Marys and Elizabeths they had married; making in all two handsome duodecimo pages, and ending with the arms and motto:—“Principal seat, Kellynch Hall, in the county of Somerset,” followed once more by Sir Walter’s handwriting in this conclusion:—

“Heir presumptive, William Walter Elliot, Esq., great grandson of the second Sir Walter.”

Vanity formed both the beginning and the end of Sir Walter Elliot’s character: vanity of appearance and of rank. He had been notably handsome when young; and at fifty-four remained a very fine-looking man. Few women could dwell more upon their own appearance than he did, nor could the valet of a newly created lord take greater pleasure in his social position. He regarded the gift of beauty as second only to that of a baronetcy; and Sir Walter Elliot, possessing both advantages, was the continual object of his most ardent respect and devotion.

His looks and his station had one just title to his affection, for to them he must have owed a wife whose character was far superior to anything his own could have merited.

We arrived at Kishan on the seventh of July. The weather throughout our journey had been calm and clear. Every day, before dawn, we left our camp for the night and watched the shadows withdraw from hill and valley before the golden glory of the rising sun. The soldiers with us, in their national liveliness, took eager pleasure in the beauty of nature. They greeted the rising sun with triumphant music, while birdsong, heard in brief bursts, filled the pauses between the notes. At noon, we set up our tents in a shaded valley or a leafy mountain wood, where a stream murmuring over pebbles invited grateful sleep. Our evening march, quieter though it was, delighted us even more than the restless spirit of the morning. If the band played, they unconsciously chose tunes of restrained feeling: a lover's farewell or a song of sorrow at absence, followed and ended by a solemn hymn that suited the peaceful beauty of evening and lifted the mind toward lofty religious thoughts. Often every sound fell silent so that we could listen to the nightingale, while fireflies danced in bright patterns and the soft call of the aziolo promised fair weather to the travellers. When we passed through a valley, gentle shadows surrounded us, with rocks coloured in lovely shades. When we crossed a mountain, Greece lay below like a living map, its famous peaks cutting the sky and its rivers winding in silver lines through fertile land. Almost afraid to breathe, we English travellers looked in ecstasy on this splendid scene, so unlike the quiet colours and melancholy beauty of our native landscape. After we left Macedonia, the fertile but flat plains of Thrace offered fewer beauties; yet the journey remained interesting. An advance guard announced our approach, and the country people quickly began to move about, preparing to honour Lord Raymond.

The mental qualities described as analytical are, in themselves, scarcely open to analysis. We recognize them only through their effects. Among other things, we know that, when possessed in excess, they are always a source of the keenest pleasure to their owner. Just as a strong man takes pride in his physical power, delighting in exercises that put his muscles to work, so the analyst rejoices in that mental activity which disentangles. He finds pleasure even in the most trivial pursuits that call his talent into use. He enjoys riddles, puzzles, and hieroglyphics, displaying in his solutions to each a sharpness that seems supernatural to ordinary understanding. His conclusions, produced by the very spirit and essence of method, truly have all the appearance of intuition.

The power of resolving things again may perhaps be greatly strengthened by mathematical study, especially by its highest branch, which has unjustly been called analysis above all others merely because of its backward operations. Yet calculation is not, in itself, analysis. A chess player, for instance, performs the former without making any effort at the latter. It follows that chess is greatly misunderstood in its effects on the mind. I am not writing a treatise now, but merely introducing a rather unusual narrative with observations made somewhat at random; I will therefore take this opportunity to assert that the higher powers of reflective thought are more clearly and more usefully exercised by the modest game of draughts than by all the elaborate frivolity of chess. In chess, where the pieces move in different and bizarre ways and have various, changing values, mere complexity is mistaken—an error not uncommon—for depth. Attention is strongly demanded. If it lapses for a moment, an oversight occurs, bringing loss or defeat. Since the possible moves are not only numerous but intricate, the chances of such oversights multiply; and in nine cases out of ten, it is the more concentrated player, rather than the more acute one, who wins. In draughts, by contrast, where the moves are uniform and vary little, the likelihood of carelessness is reduced; and, with mere attention comparatively unoccupied, whatever advantages either player gains come through superior acumen. To make this less abstract, imagine a game of draughts in which only four kings remain, and in which, naturally, no oversight can be expected. It is clear that victory can then be decided, assuming the players are otherwise equal, only by some subtle move resulting from a powerful effort of intellect.

I would go abroad and become a nun—not for religion, since I was not Catholic, but so that I might be shut away from the world forever. There I would find solitude in which to weep, and never hear the voices of life.

But my father—my beloved, most unhappy father? Would he die? Would he never overcome the fierce passion that now ruled him without mercy? Might he not, many years from then, when age had cooled the burning feelings he now suffered, become a father to me again? This thought smoothed my brow, and I felt—and wept to feel it—a sad half-smile soften the suffering on my lips. I dared to hope for a better future. Years would have to pass, but hope would give them wings; or, if they passed slowly, they would still pass, and I had not lost my father forever. Let him spend another sixteen years wandering alone. Let him once more speak his wild complaints to vast forests and terrible waterfalls in another land. Let him again face dreadful dangers and hardships that crush the soul. Let the hot southern sun burn his passion-worn cheeks again, and cold night rain fall upon him and chill his blood.

To such a life, miserable father, I give you! Go! Let your days be spent among savages, and your nights beneath the open sky. Let your limbs grow weary, your heart grow cold, and all youth die within you!

Mr. Attorney-General told the jury that the prisoner before them, though young in age, was already experienced in the treasonable acts that demanded his life. His correspondence with the public enemy, he said, had not begun today, yesterday, last year, or even the year before. It was certain that, for longer than that, the prisoner had been travelling back and forth between France and England on secret business for which he could give no honest explanation. If treason could ever prosper—which, happily, it never could—the true wickedness and guilt of his dealings might have remained hidden. Providence, however, had moved a person beyond fear and beyond reproach to uncover the prisoner’s plans and, horrified by them, reveal them to his Majesty’s Chief Secretary of State and most honourable Privy Council. This patriot, he said, would appear before them. His position and conduct were, altogether, sublime. He had been the prisoner’s friend, but, in an hour both fortunate and terrible, had discovered his infamy and resolved to sacrifice the traitor he could no longer keep in his heart upon the sacred altar of his country. “If ye truly are freemen, ye have nothing to fear—the God-given liberties of Britain surround ye as shield and shelter! (Applause.) Ye shall soon see. Bring forth your proof.”

You see, he knew his own laws as people so often know laws: by their words, not their results. Laws take on a meaning, and become very clear, when they are applied to yourself.

We went together to the House that evening. Raymond, though he knew that the coming debate would discuss and decide his plans and hopes, was cheerful and unconcerned. As we entered the coffee-room, a murmur like ten thousand hives of swarming bees deafened us. Groups of politicians stood together, their faces anxious, their voices loud or low. The aristocratic party, the richest and most powerful men in England, seemed less disturbed than the rest, since the question was to be debated without their involvement. Ryland and his supporters stood near the fire. Ryland was of humble birth and enormous wealth, inherited from his father, a manufacturer. As a young man, he had seen the king abdicate and the Houses of Lords and Commons joined together. He had supported these gains by the people, and had spent his life strengthening and increasing them. Since then, the influence of the landowners had grown; at first Ryland had not been sorry to see Lord Raymond’s schemes draw away many of his opponents’ followers. But matters had now gone too far. The poorer nobles welcomed the return of sovereignty, believing it would restore the power and rights they had lost. The nearly dead spirit of royalty stirred again in men’s minds; and they, willing slaves and self-made subjects, were ready to bow their necks beneath the yoke. Some upright and courageous spirits still remained, pillars of the state; but the word republic had become dull to common ears, and many—whether a majority, events would show—longed for the glitter and display of royalty. Ryland was driven to resist. He declared that only his patience had allowed this party to grow; but the time for tolerance had passed, and with one sweep of his arm he would clear away the cobwebs that blinded his countrymen.

It is only four o’clock, but it is winter, and the sun has already gone down. No clouds cross the clear, frosty sky to catch its slanting rays, yet the air itself has a faint rosy colour, reflected again on the snow covering the ground. I live in a lonely cottage on a broad, empty heath; no sound of life reaches me. Before me lies the desolate plain, white except for a few black patches made by the midday sun on the tops of sharp little hills, where the snow, slipping as it fell, lay thinner than on the level ground. A few birds peck at the hard ice over the pools—for the frost has lasted a long time.

I am in a strange state of mind. I am alone—entirely alone—in the world. Misfortune has passed over me like a blight and left me withered. I know that I am about to die, and I feel happy—joyful. I feel my pulse; it beats quickly. I lay my thin hand on my cheek; it burns. A small, swift spirit remains within me, now giving off its final sparks. I shall never see the snow of another winter. I truly believe I shall never again feel the life-giving warmth of a summer sun. It is with this belief that I begin to write my tragic history. Perhaps a history like mine should die with me, but some feeling I cannot explain urges me onward, and I am too weak in body and mind to resist even the slightest impulse. While life was strong in me, I believed there was a sacred horror in my story that made it unfit to speak of; now, as I am about to die, I profane its mysterious terrors. It is like the wood of the Eumenides, which none but the dying may enter; and Oedipus is about to die.

What am I writing? I must gather my thoughts. I do not know whether anyone will read these pages except you, my friend, who will receive them when I die. I do not write to you alone, because I would take pleasure in speaking of our friendship in a way that would be unnecessary if you were the only reader. So I shall tell my story as though I were writing for strangers. You have often asked why I live alone; why I weep; and, above all, why I keep such an unkind, impenetrable silence. In life I did not dare tell you; in death I reveal the mystery. Others may turn these pages carelessly: but to you, Woodville, kind and loving friend, they will be dear—the precious remains of a heartbroken girl who, even as she dies, is still warmed by gratitude toward you. Your tears will fall upon the words that record my misfortunes; I know they will. And while I still live, I thank you for your sympathy.

Mrs. Elton was, on this second meeting and on every meeting after it, exactly as Emma had first found her: self-important, presumptuous, overfamiliar, ignorant, and badly mannered. She had some beauty and some accomplishments, but so little sense that she believed she had come, with superior knowledge of the world, to brighten and improve a country neighbourhood. She imagined that Miss Hawkins had held a position in society which only Mrs. Elton’s own importance could exceed.

There was no reason to think Mr. Elton saw his wife differently. He seemed not only happy with her, but proud of her. He looked as if he congratulated himself on bringing to Highbury a woman whom not even Miss Woodhouse could equal. Most of her new acquaintances were ready to praise her, or were not used to judging people closely. Following Miss Bates’s kindly lead, or assuming that the bride must be as clever and agreeable as she said she was, they were quite satisfied. Thus Mrs. Elton’s praises passed easily from person to person, as such praise should, with no obstacle from Miss Woodhouse, who willingly added her own first approval and said pleasantly that Mrs. Elton was “very pleasant and very elegantly dressed.”

In one way, Mrs. Elton became even worse than she had seemed at first. Her feelings toward Emma changed. Probably offended by the little encouragement Emma gave to her offers of friendship, she withdrew in return and gradually became much colder and more distant. Though this was agreeable in itself, the ill-will behind it naturally increased Emma’s dislike. Her manner toward Harriet, and Mr. Elton’s as well, was unpleasant. They treated her with sneering neglect. Emma hoped it would quickly help cure Harriet; but the feelings that led them to behave so made both of them seem much worse to her. There could be little doubt that poor Harriet’s attachment had been shared freely between husband and wife, and that Harriet’s part in the story had probably been told too, in the light least favourable to her and most comforting to him. Naturally, she was the object of their shared dislike. Whenever they had nothing else to discuss, it must have been easy to begin criticizing Miss Woodhouse; and the hostility they did not dare show Emma openly found a wider outlet in their contemptuous treatment of Harriet.
