When he came to the door, he turned the key and opened it. He did not so much as look at the murdered man. He felt that the secret of it all was not to grasp the reality of the situation. The friend who had painted the fatal portrait, from which all his suffering had sprung, had passed out of his life. That was sufficient.

Then he thought of the lamp. It was a somewhat strange thing of Moorish design, fashioned from dull silver, inlaid with arabesques of polished steel, and set with rough turquoises. Perhaps his servant would notice its absence, and questions might follow. He paused for an instant, then went back and lifted it from the table. He could not avoid seeing the dead body. How motionless it was! How ghastly white those long hands appeared! It resembled some horrible wax figure.

After locking the door behind him, he stole softly downstairs. The woodwork creaked and seemed to moan as though in agony. More than once he halted and listened. No: all was quiet. It was only the noise of his own steps.

On reaching the library, he noticed the bag and coat in the corner. They had to be concealed somewhere. He opened a secret cupboard in the wainscoting, one in which he kept his own odd disguises, and placed them inside. He could burn them easily enough later. Then he took out his watch. It was twenty minutes before two.

He seated himself and began to reflect. Every year—almost every month—men were hanged in England for what he had done. There was a frenzy of murder abroad. Some crimson star had drawn too near the earth.... Yet what proof was there against him? Basil Hallward had left the house at eleven. Nobody had seen him return. Most of the servants were at Selby Royal. His valet had gone to bed.... Paris! Yes. Basil had gone to Paris, by the midnight train, as he had meant to do. Given his peculiar, secluded habits, months would pass before suspicion was awakened. Months! Everything might be destroyed well before that.

A sudden idea came to him. He put on his fur coat and hat and went into the hall. There he stopped, hearing the slow, weighty step of the policeman on the pavement outside, and seeing the gleam of the bull's-eye reflected in the window. He waited, holding his breath.

A few moments later, he lifted the latch and slipped outside, closing the door very softly behind him. Then he began to ring the bell.

After a while, midnight rang out from the great tower at Westminster, and with every stroke of the deep bell the night itself seemed to shudder. Then the railway lights were extinguished, leaving one lone lamp shining like a great ruby atop a gigantic mast, and the city’s roar grew quieter.

At two o’clock he rose and walked towards Blackfriars. Everything looked so unreal—like some bizarre dream. The houses across the river appeared to be made of darkness. It was as though silver and shadow had remade the world. The vast dome of St. Paul’s rose through the dim air like a bubble.

As he neared Cleopatra’s Needle, he saw a man bent over the parapet. When he came closer, the man looked up, and the gaslight fell directly on his face.

It was Mr. Podgers, the palmist. No one could have mistaken that fat, slack face, those gold-rimmed spectacles, that weak, unhealthy smile, or that sensual mouth.

Lord Arthur stopped. A dazzling idea came to him, and he crept quietly up behind the man. In an instant, he seized Mr. Podgers by the legs and hurled him into the Thames. There was a rough curse, a heavy splash, and then silence. Lord Arthur leaned over anxiously, but he could see nothing of the palmist except a tall hat spinning in an eddy of moonlit water. After a while, that too sank, and no sign of Mr. Podgers remained. Once he thought he saw the bulky, misshapen figure swimming towards the steps by the bridge, and a dreadful sense of failure seized him; but it proved to be only a reflection, which vanished when the moon emerged from behind a cloud. At last, it seemed that he had fulfilled destiny’s decree. He let out a deep sigh of relief, and Sybil’s name rose to his lips.

‘Have you dropped something, sir?’ a voice suddenly asked behind him.

He turned and saw a policeman carrying a bull’s-eye lantern.

‘Nothing important, sergeant,’ he replied with a smile. Then, hailing a passing hansom, he climbed in and told the driver to take him to Belgrave Square.

I was paddling away, all in a sweat to turn him in; but when he said that, it seemed to take all the strength out of me. I went slower then, and wasn’t altogether sure whether I was glad I had started or not. When I was fifty yards away, Jim says:

“Dah you goes, de ole true Huck; de on’y white genlman dat ever kep’ his word to ole Jim.”

Well, I felt downright sick. But I says, I got to do it—I can’t get out of it. Just then a skiff came along with two men in it carrying guns, and they stopped, and so did I. One says:

“What’s that over yonder?”

“A bit of a raft,” I says.

“Do you belong to it?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Any men aboard?”

“Only one, sir.”

“Well, five niggers have run off to-night up yonder, above the bend’s head. Is your man white or black?”

I didn’t answer right away. I tried, but the words wouldn’t come. For a second or two I tried to stiffen up and say it, but I wasn’t man enough—didn’t have the courage of a rabbit. I saw I was giving way; so I quit trying, and says:

“He’s white.”

“I reckon we’ll go see for ourselves.”

“I wish you would,” says I, “because it’s pap there, and maybe you’d help me tow the raft ashore where the light is.”

But my father stood beside me, comforting me and banishing bitter recollections with cheerful hopes: I thought it sweet to mourn, since he might wipe away my tears.

Again he turned my mind from its grief by setting it beside his own despair when he lost my mother. Even then I trembled at the image he gave of his passions: he possessed a poet’s fancy, and in describing the tempest that had rent his feelings, he stamped his words with life so strongly that, trembling, I believed them. I marvelled that he could ever have resumed the duties of life after his wild thoughts had seemed to make him akin to the unearthly; so awful were the ideas he expressed while he spoke that the human heart appeared too limited to contain them. His emotions seemed more suited to a spirit dwelling amid earthquake and volcano than to one imprisoned in a mortal frame and human features. Yet these were only recollections; he had altered since that time. He was now wholly love and gentleness; and when I lifted my eyes to him in wonder as he spoke, the smile upon his lips showed that his heart was filled with the mildest affections.

Two months after my aunt’s death, we moved to London, where my father guided me toward more serious studies than those which had formerly engaged me. My progress was his pleasure; throughout my studies he remained with me, helping or sharing in every lesson. We mixed much in society, and not a day went by without my father seeking to adorn it with some fresh delight. The fond attachment he felt for me, and the love and reverence with which I repaid it, threw enchantment over every instant. The hours passed slowly, because each minute was occupied; in one week we lived more than many live through several months, and the change and freshness of our pleasures lent each its relish.

We were continually taking excursions together. Whether we went to behold lovely landscapes, to view fine paintings, or at times with no purpose beyond pursuing whatever amusement might offer itself, I was always happy near my father. I regretted it whenever a third person joined us; yet if I cast an uneasy glance toward my father, his eyes, resting on me and shining with tenderness, at once brought joy back to my heart. O hours of deepest delight! Brief though ye were, memory has stretched ye into the length of a whole life when I look back through the mist of grief that rose so soon afterward, as though to hide ye from my sight.

“But, in truth, once an ascent has been made to any particular altitude, the weight of air passed through in any subsequent ascent is not at all proportional to the added height attained (as may plainly be inferred from what has already been said), but bears a ratio continually diminishing. It is therefore clear that, however high we ascend, we cannot, in the literal sense, reach a boundary beyond which atmosphere ceases to exist. It must be there, I reasoned, though it may be there in a condition of infinite tenuity.

“On the other hand, I knew that arguments had not been lacking to establish the existence of an actual and fixed boundary to the atmosphere, beyond which no air whatever is present. Yet one circumstance, overlooked by those who maintain such a boundary, seemed to me—though not a direct disproof of their doctrine—nevertheless a matter deserving the gravest inquiry. In comparing the intervals between the successive returns of Encke’s comet to its perihelion, after allowing, with the utmost precision, for every disturbance caused by planetary attraction, it is found that these periods are gradually shortening; in other words, the major axis of the comet’s ellipse is becoming less, by a slow yet wholly regular diminution. This, then, is exactly what should occur if we assume that the comet encounters resistance from an exceedingly rare ethereal medium diffused throughout the regions of its orbit. For such a medium, by checking the comet’s speed, must increase its centripetal force through the weakening of its centrifugal force. Put differently, the attraction of the sun would continually gain strength, and the comet would be drawn closer at each revolution. Indeed, no other explanation can be given for the variation in question. But again:—The actual diameter of this same comet’s nebulosity is seen to shrink rapidly as it nears the sun, and to expand with equal rapidity as it recedes toward its aphelion. Was I not warranted in supposing, with M. Valz, that this seeming condensation of bulk arises from the compression of the same ethereal medium of which I have spoken, and which grows denser only in proportion to its nearness to the sun? The lenticular appearance known also as the zodiacal light was likewise deserving of notice. This radiance, so conspicuous in the tropics and not to be confused with any meteoric gleam, stretches obliquely upward from the horizon and generally follows the direction of the sun’s equator. It seemed to me plainly a rare atmosphere extending outward from the sun, at least beyond the orbit of Venus, and, I believed, indefinitely farther still. Indeed, I could not suppose this medium limited either to the course of the comet’s ellipse or to the sun’s immediate vicinity.

He had told the girl some false story—that a secret mystery, to be explained someday, prevented him from marrying her then. He told her what he had planned to do, if he had lived, to hide her disgrace. If he died, he begged her not to curse his memory or believe that the results of their sin would fall upon her or their child, because all the guilt was his. Monks said nothing.

“The will,” Mr. Brownlow continued for him, “was written in the same spirit as the letter. He left you and your mother an income of eight hundred pounds a year each. He divided the greater part of his property into two equal shares—one for Agnes Fleming, and the other for their child, if it were born alive and lived to come of age.”

“And think, ma’am,” said Oliver, though tears came into his eyes despite all his efforts. “Oh, think how young and good she is, and how much happiness and comfort she brings to everyone around her. I am sure—certain—quite certain—that for your sake, because you are so good; and for her own sake; and for the sake of all those she makes happy, she will not die. Many years ago, I became acquainted with a Mr. William Legrand. He came from an old Huguenot family and had once been wealthy, but a succession of misfortunes had brought him to poverty. This island is a very unusual place. It is made up of little but sea sand and is about three miles long. Nowhere is it more than a quarter mile wide. It is divided from the mainland by a barely visible creek that winds through a wilderness of reeds and mud, a favorite haunt of the marsh hen. As one might expect, the vegetation is sparse, or at least stunted. There are no trees of any size. Near the western end, where Fort Moultrie stands, and where a few wretched frame houses are occupied in summer by those fleeing Charleston’s dust and fever, one may indeed find the rough palmetto. But the entire island, except for this western point and a strip of firm white beach along the sea, is covered by a dense growth of sweet myrtle, so highly valued by English gardeners. Here the shrub often reaches fifteen or twenty feet in height, forming an almost impenetrable thicket and filling the air with its fragrance.

In the deepest part of this thicket, not far from the island’s eastern, more distant end, Legrand had built a small hut, which he occupied when I first met him by pure chance. Our acquaintance soon became friendship, for there was much in the recluse to inspire both interest and respect. I found him well educated and possessed of remarkable mental powers, though afflicted by misanthropy and prone to strange shifts between enthusiasm and melancholy. His chief pleasures were hunting and fishing, or wandering along the beach and through the myrtles in search of shells or insect specimens; his collection of the latter might have been envied by a Swammerdamm. She saw me and looked up in question; that faint look of hope was itself misery. The words died before I could say them; I felt a ghastly smile crease my lips. She understood my gesture; her head fell again, and her fingers resumed their restless work. At last I found my voice, but its sound frightened her. The unhappy girl had understood my expression, and for all the world she would not have had the story of her terrible misery formed and confirmed by harsh, irreversible words. Indeed, she seemed to want to turn my thoughts from it. She rose from the floor. “Hush,” she whispered. “After much weeping, Clara is asleep; we must not wake her.”

Lord Arthur looked so grave and miserable over the letter that the Duchess burst into peals of laughter.

‘My dear Arthur,’ she exclaimed, ‘I shall never let you see a young lady’s letter again! But what am I to say about the clock? I think it a splendid invention, and should like one myself.’

‘I don’t think very highly of them,’ said Lord Arthur, with a melancholy smile; and, after kissing his mother, he quitted the room.

On reaching his room upstairs, he threw himself upon a sofa, his eyes brimming with tears. He had done all he could to commit this murder, yet on both attempts he had failed, through no fault of his own. He had endeavoured to perform his duty, but it seemed that Destiny herself had betrayed him. He was weighed down by the sterility of good intentions, by the uselessness of striving to be noble. Perhaps it would be wiser to end the engagement altogether. Sybil would suffer, certainly, but suffering could not truly spoil a nature as noble as hers. And for himself, what did it signify? There was always some war in which a man might die, some cause for which he might surrender his life; and since life held no pleasure for him, death held no fear. Let Destiny fulfil his doom. He would do nothing to assist her.

At half-past seven he dressed and went down to the club. Surbiton was there with a group of young men, and he was compelled to dine with them. Their frivolous talk and pointless jokes failed to interest him, and the moment coffee was served he left, pleading some engagement in order to escape. As he was leaving the club, the hall-porter gave him a letter. It came from Herr Winckelkopf, requesting that he call the following evening to inspect an explosive umbrella, which discharged itself the instant it was opened. It was the newest invention, and had only just come from Geneva. He tore the letter into pieces. He had resolved to make no further experiments. Then he strolled down to the Thames Embankment and sat beside the river for hours. The moon looked through a mane of tawny cloud like the eye of a lion, while countless stars glittered in the hollow sky like gold dust scattered over a purple dome. From time to time a barge swung into the muddy current and drifted away upon the tide, while the railway signals shifted from green to scarlet as trains shrieked across the bridge.

‘Good heavens!’ the Duchess said to herself. ‘So he is some kind of palm-reader after all. How dreadful. I hope, at least, that he is a foreigner. That would not be quite so bad.’

‘I really must introduce him to you.’

‘Introduce him!’ cried the Duchess. ‘You don’t mean he is here?’ She began searching for a small tortoiseshell fan and a very worn lace shawl, so that she could leave at a moment’s notice.

‘Of course he is here. I would never think of giving a party without him. He says I have a perfectly psychic hand, and that if my thumb had been even a tiny bit shorter, I would have become a complete pessimist and entered a convent.’

‘Oh, I understand!’ said the Duchess, greatly relieved. ‘He tells fortunes, I suppose?’

‘And bad fortunes too,’ Lady Windermere replied, ‘as many as you like. Next year, for example, I am in terrible danger both on land and at sea, so I intend to live in a balloon and have my dinner sent up in a basket every evening. It is all written on my little finger, or in the palm of my hand—I forget which.’

‘But surely that is tempting Providence, Gladys.’

‘My dear Duchess, surely Providence has learned to resist temptation by now. I think everyone ought to have their hands read once a month, just to know what not to do. Naturally, one does it anyway, but it is so pleasant to have been warned. Now, unless someone fetches Mr. Podgers at once, I shall have to go myself.’

‘Let me go, Lady Windermere,’ said a tall, handsome young man standing nearby, who had been listening with an amused smile.

‘Thank you, Lord Arthur, but I am afraid you would not recognise him.’

‘If he is as remarkable as you say, Lady Windermere, I can hardly fail to find him. Tell me what he looks like, and I will bring him to you immediately.’

‘Well, he does not look at all like a palm-reader. I mean, he is not mysterious, strange, or romantic-looking. He is a short, stout man, with an odd bald head and large gold-rimmed spectacles—somewhere between a family doctor and a country lawyer. I am truly sorry, but it is not my fault. People are so irritating. All my pianists look exactly like poets, and all my poets exactly like pianists. Last season, I remember inviting a most dreadful conspirator to dinner—a man who had blown up a great many people, always wore a coat of mail, and carried a dagger up his sleeve. And do you know, when he arrived, he looked exactly like a pleasant old clergyman and told jokes all evening?’

On Saturday nights in our village, there was a pleasant feeling of tidying up and taking a quiet break before beginning life again, and this encouraged Joe to risk staying out half an hour later than usual. When the half-hour and the rum and water ran out together, Joe rose to leave and took my hand.

“Wait a moment, Mr. Gargery,” said the strange man. “I think I may have a bright new shilling somewhere in my pocket, and if I do, the boy shall have it.”

He found it among a handful of loose coins, wrapped it in crumpled paper, and gave it to me. “Yours!” he said. “Remember! Your own.”

I thanked him, staring at him much longer than good manners allowed, and gripping Joe tightly. He said good-night to Joe, and to Mr. Wopsle, who left with us, but gave me only a look from his aiming eye—or not even a look, because he closed it; yet an eye can do wonders by being hidden.

On the way home, if I had felt like talking, I would have had to do all the talking myself. Mr. Wopsle left us at the door of the Jolly Bargemen, and Joe walked home with his mouth wide open, trying to wash the rum away with as much air as possible. But I was almost stunned by the return of my old wrongdoing and my old acquaintance, and could think of nothing else.

My sister was not in too bad a temper when we came into the kitchen, and Joe was encouraged by this unusual fact to tell her about the bright shilling. “A bad one, I’ll wager,” Mrs. Joe said triumphantly, “or he wouldn’t have given it to the boy! Let’s see it.”

I took it from the paper, and it turned out to be a good one. “But what’s this?” Mrs. Joe said, dropping the shilling and snatching up the paper. “Two one-pound notes?”

They were nothing less than two thick, sweaty one-pound notes, which seemed to have been very familiar with every cattle market in the county. Joe grabbed his hat again and ran to the Jolly Bargemen to return them to their owner. While he was gone, I sat on my usual stool and stared blankly at my sister, quite sure the man would not be there.

Soon Joe returned. He said the man had gone, but that he had left word at the Three Jolly Bargemen about the notes.

Almost a year had elapsed since my father’s return, and the seasons had nearly completed their course--It was then the close of May; the woods were arrayed in their newest green, and the pleasant scent of freshly cut grass filled the fields. I imagined that the soft air and the beautiful aspect of Nature might help to awaken in him gentler emotions, and dispose him to feelings of peace and affection before the confidence I resolved to obtain from him.

I therefore selected the evening of one of these days for my endeavour. I asked him to walk with me, and conducted him to a neighbouring beech wood, where the thin shade protected us from the oblique and brilliant rays of the setting sun--After we had walked some time without speaking, I sat down beside him on a moss-covered knoll--It is strange, yet even now I seem to behold the place--many of the slender, smooth trunks were entwined with ivy, whose glossy leaves of deepest green stood in contrast with the pale bark and the light foliage of the young beech shoots springing from their parent stems--the close grass was mixed with moss, and partly strewn with the dead leaves of the preceding autumn, which the winds had driven together here and there into small heaps--a few stumps, overgrown with moss, stood around--The leaves stirred softly in the breeze, and through their green roof the clear blue sky was visible--As evening advanced, the distant trunks were coloured red by the sun, and the wind wholly ceased, while a few birds passed us on their way to evening repose.

It was here, then, that we sat together; and when you learn all that occurred--all that so terribly rent our souls even in this tranquil place, which, but for strange passions, might have been a paradise to us, you will not be surprised that I remember it, as I gazed upon it, hoping its serenity might impart serenity to me, and inspire not courage alone but persuasive language. I observed all these things, and marked them vaguely in my mind, while I tried to put my thoughts into suitable order for my purpose. My heart beat quickly as I summoned myself to address him, for I was resolved not to be turned aside; yet I trembled to think what impression my words might make upon him. At last, after much hesitation, I began:

“Your kindness towards me, my dearest father, and the affection--the excessive affection--which you showed me when you first returned, will, I trust, excuse in your eyes my daring to speak to you, though with a daughter’s tender love, yet likewise with the freedom of a friend and an equal.”

Adrian’s principal effort, once the sick had received immediate relief, had been to conceal the plague’s symptoms and advance from London’s inhabitants. He knew that terror and gloomy anticipation were potent allies of disease; that despair and anxious reflection made man’s bodily frame especially open to contagion. Thus no indecorous spectacles were visible: the shops were generally open, and the stream of passers-by was in some measure maintained. Yet, though the outward aspect of an infected city had been prevented, London, to me, who had not seen it since the visitation began, seemed greatly altered. No carriages were abroad, and grass stood high in the streets; the houses looked forsaken; most shutters were shut; and the people I passed wore a ghastly, alarmed expression, wholly unlike the customary businesslike bearing of Londoners. My lone carriage drew attention as it clattered toward the Protectoral Palace—and the fashionable streets that led there appeared yet more bleak and empty. I found Adrian’s antechamber thronged—it was the hour at which he received applicants. Reluctant to interrupt his work, I waited and observed the petitioners entering and departing. They were persons of the middle and lower ranks, whose livelihood had vanished with the stoppage of commerce and of that active pursuit of gain, in every form, peculiar to our nation. The arrivals bore an air of uneasiness, at times of terror, sharply opposed to the resigned, even contented, look of those who had been heard. In their livelier steps and brighter faces, I could perceive my friend’s influence. Two o’clock sounded, after which no one else was admitted; the disappointed withdrew in sullenness or sorrow, while I entered the audience chamber.

I was surprised by the improvement evident in Adrian’s health. He no longer drooped earthward like a spring flower too carefully reared, which, rising beyond its own strength, is bowed down even by its crown of bloom. His eyes shone, his expression was calm, and an air of gathered energy spread over his entire person, very unlike his former languor. He sat at a table beside several secretaries, who sorted petitions or recorded the notes taken during that day’s audience. Two or three petitioners still remained in attendance. I admired his fairness and forbearance. Those able to live beyond London, he urged to leave it at once, supplying them with the means to do so.

Few people could claim such a pure heart, such true humility, together with a steady trust in her own honesty and in that of others. From birth she had lived a secluded life. She lost her mother very young, but her father devoted himself to her education. He had many unusual ideas that shaped the way he raised her. She knew the heroes of Greece and Rome, and those English heroes who had lived centuries before, yet she knew almost nothing of current events. She had read few writers from the previous fifty years, but apart from that her reading was extensive. So, though she seemed less familiar with the ways of life and society than he was, her knowledge was deeper and built on firmer ground. Even if her beauty and gentleness had not charmed him, her intelligence would always have held him captive. He looked to her as his guide, and his admiration was so great that he took pleasure in increasing his own sense of inferiority whenever she inspired it.

When he was nineteen, his mother died. He left college after this event and, putting aside his old friends for a time, withdrew to the neighbourhood of his Diana, receiving all his comfort from her sweet voice and even sweeter embraces. This brief separation from his companions gave him the courage to claim his independence. He felt that, however much they might mock his planned marriage, they would not dare show their ridicule once it had happened. So, having obtained his guardian's consent, though not without difficulty, and that of his beloved's father, which was more readily granted, he told no one else of his purpose. By the time he reached his twentieth birthday, he had become Diana's husband.

He loved her passionately, and her tenderness held such a charm for him that he could think of nothing but her. He invited several college friends to visit him, but their foolishness disgusted him. Diana had lifted the veil that had kept him in boyhood: he had become a man, and he wondered how he could ever have shared the empty phrases and ideas of his fellow students, or feared for even a moment the judgment of people like them. He gave up his old friendships, not from changeability, but because they were truly unworthy of him.
